source.title: La conjecture de Weil. II
readSections: The whole paper (introduction, §0 conventions, §§1–6 and the bibliography, pp. 137–252) read on page images of the published text (Numdam scan, 117 pages, SHA-256 b06eea61bf9cb2b596c162f5befcf85d1be69828910a6107c8aa3a99c4afcc71, fetched 29 September 2026). The Numdam text layer is OCR and garbles formulas, so statements and quoted misprints were read on page images, small print on 300 dpi crops.

items.name: Frobenius eigenvalues of a Q̄_ℓ-sheaf at a closed point
items.statement: Let X₀ be a scheme of finite type over F_q and ℱ₀ a Q̄_ℓ-sheaf on X₀; an algebraic closure F of F_q is chosen and deleting the index 0 denotes extension of the base field from F_q to F (0.7). For x₀ ∈ |X₀| a closed point of X₀ and x ∈ X(F) above it, one has the Frobenius automorphism F*_{x₀} of the fibre ℱ_x of ℱ at x (I, (1.11) to (1.13), or (1.18)). Its eigenvalues are called the eigenvalues of F_{x₀} on ℱ₀.
items.note: Local Frobenius and its characteristic polynomial are the Weil I (1.11)–(1.13) conventions, reused here; restated in §1 as (1.1.8). Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family.

items.name: Punctually pure and mixed sheaves (introduction form)
items.statement: ℱ₀ is punctually pure of weight n if, for every x₀ ∈ |X₀|, the eigenvalues of F_{x₀} on ℱ₀ are algebraic numbers all of whose complex conjugates have absolute value N(x₀)^{n/2}. ℱ₀ is mixed if it is an iterated extension of punctually pure sheaves; the weights of these are the weights of ℱ₀.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'. The precise definitions are (1.2.1)–(1.2.2).

items.name: Théorème 1: Rⁱf_! of a mixed sheaf of weights ≤ n is mixed of weights ≤ n+i
items.statement: Théorème 1 (3.3.1). Let f: X₀ → S₀ be a morphism of schemes of finite type over F_q, and ℱ₀ a mixed sheaf of weights ≤ n on X [sic; X₀ is meant]. Then, for each i, the sheaf Rⁱf_!ℱ₀ on S₀ is mixed of weights ≤ n+i.
items.note: Main theorem of the paper; proved in §3, (3.3.1), p. 204 ff., by the reduction to Théorème 2 (3.2.3) sketched on p. 139. DWP.7: 'For a separated finite-type morphism f:X₀→Y₀ over a finite field and a mixed constructible rational sheaf F of weights≤w, prove R^i f_!F mixed of weights≤w+i. Construct Weil II3.3.1's dévissage'. Printed 'sur X' for 'sur X₀' (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E2).

items.name: Théorème 1 over Spec(F_q): weights of H^i_c
items.statement: For S₀ = Spec(F_q), Théorème 1 says that for every eigenvalue α of Frobenius on H^i_c(X, ℱ) there is an integer m ≤ n+i (the weight of α) such that the complex conjugates of α all have absolute value q^{m/2}.
items.note: Special case of (3.3.1), stated in §3.3. DWP.7: 'Deduce H^i_c(X,F) weights≤w+i.'

items.name: Purity of H^i(X,ℱ) for X₀ proper smooth and ℱ₀ lisse pure
items.statement: Poincaré duality sometimes allows the upper bounds to be completed by lower bounds (3.3.5). For example, if X₀ is proper and smooth and the sheaf ℱ₀ is lisse (= twisted constant) and punctually pure of weight n, then the eigenvalues of Frobenius on H^i(X, ℱ) are all of weight n+i, i.e. H^i(X, ℱ) is pure of weight n+i.
items.note: Proved in §3.3 from (3.3.1) and the duality lower bound (3.3.5). DWP.7: 'For X₀ smooth and F lisse of weights≥w, use Poincaré duality to prove H^i(X,F) weights≥w+i. ... for smooth **proper** X the whole H^i is pure.'

items.name: Weil I main theorem for proper smooth varieties
items.statement: For ℱ₀ = Q_ℓ (of weight 0) one recovers the main result of Weil I, with the hypothesis 'projective and smooth' replaced by 'proper and smooth': H^i(X, Q_ℓ) is pure of weight i.
items.note: Constant-coefficient case of the preceding item (in §3.3, the corollary (3.3.9) per DWP.7). DWP.7: 'For constant coefficients export the smooth proper nonprojective extension used by WC (3.3.9).'

items.name: Théorème 2: H^i(X, j_*ℱ) is pure of weight n+i on a proper smooth curve
items.statement: Théorème 2 (cf. (3.2.3)). Let X₀ be a proper smooth curve over F_q, j: U₀ → X₀ the inclusion of a dense open subset, and ℱ₀ a lisse sheaf, punctually pure of weight n, on U₀. Then H^i(X, j_*ℱ) is pure of weight n+i.
items.note: Proved in §3.2 (3.2.3), with 'pure' replaced by 'ι-pure' (p. 139, B). Théorème 1 reduces to it by a reduction parallel to the finiteness theorem for Rⁱf_! (SGA 4 XIV 1) plus a local study at infinity of lisse punctually pure sheaves on a curve. DWP.6: 'For j:U₀↪C₀ with C₀ smooth proper and F₀ lisse punctually ι-pure of weight w, prove H^i(C,j_*F) pure of weight w+i (Weil II3.2.3).'

items.name: Outline A(i): cohomology is a direct factor after a finite cover
items.statement: If u: X'₀ → X₀ is a finite surjective morphism whose source is a proper smooth curve X'₀, and ' denotes base change by u, the H^i(X, j_*ℱ) are direct factors of the H^i(X', j'_*ℱ'). This allows one to reduce to the case where the local monodromy of ℱ at the points of X−U is unipotent.
items.note: Proof sketch of Théorème 2; carried out in (3.2). DWP.6: 'Reduce via finite covers to the stated unipotent/tame situation, proving trace-splitting and the resulting injection/direct-summand statements with ℚ_ℓ coefficients.' The unipotence reduction uses Grothendieck's local monodromy theorem (§1.7).

items.name: Outline A(ii): duality between H^i(X, j_*ℱ) and H^{2−i}(X, j_*(ℱ^∨))
items.statement: A duality theorem ensures that H^i(X, j_*ℱ) and H^{2−i}(X, j_*(ℱ^∨)) are in perfect duality, with values in Q̄_ℓ(−1). This reduces Théorème 2 to checking that the complex conjugates α' of the eigenvalues α of Frobenius on H^i(X, j_*ℱ) have absolute value |α'| ≤ q^{(n+i)/2}. The difficult case is H¹.
items.note: Same statement as Weil I (2.12) (planned there at DWP.6/EDC.1:biduality). DWP.6: 'Prove the correct duality for j_*F; do not substitute Rj_*F without its boundary comparison.'

items.name: Outline B: reformulation via isomorphisms ι: Q̄_ℓ → C
items.statement: Let α ∈ Q̄_ℓ be an eigenvalue of Frobenius on H^i(X, j_*ℱ). The estimate to be proved is equivalent to: for every isomorphism ι: Q̄_ℓ → C, |ια| ≤ q^{(n+i)/2}. In the proof each ι is treated separately, which leads to punctually ι-pure and ι-mixed sheaves, with weights allowed to be arbitrary real numbers (1.2.6); Théorème 2 is proved with 'pure' replaced by 'ι-pure'.
items.note: Made precise in (1.2.6) and remark (1.2.11). DWP.0: 'Define Weil q-numbers of an integer weight on actual algebraic-number carriers and their all-embeddings absolute-value property. Define the separate ι-weight predicate on nonzero coefficient-field elements with real weights.' Sources list 'Weil II §§1.2/1.6'. Library audit DWP.0: Weil q-numbers and ι-weights 'absent'.

items.name: Outline C: weights of j_*ℱ at the boundary via local monodromy
items.statement: Put S₀ = X₀ − U₀. If ℱ₀ is lisse and punctually ι-pure of weight β ∈ R, the weight w_{N(x₀)}(α) = 2 log_{N(x₀)}|ια| of an eigenvalue α of F_{x₀} on j_*ℱ₀, for x₀ ∈ S₀, is of the form β − m with m an integer ≥ 0, and m is determined in terms of the local monodromy of ℱ₀ at x₀ (1.8.4). More generally w_{N(x₀)}(α) is determined for α an eigenvalue of F_{x₀} on ℱ₀ in the sense of (1.10.2).
items.note: Proved in (1.8.4) (and (1.10.2)); first step w_{N(x₀)}(α) ≤ β+2 by Grothendieck's formula for Z(U₀, ℱ₀, t) (the Euler product converges for w_q(t) < −β−2 after applying ι, while the right side has numerator ι det(1−Ft, H¹_c(U,ℱ)), to which the (j_*ℱ)_x for x ∈ S contribute); second step: apply this to tensor powers of ℱ₀ and its dual using the known structure of local monodromy. DWP.5: 'Prove the local weight theorem for a punctually pure lisse sheaf on an open curve, including the weights of the monodromy graded pieces and the weights of boundary invariants of j_*F.'

items.name: Outline C: reduction to H¹_c(U,ℱ) = H¹(X, j_!ℱ), weight ≤ β+1, and to β = 0
items.statement: Given the local result, it suffices to study j_!ℱ₀ instead of j_*ℱ₀: if ℱ₀ is lisse and punctually ι-pure of weight β ∈ R, one must show that the eigenvalues α of Frobenius on H¹_c(U, ℱ) = H¹(X, j_!ℱ) have weights w_q(α) ≤ β+1. One may assume β = 0, reducing to this case by twisting (1.2.7).
items.note: Carried out in (3.2). DWP.6: 'Retain the boundary monodromy weights needed to pass from j_*F to compact support on U.' Twist: DWP.5 'twist reductions used when weights are real'.

items.name: Outline D: passage to X₀×X₀ and the iteration δ ↦ δ/2
items.statement: Pass from (U₀, ℱ₀) to (U₀×U₀, ℱ₀⊠ℱ₀), ℱ₀⊠ℱ₀ = pr₁*ℱ₀ ⊗ pr₂*ℱ₀, and analyse H*_c(U×U, ℱ⊠ℱ) = H*_c(X×X, j_!ℱ⊠j_!ℱ) with a pencil of hyperplane sections of a suitable projective completion of X₀×X₀ in general position (after the cleaning A(i)). If every eigenvalue α of Frobenius on H²(X×X, j_!ℱ⊠j_!ℱ) satisfies w_q(α) ≤ 3 = 2+1, then for α an eigenvalue on H¹(X, j_!ℱ), α² is an eigenvalue on H²(X×X, j_!ℱ⊠j_!ℱ) by Künneth, giving w_q(α) ≤ 1 + 1/2. More generally, if for every curve and every sheaf of weight zero the eigenvalues on H¹(X, j_!ℱ) satisfy w_q(α) ≤ 1+δ, the goal is to show w_q(α) ≤ 2+δ on H²(X×X, j_!ℱ⊠j_!ℱ); this improves the estimate to w_q(α) ≤ 1+δ/2 on H¹, and one iterates. This iteration replaces the use of large Cartesian powers in (I.7.3).
items.note: Carried out in (3.2) with the vanishing-cycle computation (3.1). The pencil gives f: Y₀ → P¹₀ (Y₀ a blow-up of X₀×X₀ at finitely many points), 𝒢₀ the inverse image of j_!ℱ₀⊠j_!ℱ₀; Leray reduces H²(X×X, …) to H¹(P¹, R¹f_*𝒢); on an open V₀ ⊂ P¹₀ where R¹f_*𝒢₀ is lisse the generalisation (1.5.1) of (I.3.2) shows it is a successive extension of lisse punctually ι-pure sheaves; §2 gives that ℱ₀ is a direct factor of the ι-real sheaf ℱ₀⊕ℱ₀^∨; vanishing cycles give integral weights on the jumps; constant constituents contribute nothing as H¹(P¹, Q_ℓ) = 0. DWP.6: 'Construct the external-product system on C×C and a sufficiently general pencil ... Use the strict initial estimate of DWP.5 and the §3.2 iteration δ↦δ/2'.

items.name: Outline E: the weight of an H¹ is < 2
items.statement: For ℱ₀ lisse and punctually ι-pure of weight 0 (on an open U₀ of a proper smooth curve X₀), the eigenvalues α of Frobenius on H¹(X, j_!ℱ) have weights w_q(α) < 2. This separates them from those on H²(X, j_!ℱ), of weight 2.
items.note: Proved in §2 (the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin method, inspired by Mertens' proof of the non-vanishing of ζ(s) on Re s = 1). Starts the iteration of D and is used to show R¹f_*𝒢₀ is, on V₀, a direct factor of a lisse ι-real sheaf. DWP.5: 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument and the strict initial H¹ weight bound needed to start §3.2.'

items.name: Complete reducibility of geometric monodromy of a lisse ι-pure sheaf on a smooth curve
items.statement: From E one can deduce that if ℱ₀ is a lisse punctually ι-pure sheaf on a smooth curve U₀, the fibre ℱ_u of ℱ at u ∈ |U| is a completely reducible representation of the geometric monodromy group (3.4.1)(iii); cf. (3.4.14). (In §3.4: the geometric monodromy of a lisse punctually pure sheaf on a normal scheme is semisimple.)
items.note: Proved in (3.4.1)(iii), (3.4.14). Via the heuristic dictionary of [2], I, this corresponds to the semisimplicity theorem [2], II (4.2.6) for variations of Hodge structure. DWP.8: 'Prove Weil II3.4.1: ... geometric semisimplicity for punctually ι-pure lisse sheaves on a **normal** base.'

items.name: Complete reducibility of the cohomology of the fibres of a Lefschetz pencil
items.statement: If X is a nonsingular projective variety over an algebraically closed field k, (H_t)_{t∈P¹} a Lefschetz pencil of hyperplane sections of X with H_t singular for t ∈ S, and u ∈ P¹ − S, then the H^i(H_u, Q_ℓ) are completely reducible representations of π₁(P¹ − S, u).
items.note: Special case of the semisimplicity theorem: a specialisation argument reduces to k = F; X and the pencil are then defined over a finite field and the required purity follows from the Weil conjecture (Weil I) for the H_t. Used in (4.1) for hard Lefschetz. DWP.9: 'prove nondegeneracy on the invariant part from **geometric** complete reducibility'; DWP.8 supplies the semisimplicity.

items.name: Hard Lefschetz theorem (4.1.1)
items.statement: From this complete reducibility, Lefschetz's original arguments deduce the hard Lefschetz theorem on the iterated cup-product with the cohomology class of a hyperplane section (4.1.1): for X projective and smooth over an algebraically closed field, of dimension d, and η the class of a hyperplane section, η^i: H^{d−i}(X, Q_ℓ) → H^{d+i}(X, Q_ℓ)(i) is an isomorphism.
items.note: Stated in the introduction only in words; proved in (4.1.1). The displayed form is the standard statement of (4.1.1) as recorded by DWP.9: 'For X projective smooth of pure dimension d over an algebraically closed field of characteristic≠ℓ and an ample line bundle L, construct η=c₁(L) and prove η^r:H^(d−r)(X,ℚ_ℓ)→H^(d+r)(X,ℚ_ℓ)(r) is an isomorphism.'

items.name: Hard Lefschetz with coefficients in a sheaf or complex (6.2.13)
items.statement: A variant of the hard Lefschetz theorem is given for cohomology with values in a sheaf (or even a complex) (6.2.13); under dimension hypotheses, §6 generalises the local invariant cycle theorem, the global invariant cycle theorem and the hard Lefschetz theorem to pure complexes.
items.note: Proved in (6.2.13) (with (6.2.8)–(6.2.12)). DWP.9: 'Prove the source-qualified extension for a pure lisse coefficient system using Weil II6.2.13. More generally, construct the absolute theorem for a projective X and a potentially pure bounded complex K satisfying both explicit support-dimension inequalities'. LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove ... global invariant-cycle result 6.2.12'.

items.name: Local invariant cycle theorem (3.6.1)
items.statement: Purely geometric statements follow from the existence of a formalism of weights, among them the local invariant cycle theorem (3.6.1).
items.note: Named only in the introduction; proved in (3.6.1). LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants'.

items.name: Weight gradings on Q_ℓ-homotopy types (5.3.4)
items.statement: The results announced in [3] on the existence of a grading by weight on Q_ℓ-homotopy types (5.3.4) follow from the weight formalism. The definition of the Q_ℓ-homotopy type uses essentially the construction by Miller [8] and Grothendieck of a graded (anti-)commutative differential algebra attached to a simplicial set which computes its integral cohomology.
items.note: Proved in §5, (5.3.4); the Z{t}-de Rham complex is (5.1). No atlas stage plans rational/ℓ-adic homotopy types, Sullivan-type models or the Grothendieck–Miller algebra (searched atlas and roadmaps for 'homotopy type', 'Sullivan', 'minimal model', 'Miller': only unrelated hits). Parallel results in Hodge theory: [12], [9].

items.name: Théorème 1 simplifies the applications of Weil I (3.7)
items.statement: Théorème 1 fits into a formalism much easier to handle than Weil I; in (3.7) it is shown how it simplifies the proofs of the applications given in (I.8). For its application to bounds on trigonometric sums see SGA 4½ [Sommes trigonométriques] (especially nos 1, 2, 3, 7).
items.note: Pointer only; content in (3.7). No atlas stage plans Weil I §8's applications via Weil II (FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums FF.2 consumes DWP.7 but no phrase matches (3.7)); recorded for completeness.

items.name: Scope: consequences over algebraically closed fields and over Z
items.statement: The essential results concern schemes of finite type over a finite field, with two provisos: (a) they have geometric consequences for schemes of finite type over the algebraic closure of a finite field, and specialisation arguments pass from there to an arbitrary algebraically closed base field; (b) certain results hold for schemes of finite type over Z; they follow immediately from the proofs, but not the statements, of the analogous results over a finite field, and are omitted from the survey.
items.note: Spreading-out/specialisation to arbitrary algebraically closed fields is planned at DWP.9: 'For arbitrary algebraically closed ground fields prove spreading out and smooth proper base change from the finite-field result instead of assuming every object has a finite-field model.'

items.name: Announcement: every Q̄_ℓ-sheaf on a scheme over F_q should be ι-mixed
items.statement: In (1.2) a conjecture is stated, in a more precise form, according to which on a scheme of finite type over F_q every constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaf is ι-mixed.
items.note: Stated as (1.2.9) and (1.2.10); see those items.

items.name: Announcement of determinantal weights (1.3)
items.statement: In (1.3) Grothendieck's theorem (1.3.8) is used to define the 'determinantal weights' of a lisse sheaf ℱ₀ on a smooth curve U₀. They depend only on the maximal exterior powers of the constituents of ℱ₀ and control the H⁰ (and hence the H²_c) of every sheaf deduced from ℱ₀ by passing to a space of tensors. Proposition (1.3.13), of innocuous appearance, plays the role played in (I.3.2) by the classical theory of invariants of the symplectic group.
items.note: Definition is (1.3.5); see §1.3 items.

items.name: Semicontinuity (1.10.7) and Newton = Hodge for general complete intersections
items.statement: In (1.10) the methods of (1.6)–(1.8) are applied to non-archimedean absolute values. The semicontinuity result (1.10.7) made it possible to show that, for a general complete intersection of characteristic p, the Newton polygon (defined by the slopes of crystalline cohomology) coincides with the Hodge polygon.
items.note: Proved in (1.10.7); the Newton=Hodge application is in other work (Illusie), not proved in this paper. No atlas stage plans it (searched 'Newton polygon', 'Hodge polygon' in DWP, CrystallineCohomology, WeightsInEtaleCohomology).

items.name: Equidistribution theorem (3.5) and function-field Sato–Tate
items.statement: In (3.5), from §2 and known arguments, an equidistribution theorem is deduced, a particular case of which is the analogue for a function field of the Sato–Tate conjecture (on the distribution of the Frobenius angles, for an elliptic curve over K).
items.note: Proved in (3.5). No atlas stage plans Deligne's equidistribution theorem or the function-field Sato–Tate theorem: ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 plans number-field Sato–Tate via symmetric-power automorphy only; FunctionFieldArithmetic FA.5 plans function-field Chebotarev only (searched 'equidistribut', 'Sato', 'Katz').

items.name: Weight filtration of a lisse mixed sheaf (3.4)
items.statement: In (3.4), Théorème 1 is applied to the successive extensions defining a mixed sheaf: a lisse mixed sheaf admits a 'filtration by weight' by lisse subsheaves, and the geometric monodromy of a lisse punctually pure sheaf on a normal scheme is semisimple.
items.note: Proved in (3.4.1). DWP.8: 'Prove Weil II3.4.1: weight-class decomposition moduloℤ; the unique functorial strict weight filtration on lisse mixed sheaves with integral weights; and geometric semisimplicity for punctually ι-pure lisse sheaves on a **normal** base.'

items.name: Monodromy of Lefschetz pencils (4.4)
items.statement: In (4.4) it is shown that the geometric monodromy group of the vanishing part of the cohomology of the hyperplane sections of a Lefschetz pencil (assumed sufficiently general in the wild case of characteristic 2) is Zariski dense in an orthogonal or symplectic group, or is a Weyl group; the latter case is studied in detail. (4.3) uses an ad hoc topos to transpose Lefschetz's 'Morse theory' arguments.
items.note: Proved in (4.3)–(4.4). LPV.5 plans only the odd-dimensional symplectic case needed for Weil I ('For odd n, prove that the compact monodromy image is **open** in Sp(V)'); no stage plans the orthogonal/Weyl-group cases of (4.4) (searched LPV, R34, DWP for 'Weyl group', 'orthogonal').

items.name: Théorème du pgcd (4.5)
items.statement: In (4.5) the 'gcd theorem' is deduced, used in [7] to compare the ℓ-adic and crystalline cohomologies of projective smooth varieties.
items.note: Proved in (4.5). No atlas stage plans it (searched 'pgcd', 'gcd theorem').

items.name: Stability of the category of mixed sheaves (§6.1)
items.statement: §6 develops the formalism of mixed sheaves: with proofs inspired by SGA 4½ [Th. finitude], their category is remarkably stable.
items.note: Proved in (6.1). DWP.8: 'Prove stability of the mixed category under six operations with finite-type and coefficient hypotheses, then the directional estimates'.

items.name: Pure complexes; proper direct image preserves purity (6.2.3)
items.statement: A notion of pure complex is defined, generalising that of a lisse punctually pure sheaf on a smooth scheme (6.2.4), (6.2.5). The direct image Rf_* by a proper morphism transforms pure complexes into pure complexes.
items.note: Proved in (6.2.3) with definitions (6.2.2), (6.2.4), (6.2.5). DWP.8: 'define K of weights≤w by H^i(K) having stalk weights≤w+i; define weights≥w by DK of weights≤−w ... Purity means both bounds. ... Proper direct image preserves purity by duality.' Sources of DWP.8 include 6.2.1–6.2.6.

items.name: Convention: 'schemes' are noetherian separated algebraic spaces with ℓ invertible
items.statement: Throughout, unless expressly stated otherwise, a prime number ℓ is fixed and one only considers noetherian separated algebraic spaces on which ℓ is invertible; they are simply called schemes. The reader who dislikes algebraic spaces may replace 'algebraic space' by 'scheme' in (0.1).
items.note: Algebraic spaces: SF.1 'Prove effective fpqc/fppf descent ... algebraic-space quotients'. Not in Mathlib (no AlgebraicSpace declaration). The paper never needs non-scheme spaces essentially; schemes suffice.

items.name: Fixed Q̄_ℓ, isomorphism ι: Q̄_ℓ ≅ C, meaning of 'faisceau', H*(X,ℱ) for H*(X, f*ℱ)
items.statement: An algebraic closure Q̄_ℓ of the field Q_ℓ of ℓ-adic numbers is fixed. ι denotes a field isomorphism of Q̄_ℓ with C (cf. (1.2.11)); exception: in (1.10), ι also denotes a field isomorphism of Q̄_ℓ with an algebraic closure Q̄_{ℓ'} of the field of ℓ'-adic numbers. The word 'faisceau' means, depending on the number, 'sheaf for the étale topology', 'constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaf' or 'Weil sheaf' (see (1.1.5), (1.3.2)). If f: X → Y is a morphism and ℱ a sheaf on Y, one often writes H*(X, ℱ) for H*(X, f*ℱ), likewise for hypercohomology, with or without supports.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Define Weil q-numbers of an integer weight on actual algebraic-number carriers and their all-embeddings absolute-value property. Define the separate ι-weight predicate on nonzero coefficient-field elements with real weights.' Sources list 'Weil II §§1.2/1.6'. Library audit DWP.0: Weil q-numbers and ι-weights 'absent'. Mathlib has AlgebraicClosure and the abstract isomorphism theorem for uncountable algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0 of equal cardinality, but not #Q̄_ℓ = 𝔠 nor a chosen ι (library audit DWP.0).

items.name: Geometric points; localised and algebraic geometric points
items.statement: A geometric point x̄ of X is a morphism into X of the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, denoted k(x̄). It is localised at x ∈ X if x is its image in X; it is algebraic if k(x̄) is an algebraic closure of k(x). Each geometric point defines an algebraic geometric point by replacing k(x̄) by the algebraic closure of k(x) in k(x̄) (used to extend tacitly to all geometric points terminology introduced for algebraic ones). Each point x of X with separably closed residue field defines a geometric point x̄ (take the perfect closure of k(x)); x and x̄ are often identified. If f: X → Y is a morphism, a geometric point x̄ of X defines by composition a geometric point f(x̄) of Y, sometimes simply denoted x̄.
items.note: No geometric-point API in Mathlib (searched 'GeometricPoint'); Mathlib has PerfectClosure (Mathlib/FieldTheory/PerfectClosure.lean:68) and separably closed fields. SF.2's 'geometric stalks' (EDC.0: 'common notation for internal RHom, tensor, support and geometric stalks') presuppose it; no stage phrase defines geometric points as such.

items.name: 'Locally' = étale-locally; henselisation X_(x) and strict henselisation X_(x̄)
items.statement: Unless expressly stated otherwise, 'locally' means locally for the étale topology. For x a point of a scheme X, X_(x) denotes the henselisation of X at x (the spectrum of the henselisation of the local ring of X at x). For x̄ a geometric point (0.3) of X, X_(x̄) denotes the strict localisation (= strict henselisation) of X at x̄; its residue field is the separable closure of k(x) in k(x̄).
items.note: Mathlib has HenselianLocalRing (Mathlib/RingTheory/Henselian.lean:108) but no henselisation or strict henselisation construction (searched 'enselization'). LPV.0 uses henselian traits but no stage phrase constructs the henselisation of a local ring.

items.name: Smooth curve
items.statement: A smooth curve over a field k is a scheme smooth and purely of dimension 1 over k.
items.note: Composite of Mathlib notions (smooth morphisms, dimension) but no named predicate; SF.3 (per library audit) has curves only in function-field form. Kept 'missing' since no single declaration states it.

items.name: Factorisation X → Spec(k') → Spec(k) through a finite separable extension
items.statement: Let X be a scheme of finite type over a field k. If X is connected, the structural morphism X → Spec(k) admits a unique factorisation X → Spec(k') → Spec(k) with k' a finite separable extension of k and X/k' geometrically connected. In general each connected component of X admits such a factorisation. In particular this gives a mechanical procedure to reduce properties of smooth curves over finite fields to those of absolutely irreducible smooth curves over finite fields; it is often used tacitly.
items.note: Used here for smooth curves. FA.0 (function-field form): 'Prove the exact constant field is finite and geometrical connectedness follows after choosing it.' Mathlib has AlgebraicGeometry.GeometricallyConnected (Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/Geometrically/Connected.lean:40) but not this factorisation (general form: Stacks, varieties chapter).

items.name: Traits: henselian, strictly local; notation (S, η, s, η̄, s̄)
items.statement: A trait is the spectrum of a discrete valuation ring V. It is henselian if V is, and strictly local if it is henselian with separably closed residue field. 'A trait (S, η, s)' means a trait S with closed point s and generic point η. 'A trait (S, η, s, η̄, s̄)' means a trait (S, η, s) equipped with a geometric point s̄ localised at s and whose strict localisation S_(s̄) is equipped with a generic geometric point η̄.
items.note: Components are in Mathlib: IsDiscreteValuationRing (Mathlib/RingTheory/DiscreteValuationRing/Basic.lean:58), HenselianLocalRing (Mathlib/RingTheory/Henselian.lean:108); no named 'trait' and no strict localisation. LPV.0 'Construct the geometric generic/special-fiber diagram over a henselian trait' presupposes the notion.

items.name: Conventions p, q, F_q, F; index 0 for objects over F_q; X = X₀ ⊗ F
items.statement: p always denotes a prime number ≠ ℓ, q a power of p, F_q a finite field with q elements and F an algebraic closure of F_q (resp. of F_p if F_q has not been introduced). Often in force: F_q and F are fixed; objects over F_q (schemes, or sheaves on F_q-schemes) carry an index 0, and deleting it denotes extension of scalars from F_q to F; e.g. if ℱ₀ is a sheaf on the F_q-scheme X₀, ℱ is its inverse image on X = X₀ ⊗_{F_q} F. Geometric points Spec(K̄) → X₀ of X₀ are always assumed defined by a geometric point of X, i.e. K̄ is assumed equipped with an F_q-morphism F → K̄.
items.note: Same base-change bookkeeping as Weil I; WC.0: 'Specify X→Spec k, geometric base change, the coefficient prime, finite extensions, the cohomological degree and Frobenius convention in every endpoint.'

items.name: |X| = set of closed points; x̄ ∈ |X| as geometric point
items.statement: If X is a scheme of finite type over a field or over Z, |X| denotes the set of its closed points. With the notation (0.7), if X₀ is of finite type over F_q, every point x̄ ∈ |X| defines a geometric point, still denoted x̄: Spec(F) → X₀; one speaks simply of the geometric point x̄ ∈ |X|.
items.note: The set of closed points is Mathlib `closedPoints` (Mathlib/Topology/JacobsonSpace.lean:38, 'The set of closed points.'), but the identification of x̄ ∈ |X| with a geometric point Spec(F) → X₀ is not there (see (0.3)); hence not marked library. Library audit WC.1: 'Missing: closed points of a scheme with their degrees'.

items.name: Galois viewpoint: F in place of Weil I's F*
items.statement: In this article the point of view is more Galois-theoretic than in Weil I; this often leads to writing F where F* figured in Weil I.
items.note: Convention; F is the geometric Frobenius element acting by transport of structure, cf. (1.1.7), (1.1.14). Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family.

items.name: Finite filtration
items.statement: A filtration F of an object V of an abelian category is called finite if there exist n and m such that FⁿV = V and F^m = 0 [sic; F^mV = 0 is meant].
items.note: Elementary; Mathlib has filtrations in special settings but no generic 'finite filtration of an object of an abelian category' predicate matching this.

items.name: lim ind, lim proj, quoted limits in ind/pro-categories, ':='
items.statement: lim ind and lim proj denote inductive and projective limits. Quotation marks indicate a limit taken in a category of ind-objects or pro-objects; thus « lim ind » X_i denotes the ind-object defined by the (filtered) inductive system of the X_i. One writes := for an equality whose right side is the definition of the left side.
items.note: Notation. Mathlib has Ind-objects (CategoryTheory.Ind) and pro-objects only partially; the 'formal limit' convention itself is notation, used in (1.1.1)–(1.1.2).

items.name: Constructible sheaf of A-modules (A noetherian torsion)
items.statement: Let A be a noetherian torsion ring. A sheaf of A-modules ℱ on X is constructible (SGA 4 IX §2) if there is a finite partition of X into locally closed parts X_i such that the restrictions ℱ|X_i are locally constant, with fibres A-modules of finite type.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: Constructible R-sheaf (R complete noetherian local, residue char ℓ)
items.statement: Let R be a noetherian local ring of residue characteristic ℓ with maximal ideal m, complete for the m-adic topology. The category of constructible R-sheaves is the 2-projective limit of the categories of sheaves of R/I-modules, for I an open ideal of R. Explicitly: a constructible R-sheaf ℱ on X is a projective system (ℱ_I) of sheaves of R-modules indexed by the open ideals I of R such that (α) ℱ_I is annihilated by I and is constructible as a sheaf of R/I-modules; (β) for I ⊃ J the transition morphism ℱ_J → ℱ_I induces an isomorphism ℱ_J ⊗ R/I ⥲ ℱ_I. Since n ↦ mⁿ is cofinal among open ideals, one may index by n with R/I replaced by R/mⁿ.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'. SGA 5 VI (1.4.2).

items.name: R-sheaves as pro-sheaves; notation ℱ ⊗ R/I
items.statement: The functor ℱ ↦ « lim proj » ℱ_I is fully faithful from the category of constructible R-sheaves to that of pro-sheaves of R-modules (pro-objects of the category of sheaves of R-modules); any pro-sheaf in the essential image is again called a constructible R-sheaf, and one writes ℱ ⊗ R/I for ℱ_I. Justification: for (ℱ_I) as above, the projective system in J of the ℱ_J ⊗ R/I is essentially constant with value ℱ_I.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. items.name: Lisse (twisted constant) R-sheaf
items.statement: ℱ is lisse (in another terminology, constant tordu) if the ℱ ⊗ R/I are locally constant.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: Constructible E-sheaves (E finite over Q_ℓ) and lisse E-sheaves
items.statement: Let E be a finite extension of Q_ℓ and R the integral closure of Z_ℓ in E. The category of constructible E-sheaves is the quotient of the category of constructible R-sheaves by the thick subcategory of torsion sheaves. In other words: (α) there is an essentially surjective functor ℱ → ℱ ⊗ E from constructible R-sheaves to constructible E-sheaves; (β) Hom(ℱ⊗E, 𝒢⊗E) = Hom(ℱ, 𝒢) ⊗_R E. A constructible E-sheaf is lisse if it is locally of the form ℱ ⊗_R E with ℱ lisse.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: Extension of scalars ℱ ↦ ℱ ⊗_E F between coefficient fields
items.statement: For F a finite extension of E there is a functor ℱ ↦ ℱ ⊗_E F from constructible E-sheaves to constructible F-sheaves, with Hom(ℱ⊗_E F, 𝒢⊗_E F) = Hom(ℱ, 𝒢) ⊗_E F. For an iterated extension there is a canonical isomorphism (1) (ℱ⊗_E F) ⊗_F G = ℱ ⊗_E G.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'. EDC.0: 'Prove coefficient restriction/extension and reduction identities'.

items.name: Constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaves and lisse Q̄_ℓ-sheaves
items.statement: The category of constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaves is the Q̄_ℓ-linear 2-inductive limit of the categories of constructible E-sheaves, for E ⊂ Q̄_ℓ a larger and larger finite extension of Q_ℓ. In other words: (α) for E ⊂ Q̄_ℓ finite over Q_ℓ there is an E-linear functor ℱ ↦ ℱ ⊗_E Q̄_ℓ from constructible E-sheaves to constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaves inducing isomorphisms Hom(ℱ, 𝒢) ⊗_E Q̄_ℓ ⥲ Hom(ℱ⊗Q̄_ℓ, 𝒢⊗Q̄_ℓ); (β) there are canonical isomorphisms (ℱ⊗_E F)⊗_F Q̄_ℓ = ℱ⊗_E Q̄_ℓ compatible with (1); (γ) every constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaf is of the form ℱ⊗_E Q̄_ℓ for suitable E and ℱ. A constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaf is lisse if it is locally of the form ℱ⊗_E Q̄_ℓ with ℱ lisse.

items.name: Recalled formalism for ℓ-adic sheaves (Jouanolou, SGA 5 V–VI; SGA 4½)
items.statement: Constructible Z_ℓ-sheaves on X form a noetherian abelian category (SGA 5 VI (1.1.3)); lisse constructible Z_ℓ-sheaves correspond to representations of the fundamental group (VI (1.2.5)); constructible Z_ℓ-sheaves are lisse on the strata of a stratification of X (VI (1.2.6)); tensor products and inverse images are defined, and the direct images with proper support Rⁱf_! for f: X → Y a morphism of finite type of noetherian schemes (VI (2.2)). By SGA 4½ [finitude] the theory applies as well to Rⁱf_* and Rⁱf^!, for f a morphism of finite type between schemes of finite type over a regular excellent scheme of dimension ≤ 1, and likewise to the vanishing-cycle functors RⁱΨ and RⁱΦ.

RΨ_f ... and RΦ_f(K) ... bounded constructibility for the specified excellent finite-type trait setting' (source SGA 4½ [Th. finitude]).

items.name: D⁻(X, R) as 2-projective limit of D⁻(X, R/mⁿ)
items.statement: Let R be the ring of integers of a finite extension E_λ of Q_ℓ and m its maximal ideal. For X a scheme, D⁻(X, R) := 2-lim proj D⁻(X, R/mⁿ). An object K of D⁻(X, R) is identified with a projective system of complexes K_n ∈ Ob D⁻(X, R/mⁿ) with isomorphisms K_{n+1} ⊗^L_{R/m^{n+1}} R/mⁿ ⥲ K_n in D⁻(X, R/mⁿ); K_n is rather written K ⊗^L R/mⁿ.

The paper stresses that 'il s'agit d'une théorie qui n'est pas au point' and works in this ad hoc framework.

items.name: D^b_c(X, R)
items.statement: D^b_c(X, R) is the subcategory of D⁻(X, R) formed by the K such that K ⊗^L R/m is bounded with constructible cohomology. For every n, K ⊗^L R/mⁿ is then in D^b_ctf(X, R/mⁿ) (bounded complexes of finite Tor-dimension with constructible cohomology sheaves).
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: Cohomology sheaves of K ∈ D^b_c(X,R) are constructible R-sheaves
items.statement: If K is in D^b_c(X, R), the ℋⁱK := « lim proj » ℋⁱ(K ⊗^L R/mⁿ) are constructible R-sheaves. (Proof: cutting up X, reduce to the ℋⁱ(K ⊗^L R/m) locally constant; any complex with flat components representing K ⊗^L R/mⁿ has the m-adic filtration with successive quotients quasi-isomorphic to K ⊗^L R/m, so the ℋⁱ(K ⊗^L R/mⁿ) are locally constant and one studies a fibre; in the punctual case apply SGA 5 XV p. 32.)

items.name: A torsion-free R-sheaf defines an object of D^b_c(X,R)
items.statement: Conversely, if ℱ is a torsion-free constructible R-sheaf, the projective system of complexes reduced to ℱ ⊗ R/mⁿ in degree 0 is in D^b_c(X, R). (If ℱ has torsion one would replace ℱ ⊗ R/mⁿ by τ_{≥−1}(ℱ ⊗ R/m^k) ⊗^L_{R/m^k} R/mⁿ, k large enough that m^{k−n} kills the torsion of ℱ; the complex obtained is then independent of k. This case is not needed.)

items.name: Stability of D^b_ctf(X, R/mⁿ) and D^b_c(X, R) under the operations
items.statement: Under suitable finiteness hypotheses, e.g. working in the category of schemes of finite type over S with S regular of dimension ≤ 1, the categories D^b_ctf(X, R/mⁿ) are stable under the four operations Rf_*, f*, Rf_!, Rf^!, and under the internal operations ⊗^L and R Hom. All these operations commute with reduction mod mⁿ; hence they extend trivially to D^b_c(X, R). Likewise for the functors RΨ and RΦ of vanishing cycles (SGA 4½ [Th. finitude]).

items.name: ℰxtⁱ(ℱ, 𝒢) of constructible R-, E_λ- and Q̄_ℓ-sheaves
items.statement: Example. Let X be of finite type over S as above, ℱ and 𝒢 two torsion-free constructible R-sheaves on X. The sheaves ℰxtⁱ_{R/mⁿ}(ℱ⊗R/mⁿ, 𝒢⊗R/mⁿ) form a projective system, and one puts ℰxtⁱ(ℱ, 𝒢) := ℋⁱ R ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢) = « lim proj » ℰxtⁱ_{R/mⁿ}(ℱ⊗R/mⁿ, 𝒢⊗R/mⁿ). This ℰxtⁱ is again a constructible R-sheaf. The construction passes to the quotient to define ℰxtⁱ of E_λ-sheaves and extends by passage to the limit to constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaves.

items.name: D^b_c(X, R) is triangulated when Hom groups mod mⁿ are finite
items.statement: If for all K and L in D^b_c(X, R) the groups Hom(K ⊗^L R/mⁿ, L ⊗^L R/mⁿ) are finite (as for X of finite type over a finite or algebraically closed field), then D^b_c(X, R) is triangulated, the distinguished triangles being those whose reduction modulo mⁿ is distinguished for all n.

items.name: DF^b_c(X, R) and 'triangles' as two-step filtered objects
items.statement: In general triangles are advantageously replaced by filtered complexes: DF^b_ctf(X, R/mⁿ) is the derived category of the category of bounded filtered complexes (finite filtration) whose graded is of finite Tor-dimension (Illusie, Complexe cotangent et déformations I, LN 239, V, nos 1–3), and DF^b_c(X, R) := 2-lim proj DF^b_ctf(X, R/mⁿ). Instead of a triangle in D^b_c(X, R) one constructs an object of DF^b_c(X, R) whose filtration has two steps, the vertices being the two components of the graded and the underlying complex (forgetting the filtration). By abuse of language such objects of DF^b_c(X, R) are sometimes called triangles and written as short exact sequences.
items.note: No atlas stage plans filtered derived categories (searched 'filtered derived', 'DF^b', 'filtered complex' in EDC, EDS, DWP, LPV). EnhancedDerivedSheaves plans an enhancement, which would make this device unnecessary; not the same statement.

items.name: Truncation τ_{≤n} on D^b_c(X, R)
items.statement: If K is a complex of sheaves, τ_{≤n}K is the complex … Kⁱ … → K^{n−1} → Ker d → 0 …; it respects quasi-isomorphisms but not finite Tor-dimension. For K in D^b_c(X, R) and K_k a complex of sheaves representing K ⊗^L R/m^k, let τ'_{≤n}K_k be the subcomplex of τ_{≤n}K_k obtained by replacing Ker d by the subsheaf of cycles whose image in ℋⁿ(K ⊗^L R/m^k) lies in Im(ℋⁿK → ℋⁿ(K ⊗^L R/m^k)). τ'_{≤n}K_k is in D^b_ctf(X, R/m^k), and one puts τ_{≤n}K := « lim proj » τ'_{≤n}(K ⊗^L R/m^k). The construction relies essentially on R being regular of dimension 1.
items.note: Not planned by a stage phrase (EDC.5 constructs perverse t-structures on 'the existing bounded constructible derived category' but not this ad hoc truncation). Would be subsumed by an honest ℓ-adic derived category with t-structure.

items.name: D^b_c(X, E_λ) and D^b_c(X, Q̄_ℓ)
items.statement: D^b_c(X, E_λ) is the category deduced from D^b_c(X, R) by extending scalars from R to E_λ: there is an essentially surjective functor ⊗_R E_λ: D^b_c(X, R) → D^b_c(X, E_λ), with Hom(K, L) ⊗_R E_λ ⥲ Hom(K⊗E_λ, L⊗E_λ). Then D^b_c(X, Q̄_ℓ) := 2-lim ind D^b_c(X, E_λ) (limit over the extensions E_λ ⊂ Q̄_ℓ of Q_ℓ).

items.name: Known theorems for R/mⁿ-sheaves are used freely for Z_ℓ-, Q_ℓ-, Q̄_ℓ-sheaves
items.statement: In the rest of the article the known theorems for constructible sheaves of R/mⁿ-modules are used freely for Z_ℓ-, Q_ℓ- or Q̄_ℓ-sheaves; SGA 5 V, VI, XV (for the trace formula, cf. also SGA 4½ [Rapport]) and the remarks above justify the arguments; where a difficulty arises it is pointed out.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'. The trace formula is the PR196 TraceFormula supplier consumed at WC.1.

items.name: Convention in (1.1)–(1.2): 'sheaf' = constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaf
items.statement: In this number and the next, 'sheaf' simply means constructible Q̄_ℓ-sheaf. This convention is superseded by (1.3.2).
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: ℓ-adic representation of a profinite group (or of an extension of a finitely generated discrete group by a profinite group)
items.statement: An ℓ-adic representation of a profinite group π (or more generally of an extension of a discrete group of finite type by a profinite group) on a Q̄_ℓ-vector space V is a homomorphism σ: π → GL(V) such that there exist a finite extension E of Q_ℓ in Q̄_ℓ and an E-structure V_E on V such that σ factors through a continuous homomorphism of π into GL(V_E). Representations of π in an algebraic group over Q̄_ℓ are defined likewise.
items.note: Not in Mathlib/Tau Ceti as such (continuous representations exist, not the 'defined over some finite E' condition for Q̄_ℓ). Implicit in SF.2/EDC.0 sheaf–representation dictionary but no stage phrase defines it; DWP.5 'Work with genuine finite coefficient fields/lattices before extending scalars' is the closest.

items.name: Lisse sheaves ↔ continuous representations of π₁(X, x̄)
items.statement: For X connected, pointed by a geometric point x̄, there is the usual relation between lisse sheaves and continuous representations of the fundamental group π₁(X, x̄): an equivalence of categories ℱ ↦ the π₁-module ℱ_x̄. The terminology of representations is transported to sheaves.
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'. Same item as PAPER-DELIGNE-74/s1-1.9b-lisse-sheaves-representations; SGA 5 VI (1.2.5).

items.name: Simple, semisimple, Jordan–Hölder series, constituents, semisimplification of a lisse sheaf
items.statement: Whether or not X is connected, a lisse sheaf ℱ on X is simple or irreducible if it is nonzero and has no nontrivial lisse subsheaf, and semisimple if it is a sum of simple sheaves. A Jordan–Hölder series of ℱ is a finite filtration F of ℱ by lisse subsheaves with the Grⁱ_F(ℱ) irreducible or zero. The constituents of ℱ are the nonzero Grⁱ_F(ℱ) for a Jordan–Hölder series of ℱ, and the semisimplification of ℱ is the direct sum of its constituents. Constituents and semisimplification are defined up to (non-unique) isomorphism.
items.note: DWP.5 uses 'irreducible constituents' ('Construct Weil II's generalization of the fundamental estimate for ι-real systems, irreducible constituents and compatible pairings'). The abstract Jordan–Hölder theorem is Mathlib CompositionSeries.jordan_holder (Mathlib/Order/JordanHolder.lean:456), but no sheaf-level notion exists.

items.name: Frobenius substitution φ, geometric Frobenius F = φ⁻¹, Weil group W(k̄/k)
items.statement: Let k be a finite field with q elements and k̄ an algebraic closure. The Frobenius substitution φ ∈ Gal(k̄/k) is the automorphism x ↦ x^q of k̄. The geometric Frobenius F ∈ Gal(k̄/k) is the inverse of φ. The Weil group W(k̄/k) is the subgroup of Gal(k̄/k) of integral powers of F. It is isomorphic to Z and Gal(k̄/k) is its profinite completion; W(k̄/k) is often identified with Z and Gal(k̄/k) with Ẑ by the isomorphism sending F to 1.
items.note: φ is Mathlib FiniteField.frobeniusAlgEquivOfAlgebraic (Mathlib/FieldTheory/Finite/Basic.lean:363, '(· ^ q)'); geometric Frobenius, the Weil group and Gal ≅ Ẑ are not stated. Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family.

items.name: Sheaves on Spec(k) ↔ Q̄_ℓ-spaces with an automorphism F whose eigenvalues are ℓ-adic units
items.statement: For X = Spec(k) and ℱ a sheaf on Spec(k), the fibre ℱ_k̄ at the geometric point Spec(k̄) is a Q̄_ℓ-vector space on which Gal(k̄/k) acts by transport of structure. The action is continuous: n ↦ Fⁿ extends by continuity to a homomorphism of Ẑ into GL(ℱ_x̄); in other words the eigenvalues of F are ℓ-adic units. The functor ℱ → ℱ_x̄ is an equivalence of the category of sheaves on Spec(k) with that of Q̄_ℓ-vector spaces equipped with an automorphism F whose eigenvalues are ℓ-adic units.
items.note: Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family. (x̄ here denotes the geometric point Spec(k̄), as in (1.1.6).)

items.name: F_y and det(1 − F_y t, ℱ) at a point with values in a finite field
items.statement: Let X be a scheme of finite type over Z, ℱ a sheaf on X, y: Spec(k) → X a point of X with values in a finite field k, and k̄ an algebraic closure of k. The inverse image of ℱ on Spec(k) is justiciable of (1.1.7): Gal(k̄/k) acts on ℱ_k̄. By abuse of notation one writes det(1 − F_y t, ℱ) for det(1 − Ft, ℱ_k̄), and speaks of the eigenvalues of F_y acting on ℱ. If X is connected with a geometric point x̄, there is a conjugacy class of maps Gal(k̄/k) = π₁(Spec(k), Spec(k̄)) → π₁(X, x̄); F_y denotes the image of the geometric Frobenius under any of them.
items.note: Same as Weil I (1.13) local factor, planned at WC.1/SF.2 in PAPER-DELIGNE-74/s1-1.13-local-factor. Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: det(1 − F_y t, ℱ) = det(1 − F_y t, V) for ℱ lisse
items.statement: For ℱ lisse defined by a representation V of π₁(X, x̄), det(1 − F_y t, ℱ) = det(1 − F_y t, V).
items.note: Planned under the atlas convention for the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) suppliers, which have no atlas stage of their own (same decision as the accepted PAPER-DELIGNE-74 extraction): SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 'Integrate[s] CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers' (sheaf cohomology, base change, compact support) and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.0 'Import[s] the actual bounded constructible/ctf subcategories'. Library audit SF.2: 'Missing: ... Q_l coefficients, and constructible/lisse l-adic sheaves'.

items.name: Frobenius at a point over an extension is the n-th power
items.statement: In the particular case y a closed point of X with the inclusion Spec(k(y)) → X one can often restrict to the Frobenii so obtained. If z is a point of X with values in a finite field k, with image y in X, and [k : k(y)] = n, the Frobenius relative to z is the n-th power of the Frobenius relative to y.
items.note: WC.0: 'Register canonical translations between field-isomorphic point sets and compatibility with finite-extension towers.' Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family.

items.name: Weil sheaf on X₀
items.statement: Definition (1.1.10)(i). With the notation (0.7): a Weil sheaf ℱ₀ on X₀ consists of a sheaf ℱ on X equipped with an action of W(F/F_q) (1.1.7) on (X, ℱ) which induces on X = X₀ ⊗_{F_q} F the action deduced from the action of W(F/F_q) on F. (An automorphism of (X, ℱ) is a pair (f, g) of an automorphism f of X and an isomorphism g: f_*ℱ → ℱ, or equivalently f*(g)⁻¹: f*ℱ → ℱ.) The definition of Weil sheaves depends on the choice of an algebraic closure F of F_p.
items.note: DWP.5: 'distinguish Weil descent from continuous Galois descent' (the only atlas phrase touching Weil sheaves; no stage names 'Weil sheaf'). Library audit DWP.5: 'no sheaves with Frobenius action'.

items.name: Weil group W(X₀, x̄) and its topology
items.statement: Definition (1.1.10)(ii). Let x̄ be a geometric point of X. The Weil group W(X₀, x̄) is the inverse image of W(F/F_q) under the natural map of π₁(X₀, x̄) to π₁(Spec(F_q), x̄) = Gal(F/F_q). The topology of W(X₀, x̄) = π₁(X₀, x̄) ×_{Gal(F/F_q)} W(F/F_q) is the product topology: the subgroup π₁(X, x̄) = Ker(π₁(X₀, x̄) → π₁(Spec(F_q), x̄)) is open and closed.
items.note: DWP.5 'distinguish Weil descent from continuous Galois descent'. Tau Ceti has only the local Weil group of a local field (ClassFieldTheory layer 9: 'Global Weil groups are outside this roadmap').

items.name: Weil sheaves and Weil group do not change when F_q is replaced by F_p
items.statement: A scheme X₀ over F_q is also a scheme over F_p (X₀ → Spec(F_q) → Spec(F_p)), and an algebraic closure of F_q is also one of F_p. Replacing F_q by F_p changes neither the category of Weil sheaves nor the Weil group (use X₀ ⊗_{F_p} F = ∐_σ X₀ ⊗_{F_q,σ} F, σ ranging over Hom(F_q, F) ∼ Gal(F_q/F_p)).
items.note: Not planned by a stage phrase (DWP.0 plans 'finite-field base extension' for numbers only).

items.name: Sheaves on X₀ are the Weil sheaves whose W-action extends continuously to Gal
items.statement: The inverse image on X of a sheaf on X₀ is equipped with an action of Gal(F/F_q) by transport of structure. This identifies sheaves on X₀ with particular Weil sheaves (in fact, those for which the action of W(F/F_q) extends to a continuous action of Gal(F/F_q)). For Weil sheaves the analogues of Grothendieck's results for ordinary sheaves are admitted; the generalisation is easy using (1.3.14).
items.note: DWP.5: 'distinguish Weil descent from continuous Galois descent'. The admitted extension of Grothendieck's formalism (cohomology, trace formula) to Weil sheaves is not separately planned.

items.name: Lisse Weil sheaves ↔ representations of W(X₀, x̄)
items.statement: If X̃ is the universal covering of X₀, pointed by the geometric point x̄, there is an equivariant morphism (for W(X₀, x̄) → W(F/F_q)) (X̃, with action of W(X₀, x̄)) → (X, with action of W(F/F_q)). The inverse image on X̃ of a Weil sheaf is thus equipped with an action of W(X₀, x̄); if the sheaf is lisse its fibre at x̄ identifies with its global sections on X̃, giving a 'fibre at x̄' functor (lisse Weil sheaves) → (representations of W(X₀, x̄)), 'representation' as in (1.1.6). If X₀ is connected this functor is an equivalence of categories; it allows the language of representations to be transposed to lisse Weil sheaves.
items.note: DWP.5 'distinguish Weil descent from continuous Galois descent'; the underlying lisse-sheaf/π₁ dictionary is the SF.2/EDC.0 supplier. No phrase states the W(X₀,x̄) equivalence.

items.name: F_y ∈ W(X₀, x̄), well defined up to conjugacy, with image φ^{−deg y}
items.statement: Suppose X₀ connected. For y ∈ |X₀| (or more generally y a point of X₀ with values in a finite field) the Frobenii F_y lie in W(X₀, x̄), the image of F_y in Gal(k̄/F_q) being the integral power φ^{−deg(y)} (deg y = [k(y) : F_q]) of the Frobenius substitution. The element F_y of W(X₀, x̄) is well defined up to W(X₀, x̄)-conjugacy, since its centraliser in π₁(X₀, x̄) maps onto an open subgroup of Gal(k̄/F_q) (if ȳ is a geometric point localised at y, this centraliser contains a copy of Gal(ȳ/y), whose image in Gal(k̄/F_q), identified with Ẑ, is deg(y)·Ẑ).
items.note: No stage phrase plans Frobenius elements in the global Weil group of a scheme; closest are FROB conventions (WC.0/R34.1) for π₁ and DWP.5's Weil descent.

items.name: Degree map deg: W(X₀, x̄) → Z; deg F_y = deg y; image nZ
items.statement: Call degrees the right-hand arrows of the diagram (1.1.13.1) with exact rows 0 → π₁(X, x̄) → W(X₀, x̄) → Z and 0 → π₁(X, x̄) → π₁(X₀, x̄) → Ẑ (the vertical maps being the identity, the inclusion and Z ⊂ Ẑ). One has deg F_y = deg y. The degree maps are surjective if X₀ is geometrically connected; in general, if the largest finite subfield of Γ(X₀, 𝒪_{X₀}) has degree n over F_q, their images are nZ and nẐ.
items.note: Not planned by a stage phrase (FA.4 'Relate the degree map to the Galois group of constants' is for function-field class field theory, not W(X₀,x̄)).

items.name: Frobenius correspondence and Weil sheaves ↔ (ℱ, F*: F*ℱ ≅ ℱ)
items.statement: Let ℱ be a sheaf on X. If F: X → X is the Frobenius endomorphism of X, deduced by extension of scalars from the (F_q-linear) Frobenius endomorphism x ↦ x^q of X₀, and id_{X₀} × F: X → X is the action of the geometric Frobenius F ∈ Gal(F/F_q), then as in SGA 5 XV there is a canonical isomorphism (id_{X₀} × F)*ℱ ≃ F*ℱ. For ℱ₀ a Weil sheaf on X₀ one deduces a Frobenius correspondence F*: F*ℱ ⥲ ℱ, and the functor ℱ₀ ↦ (ℱ, F*) is an equivalence of the category of Weil sheaves with that of sheaves ℱ on X equipped with an isomorphism F*: F*ℱ ⥲ ℱ. An analogous result holds for constructible sheaves of Z/ℓⁿ-modules and for constructible Z_ℓ-sheaves.
items.note: Same Frobenius correspondence as Weil I (1.11) (PAPER-DELIGNE-74/s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence), here with Weil sheaves. Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family.

items.name: The Frobenius-correspondence description fails for Q_ℓ- and Q̄_ℓ-sheaves
items.statement: It is not so for Q_ℓ- or Q̄_ℓ-sheaves: take for example ℱ = Q_ℓ and F* = multiplication by u ∈ Q_ℓ^* which is not an ℓ-adic unit (this Weil sheaf does not come from a sheaf on X₀).
items.note: Elementary once Weil sheaves exist; no stage phrase. DWP.5's 'distinguish Weil descent from continuous Galois descent' is the relevant caution.

items.name: F* on Hⁱ(X, ℱ) equals the action of F ∈ W by transport of structure
items.statement: The composite F*: Hⁱ(X, ℱ) ⥲ Hⁱ(X, F*ℱ) ⥲ Hⁱ(X, ℱ) deduced from the Frobenius correspondence coincides with the action of F ∈ W(k̄/F_q) acting on Hⁱ(X, ℱ) by transport of structure. Likewise for the Hⁱ_c.
items.note: Weil I (1.15) analogue, planned at WC.0/R34.1 in PAPER-DELIGNE-74/s1-1.15-galois-action-on-cohomology. Planned as in PAPER-DELIGNE-74 (s1-1.15-geometric-frobenius, s1-1.11-frobenius-correspondence): WC.0 requires the 'Frobenius convention in every endpoint' and R34.1 proves 'the representation-convention adapter on the imported Frobenius action'; the Frobenius/trace suppliers are the upstream PR196 family.

items.name: Arithmetic and geometric fundamental groups; geometric monodromy group
items.statement: π₁(X₀, x̄) is called the arithmetic fundamental group and π₁(X, x̄) the geometric fundamental group; if X₀ is normal these are profinite groups. If ℱ₀ is a lisse Weil sheaf on X₀, its geometric monodromy group is the image of π₁(X, x̄) in GL(ℱ_x̄).
items.note: No atlas stage defines geometric monodromy groups of lisse sheaves over finite fields in these terms (searched 'monodromy group': MordellLawrenceVenkatesh and BelyiMaps only). DWP.8 uses 'geometric semisimplicity' without defining the group.

items.name: Pure number of weight n relative to q
items.statement: Definition (1.2.1). Let q be a power of a prime number and n ∈ Z. A number α is pure of weight n, rel. q, if it is algebraic and all its complex conjugates have absolute value q^{n/2}. In what follows, 'number' means 'element of Q̄_ℓ'.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Define Weil q-numbers of an integer weight on actual algebraic-number carriers and their all-embeddings absolute-value property. Define the separate ι-weight predicate on nonzero coefficient-field elements with real weights.' Sources list 'Weil II §§1.2/1.6'. Library audit DWP.0: Weil q-numbers and ι-weights 'absent'.

items.name: Punctually pure sheaf of weight n
items.statement: Definition (1.2.2)(i). Let X be a scheme of finite type over Z and ℱ a sheaf on X. ℱ is punctually pure if there is an integer n, the weight of ℱ, such that for every x ∈ |X| the eigenvalues of F_x are pure of weight n, rel. N(x).
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Mixed sheaf and its punctual weights
items.statement: Definition (1.2.2)(ii). ℱ is mixed if it admits a finite filtration whose successive quotients are punctually pure sheaves. The weights of those quotients which are nonzero are the punctual weights of ℱ. By these definitions the zero sheaf is punctually pure and of weight n for every n; it is mixed with empty set of weights.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Variant: sheaves on Spec(k) as ℓ-adic Galois representations
items.statement: Variant (1.2.3). If k is a finite field, sheaves on Spec(k) are identified with ℓ-adic representations of Gal(k̄/k); the terminology (1.2.2) is transported to them.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'. DWP.0 also plans weights of 'an actual finite-dimensional vector space with an invertible endomorphism'.

items.name: Variant: weights for Weil sheaves and Q̄_ℓ-spaces with Frobenius
items.statement: Variant (1.2.4). The same terminology applies to Weil sheaves (1.1.10), and to Q̄_ℓ-vector spaces equipped with an action of Frobenius as regards the variant (1.2.3).
items.note: DWP.0: 'On an actual finite-dimensional vector space with an invertible endomorphism, define weights via the roots of its characteristic polynomial over a splitting field.' DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Stability of punctually pure sheaves of weight n
items.statement: Stabilités (1.2.5)(i). The category of punctually pure sheaves of weight n is stable under passage to a quotient, to a subsheaf, under extension, inverse image, and direct image by a finite morphism.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Prove preservation under invariant subobjects, quotients and extensions' (linear-algebra level). DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Tensor product adds weights; dual of lisse pure has weight −n
items.statement: (1.2.5)(ii). The tensor product of two punctually pure sheaves of weights n and m is punctually pure of weight n+m. The dual of a lisse punctually pure sheaf of weight n is punctually pure of weight −n.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Prove ... products, duals, tensor powers ... charpolynomial multiplicativity, tensor/dual spectra'. DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Stability of mixed sheaves
items.statement: (1.2.5)(iii). The category of mixed sheaves is stable under the operations of (i) (quotient, subsheaf, extension, inverse image, direct image by a finite morphism) and under tensor product.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Q̄_ℓ(1) is punctually pure of weight −2
items.statement: (1.2.5)(iv). Q̄_ℓ(1) is punctually pure of weight −2.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Prove ... Tate twists'; DWP.10 acceptance: 'ℚ_ℓ(1) with weight−2'. Same fact as PAPER-DELIGNE-74/s3-3.1-tate-twist-weight.

items.name: α pure of weight n iff |ια| = q^{n/2} for all ι; algebraicity is automatic
items.statement: (1.2.6). To show that α ∈ Q̄_ℓ^* is pure of weight n it suffices to check that for every isomorphism ι of Q̄_ℓ with C the complex number ια has absolute value q^{n/2}. The number α is then automatically algebraic; otherwise ια could be any transcendental number.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Define the separate ι-weight predicate ... Prove independence of a finite splitting field, extension of embeddings'. Library audit DWP.0: ι-weights 'absent'.

items.name: ι-weight w_q(α) of a number
items.statement: Let ι be a field isomorphism of Q̄_ℓ with C, q a power of a prime number and α ∈ Q̄_ℓ^*. Put (1.2.6.1) w_q(α) := 2 log_q|ια|; this is the ι-weight of α, rel. q.
items.note: DWP.0: 'Define Weil q-numbers of an integer weight on actual algebraic-number carriers and their all-embeddings absolute-value property. Define the separate ι-weight predicate on nonzero coefficient-field elements with real weights.' Sources list 'Weil II §§1.2/1.6'. Library audit DWP.0: Weil q-numbers and ι-weights 'absent'.

items.name: Punctually ι-pure of weight β ∈ R; ι-mixed; ι-weights
items.statement: For every real number β, a sheaf ℱ is punctually ι-pure of weight β if for every x ∈ |X| and every eigenvalue α of F_x acting on ℱ one has w_{N(x)}(α) = β. ℱ is ι-mixed if it admits a finite filtration with punctually ι-pure successive quotients; the weights of those quotients which are nonzero are the (punctual) ι-weights of ℱ. The variants (1.2.3) and (1.2.4) are transposed likewise.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Analogue of (1.2.5) for ι-purity and ι-mixedness
items.statement: The analogue of (1.2.5) remains true for punctually ι-pure and ι-mixed sheaves.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct punctually ι-pure/ι-mixed lisse and constructible sheaves, their finite filtrations and weight classes modulo ℤ. ... Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real.' Sources: 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. Library audit DWP.5: 'absent'.

items.name: Every representation of W(k̄/k) is ι-mixed
items.statement: For k a finite field, a representation V of W(k̄/k) is automatically ι-mixed.
items.note: Generalized-eigenspace filtration of F; DWP.0: 'Use generalized eigenspaces, not an assumed eigenbasis' for weights of an invertible endomorphism.

items.name: Torsion sheaf Q̄_ℓ^{(b)} and twist ℱ^{(b)}
items.statement: (1.2.7) Torsion. For b ∈ Q̄_ℓ^*, Q̄_ℓ^{(b)} denotes any Weil sheaf on Spec(F_p) of rank one on which F acts as multiplication by b. For b an ℓ-adic unit it is an ordinary sheaf. If an algebraic closure F of F_p has been chosen, it is normalised by choosing an isomorphism between its geometric fibre at F and Q̄_ℓ. For X a scheme of characteristic p (i.e. over F_p), ℱ a sheaf on X and b an ℓ-adic unit (resp. X of finite type over F_p, ℱ a Weil sheaf and b ∈ Q̄_ℓ^*), ℱ^{(b)} denotes the tensor product of ℱ with the inverse image of Q̄_ℓ^{(b)}; ℱ^{(b)} is said to be deduced from ℱ by torsion (twisting).
items.note: DWP.5: 'Prove the coefficient-embedding and twist reductions used when weights are real. A formal real twist is not automatically a motivic Tate twist.'

items.name: Q̄_ℓ^{(b)} is ι-pure of weight w_p(b); twisting adds w_p(b)
items.statement: The sheaf Q̄_ℓ^{(b)} is punctually ι-pure of weight w_p(b); the torsion ℱ ↦ ℱ^{(b)} therefore increases the weights by w_p(b).
items.note: DWP.5 'twist reductions used when weights are real'; DWP.0 'products ... finite-field base extension' for the number-level computation.

items.name: Remark (1.2.8): real ι-weights are largely illusory (a posteriori from (3.4.1))
items.statement: Remark (1.2.8). In the definitions of punctually pure and mixed sheaves the weights are required to be integers; for ι-pure and ι-mixed sheaves they may be arbitrary reals. The deep theorem (3.4.1) shows a posteriori that for X of finite type over F_p this generality is largely illusory: every ι-mixed sheaf is a direct sum of sheaves deduced by torsion (1.2.7) from ι-mixed sheaves of integral weights, and every sheaf which is ι-mixed for every ι is a direct sum of sheaves deduced by torsion from mixed sheaves. Every lisse sheaf is a successive extension of irreducible lisse sheaves, and (1.3.6) shows that every lisse sheaf on X normal connected of finite type over F_p is deduced by torsion from a sheaf whose determinant (= maximal exterior power) is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group of X.
items.note: Forward reference; proved in (3.4.1) (§3.4) and (1.3.6)/(1.3.14). DWP.8: 'Prove Weil II3.4.1: weight-class decomposition moduloℤ'. The last sentence is stated for irreducible lisse sheaves in (1.3.14).

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.9): every sheaf on X of finite type over F_p is ι-mixed
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.9). On X of finite type over F_p, every sheaf is ι-mixed. It is a consequence of the more precise conjecture (1.2.10). One of the main tools, theorem (1.5.1), is a partial result in the direction of (1.2.9).
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. Later literature: follows from L. Lafforgue's proof of (1.2.10)(i) for curves (Invent. Math. 147, 2002) plus the reduction to curves stated below (1.2.10); recorded from memory, not verified here. GS.6 plans L. Lafforgue's theorem ('State the bijection between cuspidal automorphic representations with finite-order central character and irreducible continuous n-dimensional ell-adic representations with finite-order determinant ... Prove local factors, purity') but only on curves; no stage plans the higher-dimensional reduction.

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.10)(i): purity of weight 0
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.10). Let X be normal connected of finite type over F_p, and ℱ an irreducible lisse sheaf whose determinant is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group. (i) ℱ is pure of weight 0.
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. GS.6 (L. Lafforgue, curves): 'Prove local factors, purity and multiplicity conclusions in the exact theorem range.' Higher-dimensional X reduce to curves (paper, below (1.2.10)); that reduction is not planned. The paper notes that (i), (iii), (iv) follow from the case where X is a curve.

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.10)(ii): coefficients in a number field
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.10). Let X be normal connected of finite type over F_p, and ℱ an irreducible lisse sheaf whose determinant is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group. (ii) There is a number field E ⊂ Q̄_ℓ such that the polynomials det(1 − F_x t, ℱ), x ∈ |X|, have coefficients in E.
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. Later literature (from memory, not verified here): L. Lafforgue for curves; Deligne (2012, 'Finitude de l'extension de Q engendrée par des traces de Frobenius') in general. GS.6 plans the curve-case correspondence, which gives (ii) on curves only.

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.10)(iii): λ-adic units away from p
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.10). Let X be normal connected of finite type over F_p, and ℱ an irreducible lisse sheaf whose determinant is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group. (iii) For λ a non-archimedean place of E prime to p, the inverse roots in Ē_λ of det(1 − F_x t, ℱ) (the Frobenius eigenvalues) are λ-adic units.
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. Follows on curves from the Langlands correspondence of GS.6 (L. Lafforgue); not separately planned. The paper notes that (i), (iii), (iv) follow from the case where X is a curve.

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.10)(iv): p-adic slope bound
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.10). Let X be normal connected of finite type over F_p, and ℱ an irreducible lisse sheaf whose determinant is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group. (iv) For λ dividing p, the valuation of the inverse roots satisfies |v(α)/v(Nx)| ≤ 1/2 rg ℱ.
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. Not planned. Later literature proves sharper slope bounds on curves (V. Lafforgue; Drinfeld–Kedlaya); recorded from memory, not verified here. The paper notes that (i), (iii), (iv) follow from the case where X is a curve.

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.10)(v): ℓ-adic companions
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.10). Let X be normal connected of finite type over F_p, and ℱ an irreducible lisse sheaf whose determinant is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group. (v) For suitable E (perhaps larger than in (ii)) and each non-archimedean place λ prime to p, there is an E_λ-sheaf compatible with ℱ (same Frobenius eigenvalues).
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. Not planned by any stage (searched 'companion'). Later literature: L. Lafforgue (curves), Drinfeld (2012, smooth X); from memory, not verified here.

items.name: Conjecture (1.2.10)(vi): crystalline companions
items.statement: Conjecture (1.2.10). Let X be normal connected of finite type over F_p, and ℱ an irreducible lisse sheaf whose determinant is defined by a character of finite order of the fundamental group. (vi) For λ dividing p, one hopes for little crystalline companions ('petits camarades cristallins').
items.note: Conjecture in the paper. Vague by design. Not planned (PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology RD.6 plans Kedlaya's p-adic Weil II, not companions). Later literature: Abe (2018) for curves; from memory, not verified here.

items.name: Remarks on (1.2.10): reduction to curves; Drinfeld for rank 2; compatible systems
items.statement: Parts (i), (iii), (iv) of the conjecture follow from the special case where X is a curve. For ℱ of rank 2 on a curve, Drinfeld's work reduces the conjecture ((vi) excluded so far) to controlling the constant of the functional equation of the L-function attached to ℱ (namely of L(ℱ, χ): L and its twists). In particular, if ℱ belongs to an infinite compatible system of λ-adic representations, (i) to (v) hold.
items.note: Cited results of Drinfeld; GS.6 acceptance 'n=2 the Drinfeld correspondence' is the related plan, but the reduction/compatible-system statements are not planned.

items.name: Remark (1.2.11): isomorphisms Q̄_ℓ ≅ C are an expository convenience
items.statement: Remark (1.2.11). Isomorphisms between Q̄_ℓ and C are only a convenience of exposition. Each time a number is proved pure, an easy fragment of the proof suffices to establish that it is algebraic; for the rest of the arguments it would then suffice to consider the complex embeddings of the subfield of Q̄_ℓ formed by algebraic numbers, which does not require the axiom of choice.
items.note: DWP.0 separates 'Weil q-numbers ... on actual algebraic-number carriers' from 'the separate ι-weight predicate', matching this remark.

items.name: Totally real lisse sheaf
items.statement: Definition (1.2.12). Let X be a scheme of finite type over Z and ℱ a lisse sheaf on X. ℱ is totally real if for every x ∈ |X| the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of F_x acting on ℱ are totally real algebraic numbers.
items.note: Not planned by a stage phrase (DWP.5's 'ι-real systems' is the ι-variant (1.2.13)). Mathlib has NumberField.IsTotallyReal for fields, not this sheaf predicate.

items.name: ι-real lisse sheaf
items.statement: Variant (1.2.13) (useful in equal characteristic). ℱ is ι-real if for every x ∈ |X| the polynomial ι det(1 − F_x t, ℱ) has real coefficients.
items.note: DWP.5: 'Construct Weil II's generalization of the fundamental estimate for ι-real systems'.

items.name: Lisse punctually pure sheaves are direct factors of totally real ones
items.statement: Remark (1.2.14). Every lisse punctually pure sheaf ℱ is a direct factor of a lisse punctually pure totally real sheaf, namely, if it is of weight n, of ℱ ⊕ ℱ^∨(−n).
items.note: Elementary (eigenvalues of ℱ^∨(−n) are the complex conjugates of those of ℱ). Not planned by a stage phrase; used in Outline D via its ι-variant.

items.name: Lisse ι-pure sheaves (integral weight, or any weight for Weil sheaves) are direct factors of ι-real ones
items.statement: Likewise, a lisse punctually ι-pure sheaf of integral weight is a direct factor of a lisse punctually ι-pure ι-real sheaf. In these variants ℱ may be taken to be a Weil sheaf; for Weil sheaves, a lisse punctually ι-pure sheaf of arbitrary weight is a direct factor of a lisse punctually ι-pure ι-real sheaf.
