items.name: Boundary extension of an absolute-value bound for Frobenius eigenvalues
items.statement: Let b > 0. If for every closed point x of U_0 and every eigenvalue α of F_x on 𝓕_0 one has ‖ια‖ ≤ b^{deg(x)}, then for every point x of |S_0| and every eigenvalue α of F_x on j_*𝓕_0 one still has ‖ια‖ ≤ b^{deg(x)}.
items.note: Generalizes (1.8.1). Proof (p. 182) follows (1.8.1): in (1.8.1.1) the first factor converges for |t| < 1/b (resp. |t| < 1/qb in the archimedean case, (1.4.6)); the second member has no pole for |t| < 1/‖q‖b, hence for |t| < 1/b by (1.4.4) (resp. for |t| < 1/qb); so the remaining factors ι det(1 − F_x t^{deg x}, j_*𝓕_0) (x∈|S_0|) have no pole for |t| < 1/b (resp. 1/qb), giving the claim (resp. ‖ια‖ ≤ (qb)^{deg x}, from which (1.10.1) follows by passing to tensor powers of 𝓕_0 as in (1.8.1)). The printed conclusion has b^{deg(X)} (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E24). The archimedean case is the boundary estimate DWP.5 plans ('the weights of boundary invariants of j_*F'), but the non-archimedean case is not planned, so marked missing.

items.name: Frobenius eigenvalues of 𝓕_0 at a point of S_0
items.statement: Let s ∈ |S_0|, s̄, η, η̄ as in (1.8.3), and 𝓕_η̄ the representation of the Weil group W(η̄/η). The 'eigenvalues of F_s on 𝓕_0' are the eigenvalues of a lift of F_s ∈ W(s̄/s) to W(η̄/η), acting on 𝓕_η̄. This terminology is used only when the choice of lift does not matter (cf. (1.7.4)).
items.note: Local Weil group representation at a boundary point; LPV.1 plans inertia and the monodromy operator but not this eigenvalue convention for lifts of Frobenius. Used in (1.10.3)–(1.10.9).

items.name: Non-archimedean eigenvalue bounds extend to the boundary
items.statement: In the non-archimedean case, let 0 ≤ b ≤ c ≤ ∞. If for every point x ∈ |U_0| and every eigenvalue α of F_x on 𝓕_0 one has b^{deg x} ≤ ‖ια‖ ≤ c^{deg x}, then for every point s ∈ S_0 and every eigenvalue α of F_s on 𝓕_0 one still has b^{deg s} ≤ ‖ια‖ ≤ c^{deg s}.
items.note: Proof (p. 183): for s ∈ |S_0|, pass as in (1.8.4) to a finite covering to make local monodromy unipotent, I ⊂ W(η̄/η) acting by σ ↦ exp(t_ℓ(σ)·N). Lemma (1.10.1) gives ‖ια‖ ≤ c^{deg s} for eigenvalues on Ker(N); since ‖q‖ ≤ 1 the same holds on all of 𝓕_η̄ by (1.6.14.3); the lower bound follows by passing to the dual sheaf. Uses the unipotent-reduction and N (LPV.1) and (1.6.14.3). Not planned (DWP.5 is archimedean).

items.name: ℓ′-adic units at the boundary
items.statement: If for every point x ∈ |U_0| the eigenvalues α of F_x on 𝓕_0 are ℓ′-adic units (i.e. ‖ια‖ = 1), then for every point s ∈ |S_0| the eigenvalues of F_s on 𝓕_0 are again ℓ′-adic units. Moreover, by shrinking U_0, one may replace the hypothesis 'for all x ∈ |U_0|' by 'for all but finitely many', and recover the missing x for free.
items.note: Case b = c = 1 of (1.10.3). (1.10.4) remarks that applying (1.10.3) to exterior powers relates Newton polygons at x ∈ |U_0| and s ∈ |S_0|, and that for ℓ′ ≠ p eigenvalues are in practice always ℓ′-adic units, so (1.10.3) is only useful in this form.

items.name: Valuation v_N and Newton polygons (of a family, and of 𝓕_0 at a point)
items.statement: For ℓ′ = p, pass from absolute values to valuations: for N a power of p, let v_N be the valuation of 𝐐̄_p normalized by v_N(N) = 1. For a finite family (α_i)_{i∈I} of elements of 𝐐̄_p, its Newton polygon relative to N is the graph of the continuous piecewise-linear function n from [0, |I|] to 𝐑 characterized by: n(0) = 0, and if the v_N(α_i) are arranged in an increasing sequence indexed by the integers from 1 to |I|, the slope of n between j−1 and j is the j-th of these valuations. The value of n at the integer j (0 ≤ j ≤ |I|) is thus the smallest valuation of a product of j of the α_i with distinct indices. For x ∈ |X_0|, the Newton polygon of 𝓕_0 at x, relative to ι, is the Newton polygon relative to N(x) of the image under ι of the system of eigenvalues of F_x on 𝓕_0; its value at the integer j (0 ≤ j ≤ rg 𝓕_0) is the smallest of the numbers v_{N(x)}(ια) for α an eigenvalue of F_x on Λ^j 𝓕_0.
items.note: No Newton polygon (of a family of p-adic numbers or of a polynomial) found in Mathlib or Tau Ceti (grep of the declarations index for 'Newton'); no atlas stage plans Newton polygons of Frobenius. For s ∈ S_0 the eigenvalues are those of (1.10.2). Printed 'V_N … de 𝐐̄^p' (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E26).

items.name: Newton polygon at the boundary lies above the generic one, same endpoints
items.statement: Suppose that for almost all x ∈ |U_0|, 𝓕_0 has at x the same Newton polygon n relative to ι. Then for s ∈ |S_0|, the Newton polygon n_s of 𝓕_0 at s lies above n: n_s ≥ n, and has the same endpoints.
items.note: Proof (pp. 183–184): n_s ≥ n restates the upper bound (1.10.3) on absolute values of eigenvalues of F_s for the sheaves Λ^j 𝓕_0 (using the remark after (1.10.5) for 'almost all'). Equality of endpoints n_s(rg 𝓕_0) = n(rg 𝓕_0) follows since for a rank-one sheaf (here the maximal exterior power) the valuation v_{N(x)} of ια, α the eigenvalue of F_x, is independent of x (cf. (1.3.3)). A Grothendieck-type specialization statement for Newton polygons of a lisse sheaf into its boundary; not planned.

items.name: Bound on the nilpotence order of local monodromy from valuation bounds
items.statement: Let β ≤ γ, and suppose that for almost all x ∈ |U_0| the eigenvalues α of F_x on 𝓕_0 satisfy β ≤ v_{N(x)}(ια) ≤ γ. Then, if n is the integer part of γ − β, the logarithm N of the unipotent part of the local monodromy at s ∈ |S_0| satisfies N^{n+1} = 0.
items.note: (1.10.8): sharper results use the monodromy filtration M. Proof: if m is the smallest integer with N^{m+1} = 0, F_s has eigenvalues α and α·N(s)^m, and one applies (1.10.3) (in valuation form). Not planned.

items.name: Geometric monodromy mod ℓ^n of a family of pointed curves forms a lisse sheaf generically
items.statement: Let S be an irreducible scheme, f : X → S a smooth morphism purely of relative dimension 1 with geometrically connected fibres, g a section of f, and 𝓕 a lisse 𝐙_ℓ-sheaf on X. For each geometric point s̄ of S, let M^n_s̄ be the image of π_1(X_s̄, g(s̄)) in Aut((𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕)_{g(s̄)}). Then there exists an open U of S such that, for every n and every geometric point s̄ of U, M^n_s̄ is the fibre at s̄ of a lisse subsheaf M^n of 𝒜ut(g*𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕) on U.
items.note: Proof (p. 184): let I_n be the finite étale covering ℐsom(𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕, f*g*𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕) of X, so g*I_n = 𝒜ut(g*𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕); the identity gives a section g_n of I_n over g. After shrinking S one builds simultaneously the M^n and a tower of finite étale coverings X_n ⊂ I_n containing g_n, stable under M^n, fibrewise the Galois covering trivializing 𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕, with M^n = g*(X_n/X). Facts used: Aut(F/ℓF) is finite while automorphisms of F trivial on F/ℓF form a pro-ℓ group; the neutral component of g_1 in I_1 is compatible with base change over an open U_1 (EGA IV (9.7.7)), giving X_1 and M^1 = g*X_1; for 𝐋 a set of primes invertible on U_1 the maximal pro-𝐋 quotients π_1^{(𝐋)} of the geometric fibres form a 'local system' over a smaller open U (SGA 1 XIII (3.1), (3.3), (4.5)); for 𝐋 = {ℓ} it acts on g*𝓕 and the tower of quotients acting trivially on the g*𝓕/ℓ^n𝓕 gives X_n ⊂ I_n, M^n = g*X_n. Used for the general case (1.11.4) of (1.3.1). No atlas stage plans specialization of (tame / pro-𝐋) fundamental groups in families (SGA 1 XIII).

items.name: Criterion for the π_1^{(𝐋)} of the fibres to form a local system
items.statement: For the π_1^{(𝐋)}(X_s̄, g(s̄)) to form a 'local system' on S, it suffices that there exist an embedding X ↪ X̄ with X̄ proper and smooth over S of relative dimension 1 and X the complement of a subscheme T finite étale over S (SGA 1 XIII (4.4), (4.5)). It even suffices that such an embedding exist after a finite, radicial, surjective base change S′ → S (which the étale topology does not see). This is always possible over an open of S (reduce by passage to the limit to the case where S is the spectrum of a perfect field).
items.note: Cited from SGA 1 XIII; supplies the input of (1.11.1) and (1.11.3). Not planned.

items.name: Specialization of the images of inertia (and of tame inertia) in M^n
items.statement: With the notation of (1.11.1), replace S by U and suppose there exist embeddings (1.11.2) X_1 ↪ X̄_1 (complement of T_1) and X ↪ X̄ (complement of T) compatible with X_1 → X. The X_n/X_1 are tame coverings, so one has a tower of compactifications X_n ↪ X̄_n, complement of T_n (SGA 1 XIII 5). Let s̄ be a geometric point of S, t ∈ T_s̄, η_t the generic point (of the henselization at t) of X̄_s̄, k(η̄_t) an algebraic closure of k(η_t) and I_t = Gal(η̄_t/η_t); there is a conjugacy class of maps I_t → π_1(X_s̄, g(s̄)); let M^n_t be the image of I_t in M^n_s̄ (well defined up to conjugacy). Then if s̄_1 specializes to s̄_2 and t_1 to t_2, M^n_{t_1} specializes to (a conjugate of) M^n_{t_2}. This still holds if the embeddings exist only over S′/S as in (1.11.2), hence in any case over a nonempty open of S. If s̄ has characteristic p and 𝓕_s̄ on X_s̄ is tamely ramified at t ∈ T_s̄, the map I_t → M^n_s̄ factors through the tame inertia group I_t^{(p′)} ≃ 𝐙_{(p′)}(1). If 𝓕 is tamely ramified along the section τ of T/S with t = τ(s̄), it even factors through 𝐙_{(𝐋)}(1) = ∏_{ℓ′∈𝐋} 𝐙_ℓ′(1), for 𝐋 the set of primes invertible on S, giving a conjugacy class of maps φ^n_t : 𝐙_{(𝐋)}(1) → M^n_t; again, if s̄_1 specializes to s̄_2 and t_1 to t_2, φ^n_{t_1} specializes to φ^n_{t_2}.
items.note: Proof: one may assume S strictly local; then t_1 and t_2 lie on one section τ of T, which lifts to a section τ^n of T_n; M^n acts on T_n and the M^n_{t_i} are the fibres at s̄_1, s̄_2 of the stabilizer of τ^n. For the tame statement see SGA 1 XIII (2.11) 'for the proof, if not the statement'. The printed text says η_t is 'le point générique de X̄_s̄' (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E29, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E30). Not planned.

items.name: General case of (1.3.1): image of geometric π_1 in the abelianized Weil group
items.statement: (Proof of (1.3.1) in general.) For X_0 normal and geometrically connected of finite type over 𝐅_q (notation of (1.3.1)), the image of the geometric fundamental group π_1(X, x̄) in W(X_0, x̄)^{ab} is the product of a finite group of order prime to p by a pro-p-group. Equivalently: let H_1(X, 𝐙̂) be the largest abelian quotient of π_1(X, x̄) and H_1(X, 𝐙̂_{(p′)}) its largest prime-to-p quotient; the image of π_1(X, x̄) in W(X_0, x̄)^{ab} is the largest quotient of H_1(X, 𝐙̂) on which Frobenius acts trivially, and one must show that the largest quotient of H_1(X, 𝐙̂_{(p′)}) on which Frobenius acts trivially is finite.
items.note: Proof: one may assume dim X_0 ≥ 1 and make a preliminary finite extension of 𝐅_q. Take U_0 a dense quasi-projective (e.g. affine) open of X_0, embedded in a projective space 𝐏_0; let V = (U ⊗_𝐅 k(η̄)) ∩ D_η̄ be a generic linear section of dimension 1 (η̄ a geometric generic point of the Grassmannian of linear subspaces of codimension dim U − 1). By Bertini, π_1(V, v) → π_1(U, v) is surjective, and π_1(U, v) → π_1(X, v) is surjective (normality), so H_1(V, 𝐙̂_{(p′)}) → H_1(X, 𝐙̂_{(p′)}) is surjective. H_1(V, 𝐙̂_{(p′)}) does not change when V is replaced by a sufficiently general section W (SGA 1 XIII), which after finite extension is defined over 𝐅_q (from W_0); so it suffices to prove (1.3.1) for the curve W_0, done by class field theory right after (1.3.1) (the text says '(1.3.2)', PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E31). (1.3.1) is used for (1.3.4): rank-one lisse sheaves have finite geometric monodromy up to twist. No atlas stage plans (1.3.1) or the Bertini theorem for fundamental groups (LPV/R34.4 Bertini is for hyperplane-section geometry, not π_1-surjectivity).

items.name: (1.11.1) holds for any morphism of finite type
items.statement: Proposition (1.11.1) holds for every morphism f of finite type: localization on S and a Mayer–Vietoris argument reduce to f flat with normal fibres; the arguments of restriction to an open (1.11.4) then allow one to assume f smooth and quasi-projective; the hyperplane section argument then reduces to the relative-dimension-1 case of (1.11.1).
items.note: Sketch only; the statement for general f (no section g, no fibre-connectedness hypothesis is restated) is not made precise in the text. Not used later.

items.name: Abstract Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin data (Γ, ω_1, G, Σ, (x_v)) and hypotheses (A′), (A″)
items.statement: Let Γ be a group isomorphic to 𝐙 or to 𝐑, ω_1 : Γ → 𝐑*_+ a nontrivial quasi-character, G a locally compact group which is an extension of Γ by a compact group G^0, Σ a countably infinite set, and (x_v)_{v∈Σ} a family indexed by Σ of conjugacy classes in G. Hypotheses: (A′) if Γ is isomorphic to 𝐑, the extension G is trivial (this hypothesis is in fact automatically satisfied); (A″) if Γ is isomorphic to 𝐙, the centre of G maps onto a subgroup of finite index of Γ.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'then the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument … Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'; Sources 'Weil II §§1.2–1.11/2.1–2.2'. This is the abstract setting of that argument. For the proof of (2.2.10), the only case used, it suffices that G = 𝐙 × G^0 with G^0 a compact Lie group whose identity component G^00 is semisimple. (A″) is not needed for (2.1.4) (G enters only via its finite-dimensional continuous complex representations), and if G has a linear representation whose restriction to G^0 has finite kernel, (A″) holds automatically (1.3.10).

items.name: Quasi-characters ω_s, norms Nv and degrees deg(v)
items.statement: For s ∈ 𝐂 put ω_s = ω_1^s; still denote by ω_s the composite G → Γ → 𝐂* and put Nv = ω_{−1}(x_v). If Γ is isomorphic to 𝐙, let q be the number > 1 and deg the isomorphism of Γ with 𝐙 such that ω_1(γ) = q^{−deg(γ)}; then ω_s = ω_{s+2πi/log q}. Writing again deg for the composite G → Γ → 𝐙 (via deg), put deg(v) = deg(x_v).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. Printed 'ω_s = ω_{s+2πi log q}' (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E32).

items.name: Unitarizability criterion and real part ℛ(τ) of an irreducible representation
items.statement: Let g be an element of the centre of G with nontrivial image in Γ (one exists by hypothesis). A complex linear representation τ : G → GL(V) is unitarizable if and only if τ(g) is: from a hermitian structure invariant under g one gets one invariant under G by integration over the compact group G/g^𝐙. If τ is irreducible, so that τ(g) is scalar, there is a unique real number σ with |τ(g)| = ω_σ(g), and then τ·ω_{−σ} is unitarizable; σ is called the real part ℛ(τ) of τ. One has ℛ(τ·ω_s) = ℛ(τ) + ℛ(s).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. The averaging-over-a-compact-group step is Weyl's unitarian trick, planned in tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/CompactGroups Layer 1 ('Every finite-dimensional continuous representation is unitarizable'), there for compact G only.

items.name: The spaces G̃ ⊃ Ĝ of irreducible and unitary irreducible representations, as a Riemann surface
items.statement: Let G̃ be the set of isomorphism classes of irreducible representations of G, and Ĝ the subset of unitary ones. The sets {τ·ω_s | s ∈ 𝐂} (τ ∈ Ĝ) form a partition of G̃, and s ↦ τ·ω_s identifies {τ·ω_s | s ∈ 𝐂} with the quotient of 𝐂 by a discrete subgroup of i𝐑 if Γ ≃ 𝐙, and with 𝐂 if Γ ≃ 𝐑. G̃ is given the Riemann surface structure for which it is the disjoint union of these quotients.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument … Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'. Holomorphy/meromorphy 'in τ' in (2.1.4) is with respect to this structure.

items.name: Hypotheses (B′), (B″) and their reformulation for Γ ≃ 𝐙
items.statement: (B′) For every v ∈ Σ, Nv > 1. (B″) The infinite product ∏_{v∈Σ} (1 − Nv^{−s})^{−1} converges absolutely for ℛ(s) > 1. For Γ isomorphic to 𝐙 these conditions can be rewritten: deg(v) > 0, and for every ε > 0, #{v | deg(v) = n} ≤ O(q^{(1+ε)n}).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'. The text calls the hypotheses collectively (A), (B).

items.name: L-function L(τ) of the data and its convergence
items.statement: Hypothesis (B″) ensures that for τ ∈ G̃ the infinite product L(τ) = ∏_{v∈Σ} det(1 − τ(x_v))^{−1} converges absolutely for ℛ(τ) > 1. Each factor is holomorphic in τ for ℛ(τ) > 0, and L(τ) is a holomorphic function of τ for ℛ(τ) > 1. One puts L(τ, s) = L(τ·ω_s). For τ not necessarily irreducible (or virtual, i.e. in the Grothendieck group of representations of G), L(τ) and L(τ, s) are defined in the same way.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'. For the Weil-group data of (2.2.7) this is the sheaf L-function (2.2.8.1), whose conventions are planned at WeilConjectures:WC.1 / SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 per the Weil I extraction.

items.name: Example: Γ ≃ 𝐑 (Serre's setting)
items.statement: Suppose Γ ≃ 𝐑 and fix an isomorphism of the extension G with G^0 × Γ. Let x_v^0 be the component of x_v in G^0. The situation is entirely described by the compact group G^0, the family of conjugacy classes x_v^0 in G^0 and the family of real numbers Nv > 1. Axioms (A), (B) become: the infinite product ∏_v (1 − Nv^{−s})^{−1} converges absolutely for ℛ(s) > 1. This situation is considered by Serre [11], I A2.
items.note: Illustrative; the case Γ ≃ 𝐑 is treated by reference to Serre, Abelian ℓ-adic representations, I A2. Used in (2.1.9) for ζ. No atlas stage plans this abstract framework beyond DWP.5's use.

items.name: Example: Weil group of a curve over 𝐅_q
items.statement: Let X_0 be a smooth absolutely irreducible curve over 𝐅_q, K its field of fractions and x̄ a geometric point of X_0. Let G be the extension 0 → π_1(X, x̄) → W(X_0, x̄) →^{deg} 𝐙 → 0, with ω_1(n) = q^{−n}, Σ = |X_0| and x_v the geometric Frobenius F_v. Then ω_{−1}(x_v) = Nv. Condition (A″) is not in general satisfied (but cf. the remarks after (A″)). Conditions (B) are satisfied. The functions L(τ, s) are the Artin L-functions attached to the irreducible representations of Gal(K̄/K) unramified on X_0, or rather these L-functions deprived of the local factors outside |X_0| and translated in s.
items.note: Here π_1(X, x̄) (profinite) is not compact-by-Γ in the locally compact sense unless one passes to images in a linear group, as in (2.2). FunctionFieldArithmetic:FA.5 plans Artin local factors for finite Galois covers, not L-functions of arbitrary continuous representations of W(X_0, x̄).

items.name: Abstract Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin non-vanishing theorem
items.statement: With the hypotheses and notation of (2.1.1), suppose that the function L(τ) extends to a meromorphic function of τ for ℛ(τ) ≥ 1 and that, in this region ℛ(τ) ≥ 1, it is holomorphic except for a simple pole at ω_1. Then the function L(τ) does not vanish for ℛ(τ) = 1, except for at most one representation τ_0, of dimension 1 and defined by a character ω_1ε with ε of order 2.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'then the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. Proof: (2.1.4.1)–(2.1.4.6) give ν(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0 for ν(τ) the pole order of L at τω_1; the theorem then follows from Lemma (2.1.5). Used in (2.2.9) (and hence (2.2.10)).

items.name: Logarithmic derivative of L as a sum over Frobenius classes
items.statement: For a representation τ (not necessarily irreducible) put L′(τ) = (d/ds) L(τ, s)|_{s=0}. In the domain of convergence: (2.1.4.1) −(L′/L)(τ) = Σ_{v∈Σ, n>0} log Nv · Tr τ(x_v^n). The same holds for τ virtual. For τ unitary and σ real > 1, ω_σ τ is in the domain of convergence and (2.1.4.1) applied to ω_σ·τ reads: (2.1.4.2) −(L′/L)(ω_σ τ) = Σ_{v∈Σ, n>0} (log Nv · (Nv)^{−nσ}) Tr τ(x_v^n).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'. The Euler-product logarithmic-derivative identity; the Weil I analogue (1.14.2) was marked planned at WC.1/SF.2 in the Weil I extraction.

items.name: Fourier (–Laplace) transform of a measure on G
items.statement: Let μ be a measure on G, or even on the set of conjugacy classes of G. For every unitary virtual representation τ of G put (2.1.4.3) μ̂(τ) = ∫ Tr τ(g) dμ. The integral converges if the total mass of |μ| is finite; the function τ ↦ μ̂(τ) is then called the Fourier transform of μ. If τ is not required to be unitary one speaks likewise of the Fourier–Laplace transform.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'.

items.name: Positivity of the Fourier transform of a positive measure at ρ⊗ρ̄
items.statement: If μ is positive, of finite total mass, then for every unitary virtual representation ρ one has (2.1.4.4) μ̂(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0 (for μ ≥ 0).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. Immediate since Tr(ρ⊗ρ̄)(g) = |Tr ρ(g)|² ≥ 0.

items.name: −L′/L(ω_σ τ) is the Fourier transform of a positive finite measure
items.statement: Formula (2.1.4.1) expresses that, for σ > 1, Λ_σ(τ) = −(L′/L)(ω_σ τ) is the Fourier transform of the positive measure of finite total mass (2.1.4.5) μ_σ = Σ_{v∈Σ, n>0} log Nv · Nv^{−nσ} · δ[x_v^n] on G (δ[a] the Dirac measure at a). Hence for every unitary virtual representation ρ of G with real character ≥ 0, Λ_σ(ρ) ≥ 0 for σ > 1; in particular, for every unitary virtual representation ρ: (2.1.4.6) Λ_σ(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0 (σ > 1).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'.

items.name: Pole orders ν satisfy ν(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0
items.statement: For τ ∈ Ĝ, let ν(τ) be the order of the pole (minus the order of the zero) of L at τω_1; extend ν by additivity to the Grothendieck group of unitary representations of G. For τ in this group the function −(L′/L)(τ·ω_s) has only simple poles, and its residue at τω_1 (τ ∈ Ĝ) is ν(τ). Letting σ tend to 1 in (2.1.4.6), one finds for every unitary virtual representation ρ of G: ν(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument … Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'. Under the hypotheses of (2.1.4) ν(1) = 1, ν(τ) = ν(τ̄), and ν(τ) ≤ 0 for τ ≠ 1, so Lemma (2.1.5) applies.

items.name: Lemma on integer-valued functions on Ĝ with ν(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0
items.statement: Let ν be an integer-valued function on Ĝ. Suppose: a) for the trivial representation 1, ν(1) = 1; b) ν(τ) = ν(τ̄); c) ν(τ) ≤ 0 for τ ≠ 1; d) extending ν by additivity to the Grothendieck group of unitary representations of G, one has ν(ρ⊗ρ̄) ≥ 0 for every unitary representation ρ of G. Then ν(τ) = 0 for τ ≠ 1, except for at most one representation τ_0 of dimension one defined by a character of order two.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. In this lemma G appears only through its unitary representations, so it may be replaced by a compact group (its closure in the product of its unitary representations), reducing to Variant (2.1.6).

items.name: Variant of (2.1.5) for a compact group
items.statement: Same statement as (2.1.5), but this time G is a compact group (and Ĝ the set of isomorphism classes of its irreducible representations).
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. Proved in (2.1.8) from Lemma (2.1.7). Characters and multiplicities [ρ:τ] = ∫ \overline{ρ(g)} τ(g) dg with Haar probability measure dg: planned at tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/CompactGroups Layers 0 and 6.

items.name: Existence of ρ with [ρ⊗ρ̄ : τ] ≥ (1−ε) dim τ · [ρ⊗ρ̄ : 1] on a finite set T
items.statement: Let T be a finite set of irreducible representations of the compact group G. For every ε > 0 there exists a representation ρ of G such that [ρ⊗ρ̄ : τ] ≥ (1 − ε) dim τ · [ρ⊗ρ̄ : 1] for all τ ∈ T.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. Proof: the algebra X of complex linear combinations of characters is stable under φ(g) ↦ φ̄(g) and φ(g) ↦ φ(g^{−1}) and dense in the continuous central functions on G (Peter–Weyl; planned at tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/CompactGroups Layers 5–6 as L²/uniform density, not in this central uniform form). Choose ρ_0 ∈ X real, strictly positive, with ρ_0(g) = ρ_0(g^{−1}), a neighbourhood V of e with |τ(g) − τ(e)| < ε_1 τ(e) (τ ∈ T) and ∫_{G−V} |ρ_0|² ≤ ε_2 ∫_G |ρ_0|²; make its coefficients integers, write ρ_0 = Σ n(χ)χ = ρ⁺ − ρ⁻ and put ρ = ρ⁺ + ρ⁻. Then [ρ⊗ρ̄ : τ] = [ρ_0⊗ρ̄_0 : τ] + 2[ρ⁺⊗ρ̄⁻ + ρ⁻⊗ρ̄⁺ : τ] ≥ ∫|ρ_0|²τ ≥ (1−ε)τ(e)∫|ρ_0|² = (1−ε)dim(τ)[ρ⊗ρ̄ : 1]. The printed choice 'ε_1 + ε_2 < ε' does not quite suffice for the last inequality (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E33).

items.name: Σ_τ dim τ · ν(τ) ≥ 0, hence (2.1.6)
items.statement: Let T be a finite subset of Ĝ with 1 ∉ T and ρ as in (2.1.7). Since ν(σ) ≤ 0 for σ ≠ 1: 0 ≤ ν(ρ⊗ρ̄) = Σ_σ [ρ⊗ρ̄ : σ]ν(σ) ≤ [ρ⊗ρ̄ : 1]ν(1) + Σ_{τ∈T} [ρ⊗ρ̄ : τ]ν(τ) ≤ [ρ⊗ρ̄ : 1]·(ν(1) + (1−ε) Σ_{τ∈T} dim(τ)·ν(τ)). Letting ε tend to 0 and T grow, Σ_{τ∈Ĝ} dim τ · ν(τ) ≥ 0, and (2.1.6) follows.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. The final step (unstated): with ν(1) = 1, ν ≤ 0 integer-valued off 1 and ν(τ) = ν(τ̄), at most one τ ≠ 1 has ν(τ) ≠ 0, and it must be self-conjugate of dimension 1, i.e. a character of order 2.

items.name: Riemann ζ as an instance; Mertens' inequality and non-vanishing on ℛs = 1
items.statement: With the notation of (2.1.2), the case of the Riemann zeta function corresponds to G^0 = {e}, Σ = the set of primes, and Np = p. One has −ζ′(s)/ζ(s) = Σ_{p,n} log p · p^{−ns}, so that for σ > 1 the function Λ_σ(t) = −ζ′(σ+it)/ζ(σ+it) is the Fourier transform of the positive measure Σ_{p,n} log p · p^{−nσ} · δ[n log p]. It is therefore a positive (definite) function in the sense of Bochner; in particular it satisfies the inequality 3ℛΛ_σ(0) + 4ℛΛ_σ(t) + 2ℛΛ_σ(2t) ≥ 0, from which Mertens deduces the theorem of Hadamard and de la Vallée-Poussin that ζ does not vanish for ℛs = 1.
items.note: Mathlib has the conclusion: riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/Nonvanishing.lean:413, 'The Riemann Zeta Function does not vanish on the closed half-plane re s ≥ 1'), proved via the 3–4–1 Euler-factor positivity DirichletCharacter.re_log_comb_nonneg (same file, line 244). The printed inequality has coefficient 2 on ℛΛ_σ(2t) (3 + 4cos θ + 2cos 2θ = (1 + 2cos θ)² ≥ 0, also valid; the classical Mertens form has 1). Explains the chapter title; the model for (2.1.4). Printed 'det Λ_σ(t)' (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E34).

items.name: Hypotheses (C), (D) for equidistribution
items.statement: It is classical that non-vanishing of L(τ) for ℛ(τ) = 1 implies an equidistribution of the x_v; the case Γ ≃ 𝐑 is treated in detail in Serre [11], I A2. For Γ ≃ 𝐙 make the hypotheses: (C) the function L(τ) has a meromorphic continuation to ℛ(τ) ≥ 1; in this domain it has a simple pole at ω_1 and no other pole, and it does not vanish for ℛ(τ) = 1; (D) Γ is isomorphic to 𝐙.
items.note: Equidistribution (2.1.10)–(2.1.13) is not planned by DWP.5 (which plans only the positivity/non-vanishing argument) nor elsewhere; the Chebotarev roadmaps are for number fields, and DWP.3 plans a function-field Chebotarev density statement for finite quotients only. (C) is verified for curves in (2.2.9).

items.name: Conjugacy-class space G^♮ and measures μ^♮, dg, μ_0, μ_0^♮
items.statement: Let z be a central element of G of degree d > 0. The space G^♮ of conjugacy classes of G is the quotient of G by the compact group G/z^𝐙 acting by inner automorphisms. It is the disjoint union of the G^♮_n, G^♮_n the set of conjugacy classes of degree n, and multiplication by z^k induces an isomorphism of G^♮_n with G^♮_{n+kd}. Consider on G and G^♮ the measures: μ^♮ = Σ_{v∈Σ, n>0} deg(v) q^{−n deg(v)} δ[x_v^n]; dg = the Haar measure on G for which G^0 has volume 1; μ_0 = the product of dg by the characteristic function of the open set where ω_{−1} > 1; μ_0^♮ = the projection of μ_0 on G^♮.
items.note: Setup for (2.1.11)–(2.1.13). Not planned.

items.name: Holomorphy of the Fourier–Laplace transform of μ^♮ − μ_0^♮ on ℛ(τ) ≥ 0
items.statement: If (C) and (D) are satisfied, the Fourier–Laplace transform of μ^♮ − μ_0^♮ (which converges for τ ∈ G̃, ℛ(τ) > 0) extends to a holomorphic function of τ for ℛ(τ) ≥ 0.
items.note: Proof: by (2.1.4.1) the Fourier–Laplace transform of μ^♮ is −(1/log q)(L′/L)(ω_1·τ); that of μ_0^♮ vanishes outside the ω_s and equals q^{−s}/(1 − q^{−s}) at ω_s; in ℛ(τ) ≥ 0 both are meromorphic with only a simple pole, of residue 1/log q, at ω_0. (Printed 'de μ' for 'de μ^♮', PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E35.) Not planned.

items.name: Equidistribution of Frobenius classes (Γ ≃ 𝐙)
items.statement: To compare μ^♮ and μ_0^♮ on G^♮_n, bring them back to a G^♮_i with 0 ≤ i < d by translation by a power of z. Under hypotheses (C) and (D), for every i, the measure z^{−n}(μ^♮ | G^♮_{i+nd}) on G^♮_i converges vaguely to z^{−n}(μ_0^♮ | G^♮_{i+nd}) as n → ∞.
items.note: By well-known arguments (Serre [11], I A1), (2.1.12) is equivalent to (2.1.13). The limit z^{−n}(μ_0^♮ | G^♮_{i+nd}) is independent of n (μ_0^♮ is z-invariant in positive degrees). Used later for Sato–Tate type equidistribution, deferred to (3.5) (p. 196). Not planned.

items.name: Weyl-criterion form: ∫_{G^♮_n} τ (μ^♮ − μ_0^♮) → 0
items.statement: For every unitary representation τ of G, with character still denoted τ, one has ∫_{G^♮_n} τ(g)(μ^♮ − μ_0^♮) → 0 as n → ∞.
items.note: Proof: for n > 0 put a_n = ∫_{G^♮_n} τ(g)(μ^♮ − μ_0^♮). At τ·ω_s the Fourier–Laplace transform of μ^♮ − μ_0^♮ equals Σ a_n q^{−ns}; by (2.1.11) the power series Σ a_n t^n is holomorphic for |t| ≤ 1, hence on a slightly larger disc, so a_n decays like a geometric series. Not planned.

items.name: Complex group G_𝐂, extension of 𝐙 by G_𝐂^0, and its compact form G_𝐑
items.statement: Conventions (0.7) are in force. Let G_𝐂 be a group scheme over 𝐂, extension of 𝐙 by an algebraic group G_𝐂^0 whose neutral component G_𝐂^00 is semisimple: (2.2.1.1) 0 → G_𝐂^0 → G_𝐂 → 𝐙 → 0. By (1.3.10) the centre Z_𝐂 of G_𝐂 maps onto a subgroup of finite index of 𝐙, so G_𝐂/Z_𝐂 is an algebraic group (of finite type). Choose a maximal compact subgroup U of G_𝐂/Z_𝐂 and let G_𝐑 be its inverse image in G_𝐂. The intersection G_𝐑^0 of G_𝐑 with G_𝐂^0 is a maximal compact subgroup of G_𝐂^0, and there is an exact sequence (2.2.1.2) 0 → G_𝐑^0 → G_𝐑 → 𝐙 → 0.
items.note: Structure theory of complex algebraic groups (maximal compact subgroups, all conjugate). DWP.5 plans (2.2.10) but not this group-theoretic machinery; tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/LieGroups and ReductiveGroupsPartII mention maximal compact subgroups for real Lie/reductive groups but do not plan this extension-of-𝐙 construction. Used to put Frobenius classes into a group of type (2.1.1).

items.name: Elements of G_𝐑 conjugate in G_𝐂 are conjugate in G_𝐑
items.statement: Two elements of G_𝐑 that are conjugate in G_𝐂 are conjugate in G_𝐑.
items.note: Proof: for a compact group K, conjugacy classes are separated by characters of irreducible complex representations, and these extend to algebraic representations of the complexification K_𝐂; hence two elements of K conjugate in K_𝐂 are conjugate in K. Apply this to the compact group G_𝐑/Z′, Z′ the subgroup of G_𝐑 generated by a central element of nonzero degree, noting that two elements of G_𝐑 of the same degree are conjugate if their images in G_𝐑/Z′ are. Separation of conjugacy classes by characters follows from Peter–Weyl (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/RepresentationTheory/CompactGroups Layers 5–6, class-function completeness); the algebraicity of representations of the complexification (Chevalley/Tannaka) is not planned. Gives uniqueness in (2.2.6).

items.name: Semisimple/unipotent elements and Jordan decomposition in G_𝐂
items.statement: An element of G_𝐂 is called semisimple if its image in the algebraic group G_𝐂/Z_𝐂 is, and unipotent if it lies in G_𝐂^0 and is unipotent in that algebraic group. Every element g of G_𝐂 can be written uniquely as a product g = g_s g_u = g_u g_s with g_s semisimple and g_u unipotent. This follows from the same fact for G_𝐂/Z_𝐂 and from the fact that the unipotent elements of G_𝐂 map bijectively onto those of G_𝐂/Z_𝐂.
items.note: Tau Ceti has the multiplicative Jordan decomposition in GL(V) over a perfect field (tauceti:LinearMap.GeneralLinearGroup.eq_jordanDecomposition_iff, TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/JordanChevalley/Multiplicative.lean:246; existence at line 139), not for elements of an abstract algebraic group or of this extension G_𝐂; so marked missing. Used in (2.2.6).

items.name: Monodromy data: morphism of extensions W(X_0, x̄) → G with conditions a), b), c)
items.statement: Let X_0 be a scheme of finite type over 𝐅_q, normal and geometrically connected, with base point x̄ ∈ X. The Weil group W(X_0, x̄) is an extension (1.1.13.1) of 𝐙 by the geometric fundamental group π_1(X, x̄). Let there be a morphism of extensions from 0 → π_1(X, x̄) → W(X_0, x̄) → 𝐙 → 0 to 0 → G^0 → G → 𝐙 → 0 (identity on 𝐙), satisfying: a) G^0 is an algebraic group over 𝐐̄_ℓ, extension of a finite group by a semisimple group (this implies that G has faithful linear representations); b) G^0 can be defined over a sufficiently large finite extension E of 𝐐_ℓ in 𝐐̄_ℓ, and G^0(𝐐̄_ℓ) is the union of the topological groups G^0(F), F a finite extension of 𝐐_ℓ in 𝐐̄_ℓ containing E; the first vertical arrow π_1(X, x̄) → G^0(𝐐̄_ℓ) factors through a continuous homomorphism of π_1(X, x̄) into some G^0(F), and the image of π_1(X, x̄) is Zariski-dense in G^0; c) there exists a linear representation V of G, whose restriction to G^0 has finite kernel, such that the corresponding lisse sheaf is ι-mixed.
items.note: Consequences recorded in the text: for every linear representation (V, τ) of G^0 (resp. G), V^{G^0} = V^{π_1(X, x̄)}; each linear representation (V, τ) of G defines an ℓ-adic representation of W(X_0, x̄), hence a lisse sheaf 𝓕_0(τ) with an isomorphism of W(X_0, x̄)-representations 𝓕_0(τ)_x̄ ≃ V, and V^{G^0} = V^{π_1(X, x̄)} = H^0(X, 𝓕(τ)). By (2.2.8)(i), 𝓕_0(τ) is then ι-mixed for every (V, τ); conjecture (1.2.9) would imply c) always holds. Printed 'G(F)' and 'W_1(X_0, x̄)' (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E36, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E37). Geometric monodromy group formalism; not planned as such (DWP.5 plans 2.2.10 only).

items.name: Example: the Zariski closure group of a semisimple ι-mixed lisse sheaf
items.statement: Let 𝓕_0 be an ι-mixed lisse sheaf on X_0, V = 𝓕_{0x̄}, and suppose the restriction to π_1(X, x̄) of the representation V of W(X_0, x̄) is semisimple (for example, 𝓕_0 semisimple). Define G as in (1.3.7); the proof of (1.3.9) shows that the hypotheses of (2.2.4) are satisfied. Extending scalars from 𝐐̄_ℓ to 𝐂 via ι gives an exact sequence (2.2.1.1); choose G_𝐑 as in (2.2.1).
items.note: Relies on (1.3.7), (1.3.9) of an earlier section. The situation used in (2.2.10).

items.name: Semisimple part of Frobenius is conjugate into the compact form
items.statement: Let v ∈ |X_0| and let ιF_v be the image of a geometric Frobenius F_v ∈ W(X_0, x̄) under the composite W(X_0, x̄) → G →^ι G_𝐂. The semisimple component (ιF_v)_s of ιF_v is conjugate to an element of G_𝐑, and the latter is unique up to G_𝐑-conjugacy.
items.note: Uniqueness from (2.2.2). Existence: take V as in (2.2.4) c) with constituents V_α; replacing V by ⊕V′_α, V′_α obtained from V_α by torsion (1.2.7), one may assume G acts on V through G/Z′ with deg Z′ of finite index in 𝐙; the sheaves from the constituents are punctually ι-pure of determinantal weight 0 (cf. (1.3.12)), hence of weight 0, so every Frobenius eigenvalue has |ια| = 1; thus τ(ιF_v)_s generates a relatively compact subgroup of GL(V_𝐂); since V_𝐂 is a finite-kernel representation of the algebraic group G_𝐂/Z′_𝐂, τ(ιF_v)_s = τ((ιF_v)_s) and the image of (ιF_v)_s^𝐙 in G_𝐂/Z′_𝐂 is relatively compact, hence in a maximal compact subgroup; these being conjugate, (ιF_v)_s lies in a conjugate of G_𝐑. Uses (1.3.12) (determinantal weights) and (2.2.3). Not planned.

items.name: Frobenius data of type (2.1.1) attached to G_𝐑
items.statement: Let G_𝐑 be as above, an extension of 𝐙 by the compact group G_𝐑^0, and take Σ = |X_0|, x_v = the conjugacy class in G_𝐑 of a conjugate of (ιF_v)_s, and ω_1 : g ↦ q^{−deg(g)}. These data are of type (2.1.1) and satisfy axioms (A) and (B′). The infinite product in (B″) is the one defining the zeta function ζ of X_0; it converges for ℛs > dim X_0 (1.4.6). Hence: if dim X_0 = 1, axioms (A), (B) hold; if dim X_0 = N, they hold if one takes for ω_1 not q^{−deg g} but q^{−N deg g}. The choice (2.2.7) of ω_1 is kept and the statements of (2.1) are modified accordingly when N > 1; for example, for τ unitary the products L(τ, s) converge for ℛs > N.
items.note: x_v well defined by (2.2.6). The convergence for ℛs > dim X_0 is (1.4.6) of an earlier section (Weil I-type Euler product convergence, planned at WC.1 per the Weil I extraction). The data package itself is not planned.

items.name: Representations of G, G_𝐂, G_𝐑 are equivalent; weight of 𝓕_0(τ_ℓ)
items.statement: (i) The functors 'extension of scalars by ι' and 'restriction to G_𝐑' are equivalences of categories: (linear representations of G) → (linear representations of G_𝐂) → (continuous complex representations of G_𝐑). For τ a continuous complex representation of G_𝐑, let 𝓕_0(τ_ℓ) be the sheaf deduced from the corresponding ℓ-adic representation τ_ℓ of W(X_0, x̄). If τ is irreducible, this sheaf is punctually ι-pure of weight −2ℛ(τ) (the print has 2ℛ(τ), see PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E38).
items.note: 'Verification left to the reader.' Relates the L-functions of (2.1) to the ℓ-adic series Z of I.(1.14). Sign: ω_1(g) = q^{−deg g} and F_v has degree deg v, so |τ(F_v)| = q^{−ℛ(τ) deg v} on eigenvalues, i.e. weight −2ℛ(τ) (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E38, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E39). Only used with ℛ(τ) = 0 in (2.2.9)–(2.2.10). Weight bookkeeping conventions: DWP.0 / R34.1; the equivalence of categories (complex representations of a compact form ↔ algebraic representations of the complexification) is not planned.

items.name: L(τ, s) is the sheaf L-function at t = q^{−s}
items.statement: (ii) Put Z(𝓕_0(τ_ℓ), t) = ∏_{x∈|X_0|} det(1 − F_x t^{deg x}, 𝓕_0(τ_ℓ))^{−1}. The function L(τ, s), defined for ℛs large enough, has the following expansion in powers of q^{−s}: (2.2.8.1) L(τ, s) = ιZ(𝓕_0(τ_ℓ), t)|_{t=q^{−s}}.
items.note: Sheaf L-function conventions are planned, as in the Weil I extraction for (1.14.1), under the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting (PR196) supplier via SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 ('Integrate CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers') and WeilConjectures:WC.1 ('Consume the coefficientwise Euler product and determinant formula'). The printed formula places the exponent −1 inside the determinant (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E38, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E39). The comparison with L(τ, s) of (2.1) is immediate from x_v = (ιF_v)_s (semisimplification does not change det).

items.name: For curves, L(τ) satisfies condition (C)
items.statement: If dim(X_0) = 1, the function L(τ) satisfies condition (C) of (2.1.10): meromorphic continuation to ℛ(τ) ≥ 1, a simple pole at ω_1 and no other pole there, and no zero on ℛ(τ) = 1.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'Prove convergence, poles, multiplicities'; the corollary feeds the strict initial bound (2.2.10). Proof: verify the hypotheses of (2.1.4): a) if the irreducible τ is unitary and not of the form ω_{it}, L(τ, s) is holomorphic for ℛs ≥ 1: the restriction of τ to G_𝐑^0 is nontrivial, so is that of τ_ℓ to π_1(X, x̄), the denominator of (2.2.9.1) is 1, conclude by (2.2.8)(ii); b) L(ω_s) = ζ_{X_0}(s) is meromorphic for ℛs ≥ 1 with only a simple pole at ω_s = ω_1 (classical; cohomologically via (2.2.9.1) — (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E40)). Then (2.1.4) gives (C) except possibly for a zero at ω_1·ε with ε of order 2; ε corresponds to a double covering X′_0 of X_0 and ζ_{X′_0}(s) = ζ_{X_0}(s)·L(ω_s·ε) has a simple pole at s = 1, so L cannot vanish there.

items.name: Cohomological expression of Z(𝓕_0(τ_ℓ), t) on a curve
items.note: Grothendieck's trace/rationality formula for a lisse sheaf on a curve (Weil I (1.14.3) analogue), planned per the Weil I extraction convention under the upstream CohomologicalPointCounting supplier at WeilConjectures:WC.1 ('its cohomological rational realization') and SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 ('Integrate CohomologicalPointCounting suppliers', compact support). For τ irreducible unitary nontrivial on G_𝐑^0, H^0_c = H^2_c = 0 (the latter by duality) so Z is the polynomial det(1 − Ft, H^1_c).

items.name: Strict initial weight bound on H^1_c of a pure lisse sheaf on a curve
items.statement: Let X_0 be a smooth curve over 𝐅_q and 𝓕_0 a lisse sheaf, ι-pure of weight β, on X_0. Then if α is an eigenvalue of F on H^1_c(X, 𝓕), one has w_q(α) < β + 2.
items.note: DWP.5 ('Weil II local weights and the analytic preparation'): 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument and the strict initial H¹ weight bound needed to start §3.2'; Sources 'especially … 2.2.10'. Improves the trivial bound w_q(α) ≤ β + 2 of (1.8.2); improved in (3.2). Proof (p. 196): invariant under finite extension 𝐅_q → 𝐅_{q^n} (F ↦ F^n, w_q ↦ w_{q^n}); H^1_c is a sum over connected components, so X_0 absolutely irreducible; the long exact sequence of H^1_c for 0 → 𝓕′_0 → 𝓕_0 → 𝓕″_0 → 0 reduces to 𝓕_0 irreducible; then (2.2.5) applies; passing to a covering (cohomology of X injects into that of a covering) and extension of scalars one may take G = G^0 × 𝐙; with τ_ℓ the natural representation on 𝓕_{0x̄} (G as in (1.3.7)), 𝓕_0 = 𝓕_0(τ_ℓ); reduce by torsion (1.2.7) to β = 0, so τ restricted to G_𝐑 is unitary; by (2.2.9) L(τ·ω_s) is holomorphic and invertible for ℛs ≥ 1 except for a simple pole where τω_s = ω_1; conclude by (2.2.8.1), (2.2.9.1). Consumed by §3 ((3.2)).

items.name: Lefschetz-pencil set-up for an open surface with tame coefficients
items.statement: Let S be a smooth projective surface over an algebraically closed field k, D a divisor with normal crossings on S, V = S − D, j: V ↪ S the inclusion and ℱ a sheaf on V tamely ramified along D; the aim is to study H^*_c(V, ℱ) by Lefschetz pencils. Embed S in a projective space P and sweep it by a pencil of hyperplanes (H_t)_{t∈A*}: A* is a line in the dual projective space P̌, parametrizing the hyperplanes containing a codimension-2 linear subspace A of P (the axis); for t ∈ A*, S_t = S ∩ H_t; S̃ ⊂ S × A* is the space of pairs (x,t) with x ∈ H_t; Ṽ is the inverse image of V in S̃. The first and second projections give the diagram (3.1.1.1): π: S̃ → S, π: Ṽ → V, j: V ↪ S, j: Ṽ ↪ S̃, f: S̃ → A*, f: Ṽ → A*; the fibres of f: S̃ → A* are the S_t.
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Construct the external-product system on C×C and a sufficiently general pencil after finite base extension. Import LPV's geometric existence and local vanishing-cycle operations'. The incidence variety/axis/pencil line are constructed at LPV.3: 'Construct the dual projective space, incidence variety, conormal/dual variety, axis and pencil parameter line ... Identify the incidence total space with the blowup along the smooth codimension-two axis'. Used in (3.2.6) with S = X×X, D the boundary, ℱ = 𝒢 = ℱ⊠ℱ.

items.name: General-position hypotheses (A)–(D) and exceptional points/fibres
items.statement: (A) The axis A is transverse to S and disjoint from D; hence S̃ is smooth, obtained from S by blowing up the finite set S∩A, none of whose points lies on D, so D is identified with a divisor of S̃. (B) The only singularities of f are ordinary quadratic points, none on D. (C) On the normalization D' of D, the only singularities of f are ordinary quadratic points, none above a singular point of D. A point of S is exceptional if it is (a) a critical point of f on S, (b) a critical point of f on D', or (c) a singular point of D; a fibre S_t (t∈A*) is exceptional if it contains an exceptional point, and then t is called exceptional. (D) Each exceptional fibre contains only one exceptional point. Consequently (3.1.1.2) the exceptional fibres are of one of three types: (a) S_t a curve with an ordinary double point with distinct tangents; (b) D tangent to S_t; (c) two branches of D meet on S_t.
items.note: LPV.3 plans the transversality/ordinary-singularity openness for pencils on smooth projective X: 'Prove openness of the required transversality, smooth-axis and ordinary-singularity conditions ... the singular-value set finite with one ordinary quadratic singularity in each singular fiber'. The relative version with a normal-crossings boundary (conditions (C),(D) on D') is used in DWP.6 ('a sufficiently general pencil after finite base extension'); no stage spells out the conditions on D' explicitly.

items.name: Compact-support cohomology of the blown-up open surface
items.statement: The cohomologies of V and Ṽ are related by a canonical isomorphism H^*_c(Ṽ, π*ℱ) ≅ H^*_c(V, ℱ) ⊕ (H^0(V∩A, ℱ)(−1) placed in degree 2).
items.note: Blow-up formula for the blow-up of the finite set S∩A ⊂ V. DWP.4 ('Weil I: dimension induction'): 'Use the blowup cohomology comparison and Leray spectral sequence'; EDC.4 ('Weak Lefschetz, projective bundles and blowups') owns the blowup maps. Only the injectivity (3.1.1.4) is used later.

items.name: Injectivity of π* on compact-support cohomology
items.statement: π*: H^*_c(V, ℱ) ↪ H^*_c(Ṽ, π*ℱ) is injective; indeed the transpose by Poincaré duality of π*: H^*(V, ℱ) → H^*(Ṽ, π*ℱ) is a retraction of (3.1.1.4).
items.note: Used in (3.2.13) to bound Frobenius weights on H^2_c(V,𝒢) by those on H^2_c(Ṽ,π*𝒢). Poincaré duality on the smooth surfaces V, Ṽ: EDC.2 ('Smooth trace, relative purity and Poincaré duality'); the blow-up comparison at EDC.4.

items.name: Leray spectral sequence of the pencil and lissity of R^q f_!
items.statement: E_2^{pq} = H^p(A*, R^q f_! π*ℱ) ⇒ H^{p+q}_c(Ṽ, π*ℱ). The sheaves R^q f_! π*ℱ = R^q f_*(j_! π*ℱ) are lisse except at the exceptional values of f.
items.note: Leray for f_! = f_* ∘ j_! (S̃ proper over A*); lissity away from exceptional values via local acyclicity of the tame pair. DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Analyze Leray and the weight-integral constituents of R¹f_*'. Used in (3.2.13).

items.name: Vanishing cycles at an exceptional value and the specialization sequence
items.statement: Let t be an exceptional value of f, A*_(t) the henselization of A* at t (a strictly henselian trait) and η̄ a geometric generic point of A*_(t). Apply vanishing-cycle theory to the inverse image of (S̃, j_!π*ℱ) over A*_(t). The vanishing-cycle sheaves Φ^q = Φ^q(j_!π*ℱ) are concentrated at the exceptional point x of S_t, and there is a long exact sequence … →∂ (R^q f_! π*ℱ)_t → (R^q f_! π*ℱ)_η̄ → Φ^q_x →∂ …
items.note: LPV.0: 'Construct specialization and the triangle i*K→RΨ_f(j*K)→RΦ_f(K)→ ... Show smoothness/local acyclicity gives the expected vanishing-cycle vanishing ... Prove the long exact specialization sequence'. Here the sheaf is j_!π*ℱ (tame along D), so local acyclicity away from x uses tameness; DWP.6 plans 'the coefficient-specific local calculation of Weil II3.1'.

items.name: Filtration with constant graded pieces near D under unipotent local monodromy
items.statement: Assume moreover (E): the local monodromy of ℱ around D is unipotent. For d ∈ D let S_(d) be the strict localization of S at d and V_(d) the inverse image of V in S_(d). Hypothesis (E) ensures that the inverse image of ℱ on V_(d) admits a finite filtration F (by lisse subsheaves) such that the Gr^i_F(ℱ) are constant on V_(d). Write Gr^i_F(ℱ)_d for the fibre at d of the constant extension of Gr^i_F(ℱ) to S_(d); it is H^0(V_(d), Gr^i_F(ℱ)).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Reduce via finite covers to the stated unipotent/tame situation'; 'prove the coefficient-specific local calculation of Weil II3.1'. Unipotent-monodromy linear algebra is LPV.1.

items.name: The orientation group ε(B)
items.statement: If B is a set with two elements, ε(B) is a group equipped with two opposite isomorphisms with Z, indexed by B; for example Λ²Z^B or Z^B/(Z diagonal).
items.note: Elementary bookkeeping device for the sign ambiguity of vanishing cycles (branches of S_t at a node, points of D over a tangency, branches of D). Not an atlas item; LPV.2 plans an 'orientation ambiguity' of the vanishing module but not this Z-torsor. Trivial to formalize (e.g. the quotient Z^B/diagonal).

items.name: Vanishing cycles at a node of S_t (case (a))
items.statement: Case (a) (x a critical point of f on S, off D). Since j_!π*ℱ is lisse at x, Φ^*_x(j_!π*ℱ) = Φ^*_x(Q̄_ℓ) ⊗ ℱ_x, and Φ^*_x(Q̄_ℓ) is given by Picard–Lefschetz theory in relative dimension 1: Φ^q_x(Q̄_ℓ) = 0 for q ≠ 1 and, B being the two-element set of branches of S̃_t at x, Φ^1_x(Q̄_ℓ) = Q̄_ℓ(−1) ⊗ ε(B). In total: (3.1.3.1) Φ^q_x(j_!π*ℱ) = 0 for q ≠ 1 and (3.1.3.2) Φ^1_x(j_!π*ℱ) ≅ ℱ_x(−1) ⊗ ε(B).
items.note: LPV.2: 'Compute the required quadric cohomology and local nearby/vanishing cycles; prove concentration in the middle degree and identify the rank-one vanishing module, its twist, variation pairing and orientation ambiguity'. The tensoring with a lisse ℱ is the 'coefficient-specific' part of DWP.6.

items.name: Kummer description of the vanishing cycle at a node
items.statement: (Not used later.) The isomorphism (3.1.3.2) comes from isomorphisms (3.1.3.3) Z/ℓ^n ⥲ H^1(W, μ_{ℓ^n}) = Φ^1_x(Z/ℓ^n(1)), where W is the variety of vanishing cycles at x; if u and v are local equations of the two branches of S_t at x, the canonical generator of H^1(W, μ_{ℓ^n}) is defined by the Kummer covering T^{ℓ^n} = u v^{−1}.
items.note: Explicit Milnor-fibre description of the rank-one vanishing module in relative dimension 1; the author says it is not used. LPV.2 identifies the vanishing module and its twist but does not plan this Kummer-cover generator. Recorded for completeness.

items.name: Vanishing cycles at a tangency of D with S_t, constant coefficients (case (b))
items.statement: Case (b) with ℱ = Q̄_ℓ. From the short exact sequence (3.1.4.1) 0 → j_!Q̄_ℓ → Q̄_ℓ → Q̄_ℓD → 0: the Φ^*_x vanish for the constant sheaf Q̄_ℓ since f is smooth at x; for Q̄_ℓD they coincide with the analogous groups computed on D; the long exact Φ^*_x sequence gives (3.1.4.2) Φ^q_x(j_!Q̄_ℓ) ≅ Φ^{q−1}_x(D, Q̄_ℓ). If B is the set of the two points of the henselization D_(x) above η̄, then (3.1.4.3) Φ^q_x(j_!Q̄_ℓ) = 0 for q ≠ 1 and (3.1.4.4) Φ^1_x(j_!Q̄_ℓ) = Q̄_ℓ ⊗ ε(B).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'prove the coefficient-specific local calculation of Weil II3.1 for the possible singularities of this sheaf'. The relative-dimension-0 quadratic point on D (two points of D_(x) over η̄, Φ^0 = Q̄_ℓ⊗ε(B)) is the 0-dimensional case of LPV.2's ordinary quadratic singularity.

items.name: Vanishing cycles at a tangency, unipotent coefficients (case (b))
items.statement: In the general case (hypothesis (E)), with F a filtration as in (3.1.2), one finds by dévissage that (3.1.4.5) Φ^q_x(j_!π*ℱ) = 0 for q ≠ 1, and that Φ^1_x(j_!π*ℱ) admits a filtration F with (3.1.4.6) Gr^i_F Φ^1_x(j_!π*ℱ) = Gr^i_F(ℱ)_x ⊗ ε(B).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'prove the coefficient-specific local calculation of Weil II3.1'. Used in (3.2.9) to show Φ^1 has successive quotients ι-pure of integer weight.

items.name: Vanishing cycles where two branches of D meet on S_t, constant coefficients (case (c))
items.statement: Case (c): let B be the two-element set of branches of D through x and i the projection into S or S̃ of the normalization D' of D. Near x there is an exact sequence (3.1.5.1) 0 → j_!Q̄_ℓ → Q̄_ℓ → i_*Q̄_ℓ → Q̄_ℓx ⊗ ε(B) → 0. Since f is smooth at x and f∘i is smooth at the two points of D' above x, the Φ^*_x vanish for Q̄_ℓ and i_*Q̄_ℓ, whence (3.1.5.2) Φ^q_x(j_!Q̄_ℓ) = Φ^{q−2}_x(x, Q̄_ℓx ⊗ ε(B)). The Φ^q_x(x, Q̄_ℓx ⊗ ε(B)) vanish for q ≠ −1 and Φ^{−1}_x(x, Q̄_ℓx ⊗ ε(B)) = Q̄_ℓ ⊗ ε(B).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'prove the coefficient-specific local calculation of Weil II3.1 for the possible singularities of this sheaf'. Uses the vanishing-cycle formalism of LPV.0 (vanishing for smooth maps; value on a skyscraper at a point of the special fibre).

items.name: Vanishing cycles at a crossing of D, unipotent coefficients (case (c))
items.statement: This gives Φ^q_x(j_!Q̄_ℓ) and, by dévissage, Φ^q_x(j_!π*ℱ): (3.1.5.3) Φ^q_x(j_!π*ℱ) = 0 for q ≠ 1 and, for F as in (3.1.2), (3.1.5.4) Gr^i_F Φ^1_x(j_!π*ℱ) = Gr^i_F(ℱ)_x ⊗ ε(B).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'prove the coefficient-specific local calculation of Weil II3.1'. Together with (3.1.3), (3.1.4): at every exceptional point Φ^* is concentrated in degree 1 and, under (E), is filtered with pieces Gr^i_F(ℱ)_x ⊗ ε(B) (twisted by (−1) in case (a)).

items.name: Real coefficients of the H^i_c characteristic polynomials of an ι-real pure sheaf on a curve
items.statement: (Conventions (0.7).) Let X_0 be a smooth absolutely irreducible curve over F_q and ℱ_0 a lisse sheaf on X_0 which is punctually ι-pure and ι-real. Then the polynomials ι det(1 − F t, H^i_c(X, ℱ)) have real coefficients.
items.note: Proof: in Grothendieck's formula (1.4.7.1) the local factors are real and so the rational function is real; with β the weight of ℱ_0, by (1.4.4) and (2.2.10) the zeros of ι det(1−Ft, H^2_c) are exactly the poles of absolute value q^{−(β+2)/2}, a set stable under conjugation; H^0_c is 0 if X_0 is affine and dual to H^2_c(X, ℱ^∨(−1)) if projective; hence the numerator ι det(1−Ft, H^1_c) is real. DWP.6's Sources: 'Weil II §§3.1–3.2, including3.2.3–3.2.15'; DWP.5 constructs the ι-real estimate ('Weil II's generalization of the fundamental estimate for ι-real systems'). Trace formula/L-function convention: WC.0/WC.1, SF.2 (as in the Weil I extraction). Used in (3.2.7).

items.name: Real coefficients without absolute irreducibility
items.statement: The arguments of (0.5) show that (3.2.1) holds without the hypothesis of absolute irreducibility.
items.note: Needed because the fibres Y_1 of the pencil in (3.2.7) are curves over k(x) that need not be absolutely irreducible. DWP.6 Sources cover §3.2; the component/Weil-restriction argument of (0.5) is outside this range.

items.name: Purity of H^i(X, j_*ℱ) on a projective smooth curve
items.statement: Let X_0 be a projective smooth curve over F_q, j: U_0 ↪ X_0 a dense open subset and ℱ_0 a lisse sheaf, punctually ι-pure of weight β, on U_0. Then the eigenvalues α of F on H^i(X, j_*ℱ) satisfy w_q(α) = β + i.
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'For j:U₀↪C₀ with C₀ smooth proper and F₀ lisse punctually ι-pure of weight w, prove H^i(C,j_*F) pure of weight w+i (Weil II3.2.3)'. Key input of the fundamental theorem (3.3.1). Proof completed in (3.2.15).

items.name: H^1(X, j_*ℱ) as parabolic cohomology
items.statement: For i = 1, the group H^1(X, j_*ℱ) is also the image of H^1_c(U, ℱ) in H^1(U, ℱ) (cf. the 'parabolic' cohomology groups met in the study of modular forms).
items.note: Standard consequence of the localization sequences for j_! ⊂ j_* on a curve. DWP.6: 'Retain the boundary monodromy weights needed to pass from j_*F to compact support on U'; 'Prove the correct duality for j_*F; do not substitute Rj_*F without its boundary comparison'. Also the key identity in (3.7.1).

items.name: Lemma (3.2.4)(k): weight bound 1 + 2^{−k} on H^1_c
items.statement: Let k ≥ 0. Let U_0 be a smooth curve over F_q and ℱ_0 a lisse sheaf on U_0, punctually ι-pure of weight 0. Then the eigenvalues α of F on H^1_c(U, ℱ) satisfy w_q(α) ≤ 1 + 2^{−k}. (Proved by induction on k; for k = 0 it follows from (1.8.2).)
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Use the strict initial estimate of DWP.5 and the §3.2 iteration δ↦δ/2, with all inequalities/rounding justified, to get the sharp upper bound'. DWP.5: 'the strict initial H¹ weight bound needed to start §3.2' (the base case (1.8.2)).

items.name: Corollary (3.2.5)(k): extension to H^1_c(X, 𝒢) of a sheaf generically lisse
items.statement: If U_0 is a dense open subset of a curve X_0, j: U_0 ↪ X_0, and 𝒢_0 a sheaf on X_0, the long exact cohomology sequence of 0 → j_!j*𝒢_0 → 𝒢_0 → 𝒢_0/j_!j*𝒢_0 → 0 gives a surjection H^1_c(U, j*𝒢) = H^1_c(X, j_!j*𝒢) ↠ H^1_c(X, 𝒢). If U_0 is smooth and j*𝒢_0 is lisse and punctually ι-pure of weight β, then by (3.2.4)(k) and a twisting argument (1.2.7) the eigenvalues of F on H^1_c(X, 𝒢) satisfy w_q(α) ≤ β + 1 + 2^{−k}.
items.note: Surjectivity because 𝒢_0/j_!j*𝒢_0 is punctual, so its H^1_c vanishes. DWP.6 plans the §3.2 iteration and sources '3.2.3–3.2.15'. Used in (3.2.11) for H^1(A*, Gr_G^i R^1f_!π*𝒢).

items.name: Set-up for the induction step: the surface X_0 × X_0 and hypotheses (A)–(C)
items.statement: Let k ≥ 0; assume (3.2.4)(k) and its corollary (3.2.5)(k), and prove (3.2.4)(k+1), first under hypotheses (A)–(C). Let X_0 be the projective smooth curve containing U_0 as a dense open. (A) The sheaf ℱ on U is tamely ramified, with unipotent local monodromy, at the points of X − U. Let S_0 = X_0 × X_0, V_0 = U_0 × U_0, D_0 the normal-crossings divisor of S_0 complementary to V_0; embed S_0 in a projective space P_0 and sweep S_0 by a pencil of hyperplanes with axis A_0 ⊂ P_0, chosen so that (B) S, D and the pencil with axis A satisfy the general-position conditions (A)–(D) of (3.1.1); and, for convenience, (C) the exceptional points (3.1.1) are defined over F_q. The arrows of (3.1.1.1) come by extension of scalars from morphisms of F_q-schemes, denoted by the same letters f, π, j. Let T_0 be the finite set of exceptional values of f, W_0 its complement in A*_0 and w: W_0 ↪ A*_0. Let 𝒢_0 = ℱ_0 ⊠ ℱ_0 = pr_1*ℱ_0 ⊗ pr_2*ℱ_0. Hypotheses (A)–(E) of (3.1) are satisfied by (S, D, 𝒢) and the pencil with axis A.
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Construct the external-product system on C×C and a sufficiently general pencil after finite base extension. Import LPV's geometric existence and local vanishing-cycle operations'.

items.name: w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 is a direct factor of an ι-real sheaf
items.statement: The lisse sheaf w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 on W_0 is a direct factor of an ι-real sheaf. Proof: since 𝒢 is lisse and punctually ι-pure of weight 0, ℋ_0 = 𝒢_0 ⊕ 𝒢_0^∨ is punctually ι-pure and ι-real, and it suffices that R^1f_!π*ℋ_0 is ι-real on W_0. This follows from (3.2.1): for x ∈ |W_0|, Y_1 the fibre of f at x (a curve over k(x)) and Y deduced from Y_1 by extension of scalars from k(x) to F via a geometric point x̄ localized at x, (3.2.7.1) (R^1f_!π*ℋ_0)_x̄ = H^1(Y, π*ℋ), and one applies (3.2.2) for i = 1 to the restriction of π*ℋ to Y_1.
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): sources 'Weil II §§3.1–3.2, including3.2.3–3.2.15'; DWP.5: 'Construct Weil II's generalization of the fundamental estimate for ι-real systems, irreducible constituents and compatible pairings'. (3.2.7.1) is proper base change for f_! (SF.2). (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E41)

items.name: R^1f_!π*𝒢 has no sections supported in T
items.statement: The sheaf R^1f_!π*𝒢 has no section with support in T.
items.note: Proved jointly with (3.2.9) from the injectivity on the left of the five-term sequence (3.2.9.1). DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Analyze Leray and the weight-integral constituents of R¹f_*'.

items.name: Extension of the filtration G to R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 over A*
items.statement: By (3.2.8), R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 is identified with a subsheaf of w_*w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0. By (3.2.7) and (1.5.1), w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 admits a finite filtration G^• with successive quotients lisse and punctually ι-pure. It is extended to a finite filtration of R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 by G^iR^1f_!π*𝒢_0 = w_*G^iw*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 ∩ R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 (intersection in w_*w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Analyze Leray and the weight-integral constituents of R¹f_*'. The existence of the ι-pure filtration (1.5.1) for ι-real sheaves is DWP.5 ('irreducible constituents').

items.name: Non-constant graded pieces have integer weight
items.statement: If Gr^i_G R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 does not become constant on A*, its restriction to W_0 is punctually ι-pure of integer weight.
items.note: Proof: by (1.8.4) the local representations of ℱ_0 at points of X_0 − U_0 have filtrations with ι-pure quotients of integer weight, unramified by (A); by tensor product 𝒢_0 has near each x ∈ S_0 − V_0 a filtration F with Gr^i_F(𝒢_0)_x̄ ι-pure of integer weight; the vanishing cycles (3.1), concentrated at x and zero for i ≠ 1, give the five-term sequence (3.2.9.1) and short exact sequences 0 → Gr^i_G(R^1f_!π*𝒢_0)_t̄ → Gr^i_G(R^1f_!π*𝒢_0)_η̄ → A^i_t → 0 with A^i_t a subquotient of Φ^1_x̄, hence of integer weight; if A^i_t ≠ 0 then by (1.8.4) the ι-pure w*Gr^i_G(R^1f_!π*𝒢_0) has integer weight; if all A^i_t = 0 the sheaf Gr^i_G is lisse, hence constant on the simply connected projective line A*. DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Analyze Leray and the weight-integral constituents of R¹f_*. The constant constituents on ℙ¹ contribute no H¹'.

items.name: Five-term specialization sequence at an exceptional value
items.statement: Let t̄ ∈ T, x ∈ S̃ the exceptional point above it (3.1.1), t and x their images in T_0 and S_0, η̄ a geometric point localized at the generic point of A*_(t) and η the generic point of A*_0(t). Since the vanishing cycles computed in (3.1) are concentrated at x and vanish in degrees i ≠ 1, there is an exact sequence (3.2.9.1) 0 → (R^1f_!π*𝒢_0)_t̄ → (R^1f_!π*𝒢_0)_η̄ → Φ^1_x̄ → (R^2f_!π*𝒢_0)_t̄ → (R^2f_!π*𝒢_0)_η̄ → 0 (printed with π_* in place of π*).
items.note: Instance of (3.1.1.6) with Φ^q = 0 for q ≠ 1 ((3.1.3.1), (3.1.4.5), (3.1.5.3)). LPV.0 ('Prove the long exact specialization sequence from the actual triangle, including inertia and Galois equivariance'); LPV.2 ('construct the exact five-term sequence in those degrees'). Injectivity on the left gives (3.2.8).

items.name: Constituents of w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 have weight < 2
items.statement: The constituents of w*R^1f_!π*𝒢_0 are punctually ι-pure of weight < 2.
items.note: Proof: the constituents are known to be punctually ι-pure; it suffices to test the weights at one point; the lemma follows from (2.2.10) (cf. (3.2.7.1)), i.e. the strict bound on H^1_c of a curve with weight-0 coefficients. DWP.5: 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument and the strict initial H¹ weight bound needed to start §3.2'; DWP.6 plans the §3.2 argument.

items.name: Weight bound on E_2^{11} = H^1(A*, R^1f_!π*𝒢)
items.statement: The eigenvalues α of F on E_2^{11} = H^1(A*, R^1f_!π*𝒢) satisfy w_q(α) ≤ 2 + 2^{−k}.
items.note: Proof: check on each H^1(A*, Gr^i_G R^1f_!π*𝒢). If Gr^i_G is constant, this H^1 vanishes since A* is a projective line. Otherwise w*Gr^i_G R^1f_!π*𝒢 has integer weight < 2 ((3.2.9), (3.2.10)), hence weight ≤ 1, and (3.2.5)(k) applies. This integrality step is the heart of the square-improvement. DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'The constant constituents on ℙ¹ contribute no H¹. Use the strict initial estimate of DWP.5 and the §3.2 iteration δ↦δ/2'.

items.name: Weight bounds on E_2^{02} and E_2^{20}
items.statement: The eigenvalues α of F on E_2^{02} = H^0(A*, R^2f_!π*𝒢) and on E_2^{20} = H^2(A*, R^0f_!π*𝒢) satisfy w_q(α) ≤ 2.
items.note: Proof: (3.2.7.1) and a double application of (1.4.4) show that for x ∈ |A*_0| the eigenvalues of F_x on R^if_!π*𝒢_0 (i = 0, 2) satisfy w_{N(x)}(α) ≤ β + i (here β = 0, the weight of 𝒢), whence the statement. DWP.6 Sources: '3.2.3–3.2.15'. Weight bounds for H^0_c, H^2_c of curves and for H^0, H^2 over a curve are the elementary (1.4.4) estimates (DWP.5 sources §1).

items.name: Proof of (3.2.4)(k+1) under the hypotheses of (3.2.6)
items.statement: By (3.2.11), (3.2.12) and the spectral sequence (3.1.1.5), the eigenvalues α of F on H^2_c(Ṽ, π*𝒢) satisfy w_q(α) ≤ 2 + 2^{−k}. The same estimate holds a fortiori for the eigenvalues of F on H^1_c(U, ℱ) ⊗ H^1_c(U, ℱ) ⊂ H^2_c(V, 𝒢) ⊂ H^2_c(Ṽ, π*𝒢) (Künneth and (3.1.1.4)). In particular, if α is an eigenvalue of F on H^1_c(U, ℱ), then w_q(α²) ≤ 2 + 2^{−k}, hence w_q(α) ≤ 1 + 2^{−(k+1)}.
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Use the strict initial estimate of DWP.5 and the §3.2 iteration δ↦δ/2, with all inequalities/rounding justified, to get the sharp upper bound'. Künneth for H_c from the PR196 supplier (DWP.6 dependencies: 'PR196 Künneth/base change/Leray').

items.name: End of the proof of (3.2.4)(k+1): removing hypotheses (B), (C) and (A)
items.statement: The validity of (3.2.4)(k+1) is invariant under a preliminary finite extension of the base field F_q (cf. proof of (2.2.10)). Since over F there exist embeddings and pencils satisfying (B), they exist over a finite extension of F_q; over a larger finite extension (C) holds. This proves (3.2.4)(k+1) under (A) alone. The monodromy theorem gives a finite surjective covering g: U'_0 → U_0 with U'_0 smooth such that g*ℱ_0 on U'_0 satisfies (A); one concludes since g* injects H^*_c(U, ℱ) into H^*_c(U', g*ℱ).
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Reduce via finite covers to the stated unipotent/tame situation, proving trace-splitting and the resulting injection/direct-summand statements with ℚ_ℓ coefficients'. Quasi-unipotence (the 'monodromy theorem'): LPV.1 ('Prove the quasi-unipotence theorem in the geometric coefficient setting actually used'). Existence of pencils over a finite extension: LPV.3 ('Over F_q, prove a nonempty admissible open has a point over some finite extension').

items.name: Proof of (3.2.3) by the upper bound and duality
items.statement: The assertion (3.2.3) is trivial for i = 0 or 2 (1.4). For i = 1, the validity of (3.2.5)(k) for all k ensures w_q(α) ≤ β + 1. Apply this to the sheaf ℱ_0^∨(1). Since H^1(X, j_*ℱ) and H^1(X, j_*ℱ^∨(1)) are in duality (SGA 4½ [dualité] (1.3) and (2.1)), one finds w_q(α^{−1}) ≤ (−β − 2) + 1, i.e. w_q(α) ≥ β + 1. The theorem follows.
items.note: DWP.6 ('Pure local systems on curves and the square-improvement argument'): 'Prove the correct duality for j_*F; do not substitute Rj_*F without its boundary comparison'; 'Apply duality to get the matching lower bound'. The upper bound uses (3.2.5)(k) for X, 𝒢 = j_*ℱ, U = U.

items.name: Fundamental theorem: R^if_! preserves mixedness with weight bound
items.statement: Let f: X → Y be a morphism of schemes of finite type over Z and ℱ a sheaf on X. If ℱ is mixed of weights ≤ n, then, for each i, R^if_!ℱ is mixed of weights ≤ n + i.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'For a separated finite-type morphism f:X₀→Y₀ over a finite field and a mixed constructible rational sheaf F of weights≤w, prove R^i f_!F mixed of weights≤w+i. Construct Weil II3.3.1's dévissage in sheaf, source and target ...'. Note the paper states it over Z (weights measured at closed points of Y, all of finite residue field); DWP.7 phrases it over a finite field — the Z-version reduces to fibres by (c). The main theorem of the paper.

items.name: Dévissage (a) in ℱ
items.statement: Let 0 → ℱ' → ℱ → ℱ'' → 0 be exact. If the R^if_!ℱ' and R^if_!ℱ'' are mixed of weights ≤ n + i, so are the R^if_!ℱ. If the R^if_!ℱ and R^if_!ℱ'' are mixed of weights ≤ n + i, so are the R^if_!ℱ' (apply the long exact cohomology sequence). If the sequence is split and R^if_!ℱ is mixed of weights ≤ n + i, so is R^if_!ℱ'.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Construct Weil II3.3.1's dévissage in sheaf, source and target ... propagate bounds through exact sequences/Leray'. The second assertion uses that mixed sheaves of weights ≤ w are stable under kernels of maps to/extension (the image of R^{i−1}f_!ℱ'' in R^if_!ℱ' has weights ≤ n+i−1 ≤ n+i).

items.name: Dévissage (b) in X
items.statement: Let j: U ↪ X be an open subset of X with complement i: S → X. If the R^i(fj)_!j*ℱ and the R^i(fi)_!i*ℱ are mixed of weights ≤ n + i, so are the R^if_!ℱ (apply (a) to 0 → j_!j*ℱ → ℱ → i_*i*ℱ → 0).
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'dévissage in sheaf, source and target'.

items.name: Dévissage (c) in Y
items.statement: Let j: V ↪ Y be an open subset of Y with complement i: T → Y. If the conclusion of (3.3.1) becomes true after base change by i and by j, it holds at the start (apply the base change theorem).
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'dévissage in sheaf, source and target ... Verify all finiteness and base-change hypotheses at each step'. Proper base change for f_!: SF.2.

items.name: Dévissage (d): transitivity
items.statement: If f = gh and the R^ig_!R^jh_!ℱ are mixed of weights ≤ n + i + j, then the R^kf_!ℱ are mixed of weights ≤ n + k (apply the Leray spectral sequence R^pg_!R^qh_! ⇒ R^{p+q}f_!).
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'propagate bounds through exact sequences/Leray'.

items.name: Dévissage (e): universal homeomorphisms of the base
items.statement: If g: Y' → Y is a universal homeomorphism, it suffices to verify (3.3.1) after base change by g (étale cohomology does not 'see' such a base change). Examples: Y' = Y_red, or Y' = the normalization of Y (assumed normal and integral) in a purely inseparable extension of its function field.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'finite/universal-homeomorphism reductions'. Topological invariance of the étale site: SF.2.

items.name: Dévissage (f): relative dimension 0
items.statement: If f has relative dimension 0 and ℱ is punctually pure, then f_!ℱ = R^0f_!ℱ is punctually pure of the same weight, and the R^if_!ℱ vanish for i ≠ 0. For such f, one concludes by (a).
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'finite/universal-homeomorphism reductions'. Stalks of f_!ℱ for quasi-finite f are sums of induced representations of stalks; purity is preserved since Frobenius at a point of degree d over y corresponds to the d-th root bookkeeping of DWP.0 ('finite-field base extension').

items.name: Generic structure of a lisse sheaf on a curve over a field
items.statement: If C is a curve over a field K and ℱ a lisse sheaf on C, the following hold for K perfect, hence in general after a finite purely inseparable extension of K: (α) there is a finite subset of C_red whose complement C' is smooth over K; (β) there is a finite surjective covering u: D → C', where D is the complement in a projective smooth curve D̄ of a divisor E étale over K, such that u*ℱ is tamely ramified along E; ℱ is a direct factor of u_*u*ℱ = Ru_*u*ℱ.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'generic smooth relative curves, finite covers and spreading out of the boundary'. The direct-factor statement is the trace splitting for a finite (generically étale) cover with Q_ℓ coefficients; the tame cover exists by Abhyankar-type/semistable-reduction arguments not spelled out in the paper.

items.name: Reduction of (3.3.1) to a smooth compactified relative curve with tame lisse sheaf
items.statement: The dévissages (b), (c), (d) reduce to f of relative dimension 1, then (a), (b) to ℱ lisse and punctually pure of weight n. Applying (α), (β) to the fibre of f at a generic point η of Y, standard limit arguments show C', D, … exist with the same properties over a neighbourhood of η in Y_red. By (c), (e) one reduces to this neighbourhood being all of Y_red and Y_red smooth, then by (b), (f), (a) to X being the complement, in X̄ projective and smooth of pure relative dimension 1 over Y, of a divisor D finite étale over Y, with ℱ tamely ramified along D (diagram X ↪j X̄ ↩i D over Y, f̄: X̄ → Y).
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Construct Weil II3.3.1's dévissage in sheaf, source and target, finite/universal-homeomorphism reductions, generic smooth relative curves, finite covers and spreading out of the boundary. Verify all finiteness and base-change hypotheses at each step'.

items.name: Final step of (3.3.1): purity of R^if̄_*j_*ℱ and weights of Gr_M(i*j_*ℱ)
items.statement: In the reduced situation, Rf_!ℱ = Rf̄_*(j_!ℱ). Consider the exact sequence 0 → j_!ℱ → j_*ℱ → i_!i*j_*ℱ → 0 and the filtration induced by the local monodromy filtration M on i_!i*j_*ℱ ((1.8.6) to (1.8.8)). The formation of these sheaves and of M is compatible with passage to fibres. Theorem (3.2.3), applied for all isomorphisms ι, gives that R^if̄_*j_*ℱ is punctually pure of weight n + i, and theorem (1.8.4) (also for all ι) gives that Gr^k_M(i*j_*ℱ), zero for k > 0, is pure of weight n + k on D (1.8.8). The morphism f̄i is finite, and it remains to apply (f), (a).
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Construct Weil II3.3.1's dévissage ...'; the input is DWP.6's export 'Export both the fixed-ι real-weight theorem and the algebraic all-embeddings integer-weight theorem' and DWP.5's local weight theorem ('the weights of boundary invariants of j_*F'). Compatibility of j_* with fibres needs tameness along the étale divisor D.

items.name: Integral sheaves (entier)
items.statement: A sheaf is called integral (entier) if the eigenvalues of the Frobenius elements are algebraic integers. (Used, via SGA 7 XXI 5 on p-adic valuations of Frobenius eigenvalues, to bound weights from below.)
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Integrality and the extra lower bounds0 and2(i−dim X) in3.3.3–4 require the separately supplied integrality/denominator theorem of SGA7 XXI5'. DWP.0 plans 'Integrality remains a separate predicate'.

items.name: Weights of an integral mixed sheaf are ≥ 0
items.statement: The weights of an integral mixed sheaf are necessarily positive (≥ 0): if an algebraic integer α is pure of weight n relative to q and of degree d, its norm is an ordinary integer whose absolute value is the product q^{nd/2} of the absolute values of its complex conjugates, so n ≥ 0.
items.note: Elementary algebraic number theory (nonzero integer norm has |N| ≥ 1). DWP.0 ('Weil q-numbers ... Integrality remains a separate predicate'); used by DWP.7's integral refinement.

items.name: Corollary (3.3.3): weight bounds for integral sheaves
items.statement: Let f: X → Y be a morphism of schemes of finite type over Z and ℱ an integral sheaf on X. If ℱ is mixed of weights ≤ n, then, for each i, R^if_!ℱ is mixed of weights between 0 and n + i. If i exceeds the maximum dimension d of the fibres, the weights lie between 2(i − d) and n + i.
items.note: Proof: by SGA 7 XXI (5.2.2) applied to the fibres of f, the sheaves R^if_!ℱ and R^if_!ℱ(i − d) are integral; combine with (3.3.1) and (3.3.2). DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Integrality and the extra lower bounds0 and2(i−dim X) in3.3.3–4 require the separately supplied integrality/denominator theorem of SGA7 XXI5; prove that theorem's exact application or omit the extra bound from a consumer'.

items.name: SGA 7 XXI (5.2.2): integrality of R^if_!ℱ and R^if_!ℱ(i−d) (cited)
items.statement: For ℱ integral and f with fibres of dimension ≤ d, the sheaves R^if_!ℱ and R^if_!ℱ(i − d) are integral.
items.note: Cited input (SGA 7 XXI, Deligne, 5.2.2), applied to the fibres of f. DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'SGA7 XXI5 is an explicit additional source for the optional integral-eigenvalue refinement, constructed here when used'.

items.name: Corollary (3.3.4): H^i_c over a finite field
items.statement: Let X_0 be a scheme of finite type over F_q and ℱ_0 a mixed sheaf of weights ≤ n on X_0. Then H^i_c(X, ℱ) is mixed of weights ≤ n + i: for each i and each eigenvalue α of F on H^i_c(X, ℱ), α is algebraic and there is an integer w ≤ n + i such that all complex conjugates of α have absolute value q^{w/2}. If ℱ_0 is integral, w ≥ 0. If moreover i exceeds the dimension d of X, w ≥ 2(i − d).
items.note: Case Y = Spec(F_q) of (3.3.1), (3.3.3); in characteristic p one may replace étale sheaves by Weil sheaves. DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Deduce H^i_c(X,F) weights≤w+i'. WC.6: 'For separated finite-type X and mixed sheaves use compact-support weights'.

items.name: Corollary (3.3.5): lower bound for ordinary cohomology on smooth X
items.statement: Let X_0 be smooth of finite type over F_q and ℱ_0 a lisse sheaf mixed of weights ≥ n on X_0. Then H^i(X, ℱ) is mixed of weights ≥ n + i.
items.note: Proof: reduce to X_0 of pure dimension N; ℱ_0^∨ is mixed of weights ≤ −n; by (3.3.3)/(3.3.4) H^{2N−i}_c(X, ℱ^∨)(N) is mixed of weights ≤ −n + (2N − i) − 2N = −n − i; Poincaré duality identifies H^i(X, ℱ) with its dual. DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'For X₀ smooth and F lisse of weights≥w, use Poincaré duality to prove H^i(X,F) weights≥w+i'. Poincaré duality: EDC.2.

items.name: Corollary (3.3.6): the image of H^i_c in H^i is pure
items.statement: Let X_0 be smooth of finite type over F_q and ℱ_0 a lisse sheaf pure of weight n on X_0. Then the image of H^i_c(X, ℱ) in H^i(X, ℱ) is pure of weight n + i.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Therefore for smooth X and lisse pure F the image of H^i_c→H^i is pure of weight w+i'. Combines (3.3.4) and (3.3.5). Used in (3.7.1). SGA 4½ [Sommes trig.] explains the application to trigonometric sums.

items.name: Couples (v(α), v(q^nα^{−1})) attached to a pure algebraic number
items.statement: Let α be an algebraic number, pure of some weight n relative to q, and normalize the p-adic valuations v of Q(α) by v(q) = 1. To α and each such v attach the couple of rational numbers (v(α), v(q^nα^{−1})), where q^nα^{−1} = ᾱ. If α is integral these numbers are ≥ 0. Their sum is n.
items.note: No atlas stage plans these p-adic slope couples (DWP.7 only plans the integrality lower bounds). Used in (3.3.8). Mathlib has p-adic valuations on number fields but nothing about this construction.

items.name: Corollary (3.3.8): location of the p-adic couples of Frobenius eigenvalues
items.statement: Suppose X of dimension ≤ d. In cohomology with proper support (or in ordinary cohomology for X proper), the couple (r, s) of (3.3.7) attached to an eigenvalue of Frobenius on H^i (constant sheaf Q̄_ℓ) lies in a lower triangle of the diagram below; in ordinary cohomology and for X smooth, (r, s) lies in an upper triangle of the same diagram.
