[Diagram: for i ≤ d, the square [0, i]² in the (r, s)-plane cut by the antidiagonal r + s = i, the lower triangle labelled H^i_c and the upper triangle labelled 'H^i, X lisse'; for i ≥ d, the square [0, d]² containing the square [i − d, d]², cut by the line r + s = i, the lower triangle of the inner square labelled H^i_c and the upper triangle of the outer square labelled 'H^i, X lisse'.] The verification is easy. One can show that, in ordinary cohomology, (r, s) always lies in the square union of the two triangles.
items.note: Deduced from (3.3.4) (with the integrality input SGA 7 XXI 5) and the duality method (3.3.5). The triangles are given only by the printed diagrams; the reading above (inner square [i−d,d]² for i ≥ d, from the integrality of R^if_!ℱ(i−d) and its dual) is our interpretation of the pictures. No atlas stage plans the p-adic (Newton-type) localization; DWP.7 plans only the archimedean integral bounds. The 'square' assertion is stated without proof.

items.name: Corollary (3.3.9): Riemann hypothesis for proper smooth varieties
items.statement: Taking X_0 proper and smooth, H^i(X, Q_ℓ) is pure of weight i; reasoning as in I (proof of (1.7) ⇒ (1.6)) one recovers the main theorem (1.6) of I with 'projective' replaced by 'proper': Let X_0 be a proper smooth variety over F_q. For each i, the characteristic polynomial det(t·1 − F*, H^i(X, Q_ℓ)) has integer coefficients, independent of ℓ (ℓ ≠ p). The complex roots α of this polynomial (the complex conjugates of the eigenvalues of F*) have absolute value |α| = q^{i/2}.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'For smooth **proper** X the whole H^i is pure ... For constant coefficients export the smooth proper nonprojective extension used by WC (3.3.9)'. WC.6: 'Use DWP.7 to extend pure cohomology and the assembled smooth-proper conclusions beyond projective varieties'; WC.3 plans the (1.7)⇒(1.6) argument.

items.name: (3.3.10): the fundamental theorem for ι-mixed sheaves with real weights
items.statement: Theorem (3.3.1) holds, with the same proof, with 'mixed' replaced by 'ι-mixed' and n replaced by β ∈ R. The only weights that can occur in R^if_!ℱ are the numbers ≤ β + i congruent mod Z to one of the weights occurring in ℱ. The argument (3.3.2) for bounding weights below no longer applies in this context, but (3.3.4) — except what concerns integral sheaves — and (3.3.5), (3.3.6) hold as stated.
items.note: DWP.7 ('The fundamental direct-image theorem and sharp cohomological bounds'): 'Give the corresponding fixed-ι real-weight version, including the allowed weights moduloℤ; do not infer integer weights from that version alone'; 'ι-mixed real-weight sheaves do not inherit those integrality conclusions'.

items.name: (3.3.11): smoothness may be replaced by a rational-homology-manifold condition
items.statement: In all of this, the hypothesis 'smooth' only appears to justify Poincaré duality. This allows one to replace 'smooth' by 'rational homology manifold': in the ℓ-adic context, 'smooth of pure dimension n' can be replaced by the condition (*) if a is the projection of X_0 to F_q, then Ra^!Q_ℓ = Q_ℓ(n)[2n]. For example, a scheme X_0 which, locally for the étale topology, is a quotient of a smooth scheme of dimension n by a finite group satisfies (*).
items.note: DWP.7 Sources: 'Weil II3.3.1–3.3.11'; the condition Ra^!Q_ℓ uses the exceptional inverse image of EDC.1 ('Construct the right adjoint f^! to the enhanced Rf!'). The finite-quotient example is asserted without proof (trace argument).

items.name: Theorem (3.4.1)(i): decomposition of an ι-mixed sheaf by weights mod Z
items.statement: (Conventions (0.7).) Let ℱ_0 be an ι-mixed sheaf on a scheme X_0 of finite type over F_q. ℱ_0 admits a unique decomposition ℱ_0 = ⊕_{b∈R/Z} ℱ_0(b), the decomposition according to the weight mod Z, in which the punctual ι-weights of ℱ_0(b) all lie in b. This decomposition, in which the ℱ_0(b) are of course almost all zero, is functorial in ℱ_0. Each ℱ_0(b) is deduced by twisting from an ι-mixed sheaf with integer punctual weights.
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): 'Prove Weil II3.4.1: weight-class decomposition moduloℤ; the unique functorial strict weight filtration on lisse mixed sheaves with integral weights; and geometric semisimplicity for punctually ι-pure lisse sheaves on a **normal** base'. Proofs: uniqueness/functoriality (3.4.6), lisse case (3.4.7), general case (3.4.8).

items.name: Theorem (3.4.1)(ii): the punctual weight filtration on a lisse mixed sheaf
items.statement: If the punctual weights of ℱ_0 are integers and ℱ_0 is lisse, ℱ_0 admits a unique finite increasing filtration W by lisse subsheaves, the filtration by punctual weight, such that Gr_i^W(ℱ_0) is punctually ι-pure of weight i. This filtration is functorial in ℱ_0. More precisely, every morphism between lisse ι-mixed sheaves with integer punctual weights is strictly compatible with their filtrations by punctual weight.
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): 'the unique functorial strict weight filtration on lisse mixed sheaves with integral weights'.

items.name: Theorem (3.4.1)(iii): geometric semisimplicity of pure lisse sheaves
items.statement: If ℱ_0 is lisse and punctually ι-pure, and X_0 is normal, then the sheaf ℱ on X is semisimple.
items.note: Proof (3.4.5): for U_0 open in X_0 (normal) and ū a geometric point, π_1(U_0, ū) → π_1(X_0, ū) is surjective, so one may replace X_0 by a smooth dense open U_0. Let ℱ' be the largest semisimple lisse subsheaf of ℱ (the sum of its irreducible subsheaves); by transport of structure it is Frobenius-stable, hence comes from ℱ'_0 ⊂ ℱ_0; put ℱ''_0 = ℱ_0/ℱ'_0. By (3.4.3), as ℱ'_0 and ℱ''_0 are ι-pure of the same weight, the extension ℱ_0 of ℱ''_0 by ℱ'_0 is geometrically trivial; if ℱ'' ≠ 0, lifting a simple subsheaf of ℱ'' into ℱ contradicts maximality; so ℱ'' = 0. DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): 'geometric semisimplicity for punctually ι-pure lisse sheaves on a **normal** base. Construct the Ext¹/Hochschild–Serre comparison and use the H¹ lower bound to kill geometrically nontrivial extensions of equal weights. The conclusion is after base change to the algebraic closure'.

items.name: Lemma (3.4.2): Ext^1 of lisse sheaves over F_q
items.statement: If ℱ_0 and 𝒢_0 are two lisse sheaves on X_0, there is an exact sequence 0 → H^0(X, ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢))_F → Ext^1(ℱ_0, 𝒢_0) → H^1(X, ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢))^F. Here F as exponent (resp. index) denotes invariants (resp. coinvariants) under W(k̄/F_q); Ext^1 is the group of extension classes in the abelian category of sheaves on X_0; the right arrow is pull-back to X: Ext^1(ℱ_0, 𝒢_0) → Ext^1(ℱ, 𝒢) = H^1(X, ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢)), landing in the F-invariant part.
items.note: Proof: a geometrically trivial extension ℰ_0 of ℱ_0 by 𝒢_0 has a splitting φ: ℱ → ℰ over X; the others are φ − f, f ∈ Hom(ℱ, 𝒢); the extension is trivial over X_0 iff φ − f can be chosen F-invariant, i.e. Fφ − φ ∈ Hom(ℱ, 𝒢) is of the form Ff − f, i.e. has zero image in Hom(ℱ, 𝒢)_F; ℰ_0 ↦ (Fφ − φ) is a bijection between geometrically trivial extension classes and Hom(ℱ, 𝒢)_F = H^0(X, ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢))_F. DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): 'Construct the Ext¹/Hochschild–Serre comparison'; the shared continuous Hochschild–Serre is ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.2.

items.name: Lemma (3.4.3): geometrically non-trivial extensions only from higher to lower weight
items.statement: If ℱ_0 and 𝒢_0 are lisse on X_0 smooth, and punctually ι-pure of weights β and γ, then there can exist a geometrically non-trivial extension ℰ_0 of ℱ_0 by 𝒢_0 only if β ≡ γ (mod Z) and β > γ.
items.note: Proof: it suffices that F acting on H^1(X, ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢)) does not have eigenvalue 1; ℋom(ℱ, 𝒢) is lisse of weight γ − β, and by (3.3.5) amplified by (3.3.10) the only weights in its H^1 are γ − β + 1 + n with n ≥ 0 an integer; the weight 0 can only occur for β ≡ γ (mod Z) and β > γ. DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): 'use the H¹ lower bound to kill geometrically nontrivial extensions of equal weights'.

items.name: Lemma (3.4.4): vanishing of Ext^1 between pure lisse sheaves
items.statement: If ℱ_0 and 𝒢_0 are lisse on X_0 smooth, and punctually ι-pure of weights β and γ, then one can have Ext^1(ℱ_0, 𝒢_0) ≠ 0 only if β ≡ γ (mod Z) and β ≥ γ.
items.note: Same proof as (3.4.3) using (3.4.2): the H^0 term is of weight γ − β, so its F-coinvariants vanish unless γ = β. DWP.8 sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'. Used in (3.4.7).

items.name: (3.4.6): stalkwise description of ℱ_0(b) and W_iℱ_0; uniqueness
items.statement: Let x ∈ |X| lie over x_0 ∈ |X_0|. For each β ∈ R let ℱ_x(β) be the sum of the generalized eigenspaces of F_{x_0} for the eigenvalues α of ι-weight β relative to q^{deg(x_0)}. Necessarily ℱ_0(b)_x = ⊕_{β∈b} ℱ_x(β), and, if the punctual weights are integers, (W_iℱ_0)_x = ⊕_{β≤i} ℱ_x(β). This proves uniqueness in (3.4.1)(i), (ii), and functoriality.
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'. Generalized eigenspace linear algebra: DWP.0 ('Use generalized eigenspaces, not an assumed eigenbasis. Prove that different pure weights have disjoint eigenvalue sets and hence no nonzero intertwiner').

items.name: (3.4.7): existence in (3.4.1)(i),(ii) for successive extensions of pure lisse sheaves on smooth X_0
items.statement: Assume X_0 smooth and ℱ_0 a successive extension of lisse punctually ι-pure sheaves. Then (3.4.1)(i), (ii) hold. Proof (formal consequence of (3.4.4) and half-exactness of Ext^1), by induction on the number of extensions: ℱ_0 is an extension of a lisse ℱ''_0 satisfying (i), (ii) by a lisse punctually ι-pure ℱ'_0 of weight β. (i): let b be the class of β in R/Z; by (3.4.4), for b' ≠ b the inverse image of ℱ''_0(b') in ℱ_0 is a trivial extension of ℱ''_0(b') by ℱ'_0; take ℱ_0(b) the inverse image of ℱ''_0(b) and ℱ_0(b') (b' ≠ b) a lifting of ℱ''_0(b'). (ii): β is an integer; by (3.4.4) the inverse image of W_{β−1}ℱ''_0 in ℱ_0 is a trivial extension of W_{β−1}ℱ''_0 by ℱ'_0; for i < β take W_iℱ_0 a lifting of W_iℱ''_0 ⊂ W_{β−1}ℱ''_0, for i ≥ β the inverse image of W_iℱ''_0.
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'.

items.name: Gluing: sheaves on X_0 as triples (j*ℱ, i*ℱ, specialization)
items.statement: Let j: U_0 ↪ X_0 be open with complement i: F_0 → X_0. The functor ℱ_0 ↦ (j*ℱ_0, i*ℱ_0, specialization arrow) is an equivalence between the category of sheaves on X_0 and the category of triples (ℱ'_0, ℱ''_0, s) consisting of a sheaf on U_0, a sheaf on F_0 and a morphism s: ℱ''_0 → i*j_*ℱ'_0.
items.note: Recalled standard gluing (SGA 4 IV 9.5). SF.2 ('localization'); EDC.0 ('Construct cohomology with support as the localization fiber'). No stage names this recollement for abelian sheaves explicitly; used in (3.4.8).

items.name: (3.4.8): proof of (3.4.1)(i),(ii) in general
items.statement: By induction on dim X_0: replacing X_0 by X_{0,red}, there is a dense open j: U_0 ↪ X_0 on which ℱ_0 satisfies the extra hypotheses of (3.4.7); the induction hypothesis applies to the complement F_0. Proof of (i): one must see that the specialization morphism s: i*ℱ_0 → i*j_*j*ℱ_0 sends (i*ℱ_0)(b) into i*j_*((j*ℱ_0)(b)); indeed by (1.8.9) and twisting, the punctual weights of i*j_*((j*ℱ_0)(b)) lie in b, so this sheaf coincides with (i*j_*j*ℱ_0)(b). Proof of (ii): uniqueness being ensured, one may assume by descent that X_0 is normal. Then ℱ_0 = j_*j*ℱ_0 and one takes W_iℱ_0 = j_*W_ij*ℱ_0; this gives Gr_i^Wℱ_0 = j_*Gr_i^W j*ℱ_0, and one applies (1.8.10).
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'; uses DWP.5's local weight theorem ((1.8.9), (1.8.10): weights of i*j_* of a mixed lisse sheaf). The print writes j : U₀ ↪ X for U₀ ↪ X₀ (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E46).

items.name: Variant (3.4.9): weight filtration and geometric semisimplicity for mixed/pure sheaves
items.statement: It follows at once from (3.4.1) that every lisse mixed sheaf admits a filtration by punctual weight by lisse subsheaves, and that every lisse punctually pure sheaf on a normal X₀ is geometrically semisimple (the print omits 'lisse' and the normality of X₀, see PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E47).
items.note: Mixed (not ι-mixed) sheaves have integer weights for all ι, so (3.4.1)(ii) applies. The semisimplicity clause needs the hypotheses of (3.4.1)(iii) (lisse, X_0 normal) — (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E47) DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): 'geometric semisimplicity for punctually ι-pure lisse sheaves on a **normal** base'.

items.name: Sheaves having potentially a property P
items.statement: Let P be a property of sheaves on schemes of finite type over a finite field (e.g. being mixed, being punctually ι-pure, …). A sheaf ℱ on a scheme X of finite type over an algebraically closed field k is said to have potentially the property P if (X, ℱ)/k is deduced by a base change x̄: Spec(k) → S from a system (X_S, ℱ_S) over S — with X_S of finite type over S, S of finite type over Z — such that the restrictions of ℱ_S to the fibres of X_S/S at the closed points of S have the property P.
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'. LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'retaining the specified arithmetic model over an integral finite-type Z[1/ℓ]-base rather than treating “potentially pure” as an empty label'; DWP.9: 'specify a genuine model witnessing potential purity'.

items.name: Example (3.4.11): R^if_*Q_ℓ of a proper smooth map is potentially punctually pure
items.statement: If f: Y → X is proper and smooth, the sheaves R^if_*Q_ℓ are potentially punctually pure. This results from a standard limit argument, to construct f_0: Y_0 → X_0/S_0 proper and smooth, and from (3.3.9) applied to the fibres of f_0.
items.note: DWP.8 ('Mixed complexes, weight filtrations and geometric semisimplicity'): sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'. Spreading out from an arbitrary algebraically closed field: DWP.9 'prove spreading out and smooth proper base change from the finite-field result instead of assuming every object has a finite-field model'; (3.3.9) is DWP.7.

items.name: Corollary (3.4.12): potentially pure lisse sheaves are semisimple
items.statement: Let X be a normal scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field k, and ℱ a lisse sheaf on X. If ℱ is potentially punctually ι-pure, it is semisimple.
items.note: Generalization of (3.4.1)(iii) via the specialization theorem (1.11.1), (1.11.5). DWP.8 sources '3.4.1–3.4.13'.

items.name: Corollary (3.4.13): semisimplicity of R^if_*Q_ℓ for proper smooth f
items.statement: Let S be a normal connected scheme over an algebraically closed field k, and f: X → S a proper smooth morphism. Then the sheaves R^if_*Q_ℓ are semisimple.

items.name: Remark (3.4.14): the case of (3.4.13) needed for hard Lefschetz
items.statement: The key point in the proof of hard Lefschetz given in (4.1.1) is a special case of (3.4.13) in which f is projective and S is a curve (an open of P^1). To treat this case it suffices to have (I.1.6) (to ensure the purity of R^if_{0*}Q_ℓ), (1.11.1) for the specialization argument, and (2.2.10) (Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin) to forbid the eigenvalue 1 in the proof of (3.4.1).
items.note: Dependency remark for §4. DWP.9: 'prove nondegeneracy on the invariant part from **geometric** complete reducibility'. Recorded as a statement of which inputs suffice (a shortcut not using (3.3.1)).

items.name: Set-up of (3.5.1): arithmetic/geometric monodromy groups and their compact forms
items.statement: Take the notations and hypotheses of (2.2): there is a commutative diagram with exact rows 0 → π_1(X, x̄) → W(X_0, x̄) → Z → 0 and 0 → G^0 → G → Z → 0, the vertical maps π_1(X, x̄) → G^0 and W(X_0, x̄) → G being inclusions (with dense image) and the identity on Z; X_0 is normal, geometrically connected of dimension N, and by (2.2.8), for every irreducible representation τ of G_R, the corresponding sheaf ℱ(τ_ℓ) is punctually ι-pure of weight 2ℛ(τ). Let G^♮_{Ri} denote the space of conjugacy classes of degree i of G^♮_R, and μ_0 the measure on G^♮_R defined in (2.1.10).
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). The objects G, G^0, G_R, ℛ(τ), μ_0 are defined in §2 (outside this range).

items.name: Analytic properties of L(τ) for representations of the monodromy group
items.statement: If τ ∈ Ĝ is an irreducible complex representation of G, the product defining L(τ) converges for ℛ(τ) > N. The formula (2.2.8.1), Grothendieck's cohomological interpretation of L-functions (1.4.5.1), and (3.3.4) modified by the second variant (3.3.10), show that L(τ) extends to a meromorphic function on G̃, which has zeros or poles only for ℛ(τ) an integer or half-integer, and that for ℛ(τ) > N − 1/2, L(τ) is holomorphic and invertible except for a simple pole at τ = ω_N. This allows one to apply the equidistribution results (2.1.10) to (2.1.12) (with ω_1 replaced by ω_N, cf. (2.2.7)).
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). Inputs: the trace formula/L-function conventions (WC.0/WC.1, SF.2 as in the Weil I extraction) and (3.3.4)/(3.3.10) (DWP.7). The absence of zeros on ℛ(τ) = N − 1/2 < ℛ < N uses the ι-mixed weight bound H^i_c of weight ≤ 2ℛ(τ)+i and the integrality mod Z of weights.

items.name: Frobenius classes of F_{q^n}-points and the measure identity (3.5.2.1)
items.statement: For every integer n > 0 let F_{q^n} be the degree-n extension of F_q in k̄ and X_(n) the scheme over F_{q^n} deduced from X_0 by extension of scalars; X_(n) is a covering of X_0, corresponding to the subgroup of W(X_0, x̄) of elements of degree divisible by n. Each point x of X_0 with coordinates in F_{q^n} defines a rational point, hence a closed point, of X_(n); F_x denotes a corresponding geometric Frobenius element and its image in W(X_0, x̄), which has degree n; F_x also denotes its image in G, and (ιF_x)_s the conjugacy class in G_R of the elements conjugate to the semisimple part of ιF_x ∈ G_C (2.2.4). If a closed point x_0 of X_0 is the image of a rational point of X_(n), its degree d divides n; conversely if d | n there are d rational points x of X_(n) over x_0, and for each F_x = F_{x_0}^{n/d} (up to conjugacy). On the space of conjugacy classes of W(X_0, x̄) one therefore has the identity of measures (3.5.2.1) Σ_{n>0, x_0∈|X_0|} deg(x) δ[F^n_{x_0}] = Σ_{n>0, x_0∈X_0(F_{q^n})} δ[F_x] (as printed; read deg(x_0) on the left and x ∈ X_0(F_{q^n}) on the right).
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). DWP.3 plans for Weil I 'conjugacy classes in finite étale quotients and the degree congruences imposed by the constant-field extension' but not this measure identity. Printed indices in (3.5.2.1) are slightly off (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E48).

items.name: Theorem (3.5.3): equidistribution of Frobenius conjugacy classes
items.statement: With the notations of (3.5.1), for every i, the measure z^{−n}(q^{−N(nd+i)} Σ_{x∈X_0(F_{q^{nd+i}})} δ[(ιF_x)_s]) on G^♮_{Ri} converges vaguely to μ_0^♮|G^♮_{Ri} = z^{−n}(μ_0^♮|G^♮_{R(nd+i)}) as n → ∞. Here z is a chosen central element of degree d > 0, used to identify the G^♮_{Ri} with one another as i runs through an arithmetic progression of ratio d.
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). Specialization of (2.1.12) using (3.5.2.1) and the analytic input of (3.5.1).

items.name: Example (3.5.4): the H^1 local system of a family of elliptic curves
items.statement: Let f: E_0 → X_0 be a family of elliptic curves parametrized by X_0, and take ℱ_0 = R^1f_*Q_ℓ. Put V = ℱ_{0x̄}. There is a natural isomorphism Λ²V ≅ Q_ℓ(−1), compatible with the action of G. Since G acts on Q_ℓ(−1) by ω_{−1}, the elements of degree n of G act on V with determinant q^n.
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). The Weil pairing / cup product Λ²H^1 ≅ H^2 = Q_ℓ(−1) for a relative elliptic curve is not planned in this form (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli owns abelian-scheme Tate modules; no stage checked for this relative statement).

items.name: Lemma (3.5.5): big geometric monodromy for non-isotrivial elliptic families
items.statement: If the modular invariant j of E/X is non-constant, the group G^0 is the whole group SL(V).
items.note: Proof: let n ≥ 3 be prime to p and X' a connected component of the covering ℐsom(E_n, (Z/n)²) of X: an étale Galois covering with group a subgroup of SL(2, Z/n), on which E_n is trivial, α: E_n ⥲ (Z/n)². With x̄' a base point over x̄, (E, α) defines u: X' → M_n (moduli of elliptic curves with level-n structure). Non-constancy of j makes u dominant, so the image of u: π_1(X', x̄') → π_1(M_n, u(x̄')) has finite index. One knows transcendentally that π_1(M_n) maps onto the subgroup of SL(H^1(E_x̄, Z_ℓ)) of elements ≡ 1 mod n. So the geometric monodromy of ℱ/X contains a finite-index subgroup of SL(H^1(E_x̄, Z_ℓ)). No atlas stage plans this (searched Sato–Tate / modular curve / monodromy stages); ModularCurvesPartII and AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli own M_n but not this ℓ-adic monodromy computation in characteristic p (which here is imported 'par voie transcendante', i.e. via lifting to characteristic 0).

items.name: The compact group SU(2)×Z, Sato–Tate measure and Frobenius angles
items.statement: Suppose j non-constant. Lemma (3.5.5) shows that G_R is SU(2) × Z, acting on ιV ≅ C² by (g, n) ↦ q^{n/2}·g. Identify the set of conjugacy classes in SU(2) with [0, π] by class of diag(e^{iθ}, e^{−iθ}) ↦ θ. The direct image of Haar measure of SU(2) is the measure (2/π) sin²θ dθ on [0, π] (printed (1/2π) sin²θ dθ, see PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E50). For x ∈ X_0(F_{q^n}), define the Frobenius angle θ(x) ∈ [0, π] by requiring that the eigenvalues of ιF_x be the numbers e^{±iθ(x)}·q^{n/2}, i.e. that the curve E_x over F_{q^n} have 1 − 2cos θ(x)·q^{n/2} + q^n rational points (the print has + 2cos θ(x), see PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E51). In G_R ≅ SU(2) × Z one has (ιF_x)_s = (θ(x), n).
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). Mathlib has Haar measure on compact groups (MeasureTheory.Measure.haar) but no SU(2) Weyl integration formula. (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E50, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E51)

items.name: Proposition (3.5.7): Sato–Tate in equal characteristic
items.statement: With the preceding notations (and for j non-constant), as n → ∞ the measure (1/q^{nN}) Σ_{x∈X_0(F_{q^n})} δ[θ(x)] tends vaguely to (2/π) sin²θ dθ, the Sato–Tate probability measure (printed (1/2π) sin²θ dθ, see PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E50).
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Weil II §3.5 function-field equidistribution (searched all roadmaps for equidistribution/Sato–Tate/Haar/Weyl: only number-field or dynamical stages such as ModularityAndLanglandsExtensions ML.3 (automorphic Sato–Tate), ArithmeticDynamics DY.4). DWP.3 plans a closed-point Chebotarev/density argument for Weil I §6, and DWP.5 the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin input (2.2.10), but not (2.1.10)–(2.1.12)/(3.5). The theorem gives in equal characteristic the equidistribution conjectured by Sato–Tate; previously obtained by H. Yoshida (Inv. Math. 19 (1973), 261–277) for certain modular families. The author says the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin theorem of §2 was proved originally to extend Yoshida's result to arbitrary one-parameter families.

items.name: Specialization map for a proper family over a henselian trait
items.statement: Let k be an algebraically closed field, S the spectrum of the henselization of k[T] at the ideal (T), s the closed point of S, η the generic point and η̄ a geometric generic point. Let f: X → S be a proper morphism. There is a specialization morphism sp*: H^*(X_s) → H^*(X_η̄); its image is contained in the invariants under the inertia group Gal(η̄/η). It is the composite (7) sp*: H^*(X_s) ⥲← H^*(X) → H^*(X_η) → H^*(X_η̄), where H^*(X) ⥲ H^*(X_s) is the proper base change isomorphism.
items.note: LPV.0: 'Construct specialization and the triangle i*K→RΨ_f(j*K)→RΦ_f(K)→'; LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'.

items.name: Theorem (3.6.1): local invariant cycle theorem
items.statement: Suppose X essentially smooth over k and X_η̄ smooth over η̄. Then, in Q_ℓ-cohomology, the morphism sp*: H^*(X_s) → H^*(X_η̄)^{Gal(η̄/η)} is surjective.
items.note: LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'. Final step: the functor W_i (part of weight ≤ i) is exact; applied to the cross (8), with W_i(H^{2N−i−1}(X_s)^∨(−N)) = 0 by (3.6.3) and W_iH^i(X_η̄)^I = H^i(X_η̄)^I by (3.6.2), it gives H^i(X_s) ↠ W_iH^i(X_η) ↠ H^i(X_η̄)^I.

items.name: Reduction of (3.6.1) to a situation defined over a finite field
items.statement: A limit argument allows one to assume that S is the henselization at a point s of a curve S' smooth over k, and that f is deduced by base change g: (S, s) → (S', s) from a proper morphism f': X' → S' with X' smooth over k and smooth over S' except above s. Using (1.11.3) one reduces to k the algebraic closure of F_q. For F_q large enough, (f', X', S', s) comes by extension of scalars from (f'_0, X'_0, S'_0, s_0) over F_q. Let (S_0, η_0, s_0) be the henselization of S'_0 at s_0 and f_0: X_0 → S_0 deduced from f'_0 by base change g_0. The Galois group Gal(η̄/η) is the inertia group of Gal(η̄/η_0); the latter acts on the cohomology of X_η̄, which allows one to speak of weights (cf. (1.7.4)).
items.note: LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'. The specialization theorem (1.11.3) for passing from an arbitrary algebraically closed k to F̄_q is outside this range.

items.name: Wang-type exact sequences for cohomology of the generic fibre
items.statement: The Z/ℓ^n cohomology of X_η is computed by the Leray (Hochschild–Serre) spectral sequence of X_η → η: (1) E_2^{pq} = H^p(I, H^q(X_η̄)) ⇒ H^{p+q}(X_η). The inertia I is an extension of Z_ℓ(1) (the ℓ-part of the tame quotient) by a profinite group I' of order prime to ℓ; for every Z/ℓ^n[I]-module V there is a spectral sequence (2) E_2^{pq} = H^p(Z_ℓ(1), H^q(I', V)) ⇒ H^{p+q}(I, V). The I'-invariants V^{I'} have a unique I'-stable complement, on which I' has neither invariants nor coinvariants, giving V^{I'} ≅ V_{I'}; moreover H^q(I', V) = 0 for q > 0, so (2) reduces to (3) H^p(I, V) = H^p(Z_ℓ(1), V^{I'}) = H^p(Z_ℓ(1), V_{I'}). For every ℓ-adic representation V of Z_ℓ(1): (4) H^0(Z_ℓ(1), V) = V^{Z_ℓ(1)}, H^1(Z_ℓ(1), V) = V_{Z_ℓ(1)}(−1), H^p(Z_ℓ(1), V) = 0 for p ≥ 2. Combining (1), (3), (4) gives exact sequences (analogous to the Wang sequences) (5) 0 → H^{i−1}(X_η̄)_I(−1) → H^i(X_η) → H^i(X_η̄)^I → 0.
items.note: LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'. LPV.1: 'Construct tame/wild inertia and the tame character t_ℓ:I→Z_ℓ(1)'. Hochschild–Serre: ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.2 (as for (3.4.2)).

items.name: Local cohomology sequence, duality with support and the cross (8)
items.statement: There is a long exact sequence of Z/ℓ^n cohomology with supports (6) → H^i_{X_s}(X) → H^i(X) → H^i(X_η) →. Since X is essentially étale over X' and X_s ⥲ X'_s, H^i_{X'_s}(X') ⥲ H^i_{X_s}(X). Replacing X'_0 by a connected component, X' is purely of dimension N. H^i_{X'_s}(X') can be interpreted as homology of X'_s: with a the projection of X to Spec(k), the adjunction between Ra_! and Ra^! applied to (Z/ℓ^n)_{X'_s} and Z/ℓ^n[i] on Spec(k) gives a perfect duality with values in Z/ℓ^n(−N) between H^i_{X'_s}(X') and H^{2N−i}(X'_s), i.e. between H^i_{X_s}(X) and H^{2N−i}(X_s). The sequences (5) and (6) thus give a cross of exact sequences (8): horizontally 0 → H^{i−1}(X_η̄)_I(−1) → H^i(X_η) → H^i(X_η̄)^I → 0, vertically H^i(X_s) → H^i(X_η) → H^{2N−i−1}(X_s)^∨(−N), with sp*: H^i(X_s) → H^i(X_η̄)^I the diagonal. By passage to the limit the cross persists in Z_ℓ-cohomology (with lim← H^{i+1}_{X'_s}(X', Z/ℓ^n) on top); possible torsion complicates the duality interpretation, but this disappears in Q_ℓ-cohomology, where (8) holds again. The arithmetic Galois group Gal(η̄/η_0) acts on this cross via its quotient Gal(F/F_q).
items.note: LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'. Duality with supports on the smooth X': EDC.1/EDC.2 (Ra^! and Poincaré duality), EDC.0 ('Construct cohomology with support as the localization fiber').

items.name: Lemma (3.6.2): H^i(X_η̄)^I has weights ≤ i
items.statement: H^i(X_η̄)^I is mixed of weights ≤ i.
items.note: Proof: H^i(X_η̄) is the fibre at η̄ of R^if_{0*}Q_ℓ on S_0; by (3.3.9) applied to the fibres of f_0 this sheaf is pure of weight i (over η_0), and one applies (1.8.8)(i). LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'. Local weight theorem: DWP.5 ('the weights of boundary invariants of j_*F').

items.name: Lemma (3.6.3): H^{2N−i−1}(X_s)^∨(−N) has weights ≥ i+1
items.statement: H^{2N−i−1}(X_s)^∨(−N) is mixed of weights ≥ i + 1. This follows at once from (3.3.4). Although not indispensable, note also that H^i(X_s) is mixed of weights ≤ i.
items.note: X_s is proper, so H^{2N−i−1}(X_s) = H^{2N−i−1}_c has weights ≤ 2N−i−1 by (3.3.4); dualize and twist. LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove Deligne II 3.6.1 for a proper family over the henselization of k[T] at (T), k algebraically closed, with total space essentially smooth over k and smooth generic fiber. Prove specialization onto inertia invariants by its weight-filtered exact-sequence argument and arithmetic spreading/descent'. DWP.7 for (3.3.4).

items.name: (3.6.4): complex-analytic local invariant cycle theorem
items.statement: Let D ⊂ C be the unit disc, f: X → D a proper morphism, with X smooth and f smooth over D* := D − {0}. If f factors through pr_2: P^n(C) × D → D, there is an analogue of (3.6.1): writing X_0 for the special fibre f^{−1}(0) and X_t := f^{−1}(t) another fibre (t ∈ D*), there is a surjective homomorphism H^*(X_0, Q) ↠ H^*(X_t, Q)^{π_1(D*, t)}. This is proved by an argument parallel to (3.6.1), the weight filtration of mixed Hodge theory replacing the one deduced from Frobenius (see J. Steenbrink, Mixed Hodge structure on the vanishing cohomology, Symp. in Math., Oslo, 1976).
items.note: No atlas stage plans the Hodge-theoretic local invariant cycle theorem (limit mixed Hodge structures). tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/HodgeStructures L2 plans mixed Hodge structures and strictness only, not Steenbrink's limit MHS. Stated with a reference, no proof.

items.name: (3.7.1): purity of the parabolic cohomology of Sym^k of an elliptic family
items.statement: Let S_0 be a smooth scheme over F_q, f: E_0 → S_0 a family of elliptic curves parametrized by S_0, and ^kW := Im(H^1_c(S, Sym^k(R^1f_*Q_ℓ)) → H^1(S, Sym^k(R^1f_*Q_ℓ))). For S_0 a curve with projective completion j: S_0 ↪ S̄_0, ^kW can also be described as H^1(S̄, j_*Sym^k(R^1f_*Q_ℓ)). The sheaf R^1f_*Q_ℓ is punctually pure of weight 1; its k-th symmetric power is therefore pure of weight k and, by (3.3.6), ^kW is pure of weight k + 1. Assertion (5.1) of [4] is a special case of this result.
items.note: Application of (3.3.6) (DWP.7: 'for smooth X and lisse pure F the image of H^i_c→H^i is pure of weight w+i') and, for curves, (3.2.3)/(3.2.3-parabolic) (DWP.6). Purity of R^1f_*Q_ℓ of weight 1 is Weil I/DWP.1 (curves/abelian varieties). This makes unnecessary the arguments of [4] (Deligne, Formes modulaires et représentations ℓ-adiques) reducing [4](5.1) to the usual Weil conjecture (I.1.6); [4](5.1) is an essential point of the proof of the Ramanujam–Petersson conjecture cited in (I.8.2). No atlas stage owns the Ramanujam–Petersson application (grep 'Ramanujam' found none); R34.5/R34.6 plan Kuga–Sato purity via DWP.

items.name: (3.7.2.1): Deligne's bound for exponential sums of polynomials
items.statement: Let Ψ: F_p → C* be a non-trivial additive character of F_p. If Q ∈ F_q[X_1, …, X_n] is a polynomial of degree d prime to p whose homogeneous part of degree d, Q_d, defines a smooth projective hypersurface, then |Σ_{x_1,…,x_n∈F_q} Ψ(Tr_{F_q/F_p} Q(x_1, …, x_n))| ≤ (d − 1)^n q^{n/2}.
items.note: Simplified proof of (I.8.4). FF.2 ('Weil and Deligne bounds'): 'State polynomial/rational exponential-sum bounds via curves and l-adic trace functions ... import actual cohomological estimates from WeilConjectures and DeligneWeightsAndPurity'. Deduced from (3.7.2.2)–(3.7.2.3).

items.name: Artin–Schreier sheaf ℱ_0(ΨQ) and the trace formula for the exponential sum
items.statement: Regard Ψ as ℓ-adic-valued rather than complex, via ι, and, as in SGA 4½ [Sommes trigonométriques], define a sheaf ℱ_0(ΨQ) on affine n-space A^n_0 over F_q using Ψ and the Artin–Schreier covering T^p − T = Q of A^n_0. Then (3.7.2.2) Σ_{x_1,…,x_n∈F_q} Ψ(Tr_{F_q/F_p} Q(x_1, …, x_n)) = Σ(−1)^i Tr(F, H^i_c(A^n, ℱ(ΨQ))) (printed with ψ and summation over F).
items.note: FF.2: 'State polynomial/rational exponential-sum bounds via curves and l-adic trace functions'. The Grothendieck trace formula is the SF.2/WC.0 supplier convention (as in the Weil I extraction). The Artin–Schreier sheaf itself is not explicitly named in a stage description; FF.2's acceptance mentions 'Artin-Schreier-trivial functions'.

items.name: (3.7.2.3): cohomology of ℱ(ΨQ) is concentrated in degree n, of dimension (d−1)^n, pure of weight n
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (3.7.2.1): H^i_c(A^n, ℱ(ΨQ)) = 0 for i ≠ n; dim H^n_c(A^n, ℱ(ΨQ)) = (d − 1)^n; and H^n_c(A^n, ℱ(ΨQ)) is pure of weight n.
items.note: Stronger than (3.7.2.1), which follows via (3.7.2.2). Proof via (3.7.3)–(3.7.4): lissity in the universal family, (1.8.12) to reduce to one polynomial, Künneth to n = 1, Q = X^d, then (I.8.11). FF.2 plans the application; DWP.7 the weight input.

items.name: Universal family of polynomials with smooth leading form
items.statement: Let S'_0 be the affine space over F_q parametrizing polynomials in n variables of degree ≤ d, and S_0 the open subset of S'_0 parametrizing those whose homogeneous part of degree d defines a nonsingular hypersurface (i.e. has discriminant ≠ 0). Let Q_S ∈ H^0(S_0, 𝒪_{S_0}[X_1, …, X_n]) be the universal polynomial over S_0; it is a section of the structure sheaf of S_0 × A^n_0 and defines a sheaf ℱ_0(ΨQ_S) on S_0 × A^n_0. Let f be the projection of S_0 × A^n_0 to S_0. The polynomial Q corresponds to a rational point of S_0, and (A^n_0, ℱ_0(ΨQ)) is the fibre of (S_0 × A^n_0, ℱ_0(ΨQ_S)) at that point.
items.note: Parameter space of polynomials and discriminant locus; no atlas stage plans this specific family (FF.2 plans the bound, not this proof route). Needed for the deformation argument (3.7.3)–(3.7.4).

items.name: Lemma (3.7.3): the R^if_!ℱ_0(ΨQ_S) are lisse on S_0
items.statement: The sheaves R^if_!ℱ_0(ΨQ_S) on S_0 are lisse.
items.note: Proof: let P^n_0 be A^n_0 with a hyperplane at infinity H_0 adjoined, f̄: S_0 × P^n_0 → S_0 and j: S_0 × A^n_0 ↪ S_0 × P^n_0. Locally for the étale topology the S-scheme S × P^n with the sheaf j_!ℱ(ΨQ_S) is constant (a product with S): clear on S × A^n, where j_!ℱ(ΨQ_S) is locally constant, and near a point h of H where Q_{Sd} does not vanish (resp. vanishes) there are local coordinates t in which Q_S = t_1^{−d} (resp. Q_S = t_2·t_1^{−d}). Hence (S × P^n, j_!ℱ(ΨQ_S)) is locally acyclic over S_0 (SGA 4½ [Th. finitude] 2.16), and R^if_!ℱ_0(ΨQ_S) = R^if̄_*j_!ℱ_0(ΨQ_S) are lisse (loc. cit., A2). No atlas stage plans this local-acyclicity computation for Artin–Schreier sheaves (LPV.0 plans generic local acyclicity via PR196, FF.2 the bound only).

items.name: (3.7.4): reduction of (3.7.2.3) to Q = Σ X_i^d and then to n = 1
items.statement: The scheme S'_0 is connected, and the sheaves R^if_!ℱ_0(ΨQ_S) are mixed. To prove (3.7.2.3) it therefore suffices, by (1.8.12), to do so for one particular polynomial Q. Take Q = Σ X_i^d. For this choice the sheaf ℱ_0(ΨQ) is the tensor product of the inverse images of analogous sheaves on the n factors A^1_0 of A^n_0, and the Künneth formula reduces (3.7.2.3) to the case n = 1, Q = X^d. For this case, see (I.8.11).
items.note: Uses (3.3.1) (mixedness of R^if_!, DWP.7) and (1.8.12) (a lisse mixed sheaf on a connected base pure at one point is pure; DWP.5/DWP.8 sources §1). The connected base needed is S_0 (an open of the irreducible S'_0; printed S'_0). FF.2 plans the exponential-sum bound; the Gauss-sum computation (I.8.11) is from the Weil I extraction.

items.name: Conventions of §4: base field, coefficients and trivialized Tate twist
items.statement: Throughout §4, except in no. 5, one works over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic p; ℓ is a prime distinct from p, and cohomology groups have coefficients in Z_ℓ, Q_ℓ or Z/m, m a power of ℓ. In (4.1) and (4.3) an isomorphism, over k, between Z_ℓ and Z_ℓ(1) is chosen, which dispenses with writing Tate twists.
items.note: DWP.9: 'The Tate twist is restored from the source's temporary geometric trivialization.' Coefficient conventions reuse EDC.0/SF.2 as in the Weil I extraction. Any formalization must restore twists (e.g. η ∈ H²(X,Q_ℓ(1)), δ ∈ Hⁿ(X_u)(n')).

items.name: Hard Lefschetz theorem
items.statement: Let X be a projective smooth variety over k, 𝓛 an ample invertible sheaf on X and η = c₁(𝓛) ∈ H²(X, Q_ℓ). Suppose X is purely of dimension n. Then for every i ≥ 0 the cup product with ηⁱ, ηⁱ∪ : H^{n−i}(X, Q_ℓ) → H^{n+i}(X, Q_ℓ), is an isomorphism.
items.note: DWP.9: 'For X projective smooth of pure dimension d ... and an ample line bundle L, construct η=c₁(L) and prove η^r:H^(d−r)(X,ℚ_ℓ)→H^(d+r)(X,ℚ_ℓ)(r) is an isomorphism.' Proof by induction on n: the case n=0 is trivial; since c₁(𝓛^{⊗m}) = m c₁(𝓛) one may replace 𝓛 by a tensor power, so assume 𝓛 very ample and admitting a Lefschetz pencil; reduced via (4.1.2)–(4.1.4) to complete reducibility (3.4.13) of the monodromy. Main result of §4; used in (4.3.9), (4.3.10), (4.4) and (4.5).

items.name: Factorization of ηⁱ∪ through a smooth hyperplane section
items.statement: Let 𝓛 be very ample and Y a smooth hyperplane section of X (in the projective embedding defined by 𝓛), so η = cl(Y). Interpreting cup product with η as the composite of restriction H*(X) → H*(Y) with its Poincaré-duality transpose (Gysin) H*(Y) → H*⁺²(X), for i ≥ 1 the map ηⁱ∪ : H^{n−i}(X) → H^{n+i}(X) factors as H^{n−i}(X) → H^{(n−1)−(i−1)}(Y) —η^{i−1}∪→ H^{(n−1)+(i−1)}(Y) → H^{n+i}(X). For i ≥ 2 the outer arrows are isomorphisms by weak Lefschetz (4.1.6); for i = 1, H^{n−1}(X) injects into H^{n−1}(Y) and its transpose H^{n−1}(Y) → H^{n+1}(X) is surjective, so η∪ : H^{n−1}(X) → H^{n+1}(X) is bijective iff (4.1.2) holds.
items.note: DWP.9: 'Reduce to very ample L and a suitable pencil. Use induction, restriction/Gysin adjunction and weak Lefschetz'. Gysin/cycle class η=cl(Y) from EDC.3 (SGA 4½ cited).

items.name: Nondegeneracy of the intersection form on the image of H^{n−1}(X)
items.statement: (cf. SGA7 XVIII (5.2.4).) The intersection form on H^{n−1}(Y) is nondegenerate on the image of H^{n−1}(X). Given the induction hypothesis (theorem (4.1.1) in dimension n−1), theorem (4.1.1) for X and 𝓛 is equivalent to this statement.
items.note: DWP.9 cites 4.1.1–4.1.6 and plans 'prove nondegeneracy on the invariant part from geometric complete reducibility'. Proved by choosing Y = Y_{t₀} in a Lefschetz pencil (SGA7 XVII (2.5)) after replacing 𝓛 by a power, then (4.1.3) + (3.4.13) + (4.1.4).

items.name: Cohomology of pencil fibres as a lisse sheaf with monodromy action
items.statement: Let (Y_t)_{t∈P¹} be a Lefschetz pencil of hyperplane sections of X with Y = Y_{t₀}, and S the set of t for which Y_t is singular. The H^i(Y_t) (t ∈ P¹ − S) are the fibres of a lisse Q_ℓ-sheaf on P¹ − S, and π₁(P¹ − S, t₀) acts on H^i(Y).
items.note: LPV.4: 'On U=P¹−S construct R^n f_*Q_ℓ as a lisse sheaf through PR196 base change, with its cup-product pairing.' Pencil existence from SGA7 XVII (2.5) is LPV.3.

items.name: Image of H^{n−1}(X) equals the monodromy invariants
items.statement: The image of H^{n−1}(X) in H^{n−1}(Y) is the subspace H^{n−1}(Y)^{π₁} of invariants under monodromy (π₁ = π₁(P¹ − S, t₀)).
items.note: DWP.9: 'The invariant-cycle input is LPV's late theorem proved using DWP.7–8, or the precisely scoped lower-dimensional induction statement of Weil II4.1.3; it must not assume the d-dimensional hard Lefschetz conclusion.' Paper: proved in SGA7 XVIII (5.6.10) under the hypothesis that Y satisfies the theorem (the induction hypothesis); over C with integral cohomology SGA7 XIX (4) (conjugated with (4.3.1) and Picard–Lefschetz); a direct Z_ℓ-proof over any k is given in (4.3) (see (4.3.2)–(4.3.3)).

items.name: Complete reducibility of the monodromy on H^{n−1}(Y) (recalled from (3.4.13))
items.statement: H^{n−1}(Y) is a completely reducible representation of π₁(P¹ − S, t₀).
items.note: Cross-section input from §3 (geometric semisimplicity of pure lisse sheaves). DWP.8: 'geometric semisimplicity for punctually ι-pure lisse sheaves on a **normal** base'; DWP.9 'from **geometric** complete reducibility'.

items.name: Nondegeneracy of an invariant form on invariants of a completely reducible representation
items.statement: Let V be a completely reducible linear representation of a group π, equipped with a bilinear form Φ that is π-invariant and nondegenerate. Then the restriction of Φ to V^π is nondegenerate.
items.note: Pure linear algebra; not found in Mathlib/Tau Ceti as a single statement (Mathlib has IsSemisimpleModule and LinearMap.BilinForm.Nondegenerate but no lemma on restriction to invariants). Proof: V = V^π ⊕ W with W a subrepresentation having no trivial quotient; W is Φ-orthogonal to V^π, so Φ = (Φ|V^π) ⊕ (Φ|W). DWP.9: 'prove nondegeneracy on the invariant part from **geometric** complete reducibility.' Applied with V = H^{n−1}(Y) to get (4.1.2).

items.name: Odd Betti numbers of smooth projective varieties are even
items.statement: The Betti numbers of odd index of a nonsingular projective variety X are even.
items.note: DWP.9: 'Export primitive Lefschetz decompositions, nondegenerate primitive pairings and odd-Betti parity under the appropriate smooth projective hypotheses.' Proof: reduce to X connected of pure dimension n; for η = c₁(𝓛), 𝓛 ample, the form Tr(ηⁱxy) on H^{n−i}(X) is nondegenerate by (4.1.1) and Poincaré duality; if n−i is odd it is alternating, so b_{n−i} = b_{n+i} is even. Deligne remarks it should hold without projectivity but he cannot prove it in characteristic ≠ 0.

items.name: Cohomological dimension of the affine complement (input)
items.statement: Let X be projective and smooth, purely of dimension n+1, and Y a smooth hyperplane section (purely of dimension n). In Z/m-cohomology, H^i(X − Y) = 0 for i > n+1 (cohomological dimension of affine varieties, SGA4 XIV (3.2)).
items.note: EDC.4: 'Using the imported affine Artin vanishing theorem and EDC.2–3 localization and duality, prove weak Lefschetz'. Artin vanishing is imported from the upstream EtaleBaseChange supplier.

items.name: Vanishing of compactly supported cohomology of X − Y in low degrees
items.statement: With X, Y as in (4.1.6), since X − Y is smooth, Poincaré duality gives H^i_c(X − Y) = 0 for i ≤ n (Z/m-coefficients).
items.note: EDC.4 plans weak Lefschetz via Artin vanishing and EDC.2 duality ('EDC.2–3 localization and duality').

items.name: Weak Lefschetz theorem (restriction form)
items.statement: With X, Y as in (4.1.6), from the long exact sequence of relative cohomology → H^i_c(X−Y) → H^i(X) → H^i(Y) →∂ one gets: H^i(X) → H^i(Y) is an isomorphism for i < n = dim(Y), and Hⁿ(X) ↪ Hⁿ(Y) is injective. By passage to the limit these results remain true in Z_ℓ- and Q_ℓ-cohomology.
items.note: EDC.4: 'prove weak Lefschetz for a smooth hyperplane section Y of a smooth projective d-fold X: restriction is an isomorphism below d−1 and injective in degree d−1'. Used in (4.1.1) proof, (4.3.2), (4.3.3), (4.3.7).

items.name: Weak Lefschetz theorem (Gysin form)
items.statement: With X, Y as in (4.1.6), the Gysin morphisms, transposes by Poincaré duality of the restriction morphisms, satisfy: H^i(Y) → H^{i+2}(X) is an isomorphism for i > n, and Hⁿ(Y) → H^{n+2}(X) is surjective. These remain true in Z_ℓ- and Q_ℓ-cohomology.
items.note: EDC.4: 'prove its dual Gysin form'.

items.name: Torsion-freeness of H_c^{n+1}(X−Y, Z_ℓ) and of Hⁿ(Y,Z_ℓ)/Hⁿ(X,Z_ℓ)
items.statement: With X, Y as in (4.1.6), in Z_ℓ-cohomology the universal coefficient formula H^i_c(X−Y, Z/ℓ) = H^i_c(X−Y, Z_ℓ) ⊗ Z/ℓ ⊕ Tor₁^{Z_ℓ}(H^{i+1}_c(X−Y, Z_ℓ), Z/ℓ) shows that H^{n+1}_c(X−Y, Z_ℓ) is torsion-free. Hence Hⁿ(Y, Z_ℓ)/Hⁿ(X, Z_ℓ) is torsion-free.
items.note: EDC.4 plans weak Lefschetz but not this integral (Z_ℓ) torsion-freeness refinement; no stage mentions it. Used implicitly in the Z_ℓ statements of (4.3).

items.name: Local theory: the vanishing cycle δ of an ordinary quadratic degeneration
items.statement: Let f: X → S be as in (I.4.2) (proper, over a henselian trait, smooth outside one ordinary quadratic singular point of the special fibre), of relative dimension n; write n = 2n' or 2n'+1. Let δ ∈ Hⁿ(X_η̄)(n') be the vanishing cycle; it is well defined up to sign. These results (the local theory of (I.3), (I.4), including the Picard–Lefschetz formula for the inertia action) hold in Z/m-, Z_ℓ- or Q_ℓ-cohomology; the proof for Z/m-cohomology, from which the others follow, is in SGA7.
items.note: LPV.2: 'identify the rank-one vanishing module, its twist, variation pairing and orientation ambiguity ... In the odd-n case prove the Picard–Lefschetz formula ρ(σ)x=x+ε_n t_ℓ(σ)⟨x,δ⟩δ ... In the even-n tame branch prove the quadratic-character reflection formula under p≠2.' Recalled from Weil I (I.3)–(I.4).

items.name: Local monodromy for n even and p = 2
items.statement: In the case n even and p = 2 (excluded in (I.4.3)), the inertia group I admits several characters of order 2. For one of them, depending on the ordinary quadratic singularity of f, the local monodromy is still given by the formula of loc. cit. (the reflection x ↦ x − (−1)^{n'}(x,δ)δ through that character).
items.note: LPV.2 plans the even-n reflection formula only 'under p≠2'; LPV.3 acceptance mentions only a 'characteristic-2 odd-fiber-dimension pencil'. The p = 2, n even case, which is the purpose of (4.2), is not planned. Proof cited to SGA7.

items.name: Image of the special fibre cohomology is the orthogonal of δ
items.statement: In the situation of (4.2.1), the image of Hⁿ(X_s) in Hⁿ(X_η̄) is the orthogonal of δ.
items.note: LPV.2: 'prove specialization is an isomorphism outside degrees n and n+1 and construct the exact five-term sequence in those degrees'; the corollary follows from that sequence. Used in (4.3.2).

items.name: Inertia invariants equal the orthogonal of δ (Z_ℓ, Q_ℓ)
items.statement: In Z_ℓ- or Q_ℓ-cohomology, the image of Hⁿ(X_s) in Hⁿ(X_η̄) (the orthogonal of δ) is also the subspace of invariants under the inertia group I.
items.note: Proof: the term (x,δ)δ in the Picard–Lefschetz formula is zero iff (x,δ) = 0 — clear if δ is not torsion, and if δ is torsion, (x,δ) is identically zero. LPV.4: 'Construct E^⊥, identify the common fixed space of the local transvections'.

items.name: Global setup of a Lefschetz pencil and the dual variety
items.statement: Notation of (I.5.6): X ⊂ P is a connected nonsingular projective variety of dimension n+1, (X_t)_{t∈D} a Lefschetz pencil of hyperplane sections of X, S the set of exceptional t ∈ D for which X_t is singular, j: U → D the inclusion of the complementary open; n = 2n' or 2n'+1. D is identified with a line of the dual projective space P^∨, and X^∨ ⊂ P^∨ denotes the image of X under the correspondence 'the hyperplane H is tangent to X at x'.
items.note: LPV.3: 'Construct the dual projective space, incidence variety, conormal/dual variety, axis and pencil parameter line.'

items.name: Transverse Lefschetz pencil
items.statement: A Lefschetz pencil is called transverse if D is transverse to X^∨ (in particular D ∩ X^∨ = ∅ if X^∨ is not a hypersurface). In the exceptional case (p = 2, n even) a Lefschetz pencil is not automatically transverse.
items.note: LPV.3 plans 'openness of the required transversality, smooth-axis and ordinary-singularity conditions' but not this notion of transversality of D to the dual variety nor the characteristic-2 distinction.

items.name: Path between geometric points (SGA1 V (5.7))
items.statement: A path between two geometric points ā and b̄ of a scheme S is an isomorphism between the functors 'fibre at ā' and 'fibre at b̄' from the category of étale coverings of S to (Sets).
items.note: LPV.4: 'Transport local vanishing cycles along explicit étale paths.' Mathlib has fibre functors of Galois categories (CategoryTheory.PreGaloisCategory.FiberFunctor) but no named notion of étale path of a scheme.

items.name: Vanishing cycle transported along a path
items.statement: For every path c, drawn on U, from u to a geometric generic point η̄_t of D_(t) (t ∈ S), one has Hⁿ(X_u, Z_ℓ) ≅ Hⁿ(X_{η̄_t}, Z_ℓ), whence a vanishing cycle ±δ_c in Hⁿ(X_u, Z_ℓ)(n') (printed '(m)').
items.note: LPV.4: 'Transport local vanishing cycles along explicit étale paths. Define E as their span'. Twist (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E55)

items.name: The set of vanishing cycles
items.statement: The set of vanishing cycles is the set of the cycles ±δ_c for c and t ∈ S varying.
items.note: LPV.4: 'Transport local vanishing cycles along explicit étale paths ... prove independence of path choices as a monodromy-stable subspace, not independence of the individual oriented vectors.'

items.name: Vanishing part Ev of Hⁿ(X_u)
items.statement: The vanishing part of Hⁿ(X_u) is the subspace generated by the λδ (λ ∈ Z_ℓ(−n'), δ vanishing).
items.note: LPV.4: 'write E for the vanishing-cycle subspace ... Define E as their span'. Denoted Ev(Y) from (4.3.1) on.

items.name: π₁(U,u) is topologically generated by conjugates of the inertia groups
items.statement: Since the projective line D is simply connected, the fundamental group π₁(U, u) is topologically generated by the conjugates of the inertia groups I_t for t ∈ S.
items.note: LPV.5: 'Prove the required topological generation of the geometric monodromy image by those local operators'. Also used in (4.3.6) and (4.3.2).

items.name: Monodromy group generated by Picard–Lefschetz transvections/reflections
items.statement: The monodromy group, image of π₁(U, u) in GL(Hⁿ(X_u, Z_ℓ)), is topologically generated by the images of the conjugates of the I_t: for n odd, by the transvections x ↦ x + λ(xδ)δ, λ ∈ Z_ℓ(1) the ℓ-primary quotient of the tame inertia group; for n even, by the reflections x ↦ x − (−1)^{n'}(xδ)δ (one has (δ,δ) = (−1)^{n'}·2).
items.note: LPV.5 (generation by local operators) with LPV.2's Picard–Lefschetz formula. Deligne adds that an unwritten theory of vanishing cycles over bases of dimension > 1 should show all ±δ are conjugate for any transverse pencil and the monodromy group independent of the transverse pencil; he proves only the weaker (4.2.6) (cf. SGA7 XVIII (6)).

items.name: Conjugacy of vanishing cycles for a generic Lefschetz pencil
items.statement: For a generic Lefschetz pencil, the vanishing cycles, taken up to sign, are all conjugate under the monodromy group.
items.note: LPV.5: 'Prove conjugacy, up to the orientation sign, of local vanishing cycles using the irreducible dual variety and the required fundamental-group/Bertini surjectivity.' Proof: if X^∨ is not a hypersurface, S = ∅ for a general pencil; otherwise X^∨ is irreducible, the critical locus S_η = D_η ∩ X^∨ over the generic line is connected, and Gal(η̄/η) acts transitively on S_η̄.

items.name: Bertini surjectivity onto π₁(P^∨ − X^∨)
items.statement: Let η be the generic point of the Grassmannian of lines in P^∨, η̄ a geometric generic point, D_η the corresponding projective line over k(η), D_η̄ its base change to k(η̄), S_η = D_η ∩ X^∨, U_η = D_η − S_η and U_η̄ = D_η̄ − S_η̄. For u ∈ U_η̄ the composite π₁(U_η̄, u) → π₁(U_η, u) → π₁(P^∨ − X^∨, u) is surjective (Bertini); the action of π₁(U_η̄, u) on the cohomology of the hyperplane section X_u factors through π₁(P^∨ − X^∨, u). Moreover S_η maps to the generic point of X^∨ with connected geometric fibre, so S_η is connected.
items.note: LPV.5: 'the required fundamental-group/Bertini surjectivity'.

items.name: Conjugacy of Picard–Lefschetz transformations for a sufficiently general pencil
items.statement: For p = 2, n even, suppose the Lefschetz pencil (X_t)_{t∈D} sufficiently general (= with axis in a suitable open subset of the Grassmannian). Then: (i) n odd: the homomorphisms from Z_ℓ(1) into the monodromy group given by the Picard–Lefschetz formulas x ↦ x + λ(xδ)δ, for δ a vanishing cycle, are conjugate to each other; (ii) n even: the reflections x ↦ x − (−1)^{n'}(xδ)δ, for δ a vanishing cycle, are conjugate to each other.
items.note: For a generic pencil it follows from (4.2.6) and the Picard–Lefschetz formulas; the general case is reached via (1.11) (specialization). LPV.5 plans conjugacy of vanishing cycles but neither the passage from generic to all sufficiently general pencils nor the p = 2, n even reflection case (LPV.2 is restricted to p≠2). Used in (4.4.1) and (4.4.9).

items.name: Vanishing cycles conjugate in Hⁿ(X_u, Q_ℓ)
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (4.2.7), the vanishing cycles, taken up to sign, are all conjugate in Hⁿ(X_u, Q_ℓ).
items.note: Proof: neglecting torsion, ±δ is determined up to sign by the corresponding Picard–Lefschetz transformation. LPV.5 'Prove conjugacy, up to the orientation sign, of local vanishing cycles' (generic pencil; the sufficiently-general/p=2 extension is not explicitly planned). Hypothesis of (4.4.1).

items.name: Pencil fibration of the blow-up along the axis
items.statement: Let P be a projective space over k, X ⊂ P projective and smooth, purely of dimension n+1, A a codimension-2 linear subspace of P meeting X transversally, and suppose the hyperplanes through A sweep out on X a Lefschetz pencil of hyperplane sections (SGA7 XVII (2.2)). Let Δ = X ∩ A, X̃ the blow-up of X along Δ, and Δ̃ ≅ Δ × P¹ the exceptional divisor. The hyperplane sections of the pencil are the fibres of a morphism f: X̃ → P¹ (SGA7 XVIII (4.1.1)). Let S be the set of critical values of f, 0 ∉ S a rational point of P¹, Y_t the fibre of f at t and Y = Y₀; diagram (4.3.1.1): Δ ↪ Δ̃, Y ↪ X̃ → X, Y → 0 ↪ P¹.
items.note: LPV.3: 'Identify the incidence total space with the blowup along the smooth codimension-two axis, prove the total space smooth, the morphism projective, and the singular-value set finite'.

items.name: Ev(Y) and its orthogonal Ev(Y)^⊥
items.statement: The vanishing part Ev(Y) of Hⁿ(Y) is as defined in (4.2.4). Ev(Y)^⊥ denotes its orthogonal for the form (x, y) = Tr(x ∪ y).
items.note: LPV.4: 'Construct E^⊥'.

items.name: H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z/m) ≅ Ev(Y)^⊥
items.statement: In Z/m-cohomology, H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z/m) ≅ Ev(Y)^⊥ ⊂ Hⁿ(Y).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'. Proof: Rⁿf_!Z/m has no section with punctual support (injectivity of specialization maps), so its H⁰ injects into Hⁿ(Y) with image the fibre at 0 of its largest constant subsheaf; the local theory (4.2.2) shows Ev(Y)^⊥ is the fibre at 0 of the largest locally constant subsheaf, which is constant since P¹ is simply connected.

items.name: Ev(Y)^⊥ equals the global monodromy invariants (Z_ℓ, Q_ℓ)
items.statement: In Z_ℓ- (or Q_ℓ-) cohomology, H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z_ℓ) and Ev(Y)^⊥ also coincide with Hⁿ(Y)^{π₁(P¹−S, 0)}.
items.note: LPV.5: 'thereby complete LPV.4's identification of E^⊥ with the global invariant subspace' (Q_ℓ). Proof: in Z_ℓ-cohomology the local theory shows Rⁿf_!Z_ℓ is the direct image of its restriction to P¹ − S, so H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z_ℓ) = H⁰(P¹ − S, Rⁿf_!Z_ℓ) = Hⁿ(Y)^{π₁(P¹−S,0)}.

items.name: Ev(Y)^⊥ is the image of Hⁿ(X) (direct proof of (4.1.3))
items.statement: Ev(Y)^⊥ is the image of Hⁿ(X) in Hⁿ(Y) (which injects by weak Lefschetz). Equivalently, Hⁿ(X) → Hⁿ(Y) → Ev(Y)^* is exact.
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13' and plans 'the precisely scoped lower-dimensional induction statement of Weil II4.1.3'. Generalizes SGA7 XIX (4) to arbitrary base field, Z_ℓ-cohomology. Proof for Z/m in (4.3.7)–(4.3.8) via (4.3.4)–(4.3.6); combined with (4.3.2) gives (4.1.3).

items.name: Cross of exact sequences in Z/m-cohomology
items.statement: In Z/m-cohomology, (4.3.3) together with Poincaré duality (the transpose of restriction being Gysin; dualization exact for Z/m-modules) gives a cross of exact sequences (4.3.3.1): 0 → Ev(Y) → Hⁿ(Y) → H^{n+2}(X) → 0 horizontally, and Hⁿ(X) ↪ Hⁿ(Y) → Ev(Y)^* vertically, where the composite Hⁿ(X) → Hⁿ(Y) → H^{n+2}(X) is cup product with η = cl(Y).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'.

items.name: Cross of exact sequences in Z_ℓ-cohomology
items.statement: The Z/ℓ^j-crosses do not pass directly to the projective limit (the Ev(Y)^* in Z/ℓ^j-cohomology need not form a projective system), but the Ev(Y) map onto each other, and if the δ_i (i ∈ B) generate Ev(Y) in ℓ-adic cohomology one can pass to the limit in the exact sequence 0 → Hⁿ(X) → Hⁿ(Y) → (Z/ℓ^j)^B, whence in Z_ℓ-cohomology the cross (4.3.3.2): 0 → Ev(Y) → Hⁿ(Y) → H^{n+2}(X) → 0 and Hⁿ(X) ↪ Hⁿ(Y) → Ev(Y)^*, with composite η∪. In Q_ℓ-cohomology one recovers surjectivity of Hⁿ(Y) → Ev(Y)^*, the transpose of the inclusion Ev(Y) ⊂ Hⁿ(Y).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'. Used in (4.3.10).

items.name: Relative cohomology of a morphism of topoi
items.statement: Let u: T' → T'' be a morphism of topoi. The triples (𝓕' on T', 𝓕'' on T'', φ: u*𝓕'' → 𝓕') form a new topos T. For 𝓕 = (𝓕', 𝓕'', φ) an abelian sheaf on T put H⁰(T'' mod T', 𝓕) = Ker(H⁰(φ): H⁰(T'', 𝓕'') → H⁰(T', 𝓕')). Deriving this functor gives the relative cohomology of T'' mod T'. It can also be built by deriving 𝓕 ↦ (H⁰(T'', 𝓕'') → H⁰(T', 𝓕')) into complexes in degrees 0 and 1; this agrees because every 𝓕 injects into some 𝓕₁ with H⁰(φ) surjective (a sum of sheaves (0, 𝓕'') and (𝓕', u_*𝓕')). For K ∈ D⁺(T) there is a triangle → RΓ(T'' mod T', K) → RΓ(T'', K'') → RΓ(T', K') →, giving a long exact cohomology sequence.
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'; the relative-cohomology topos itself is not named in any stage description, so it is only implicitly planned through the §4.3 source citation. Mathlib has no topos of such triples.

items.name: Specialization map of relative cohomology along a path
items.statement: Let X be an irreducible complete variety over k, x, y two closed points of X, and K ∈ D⁺(X). Let η̄_x and η̄_y be geometric points localized at generic points η_x, η_y of the henselizations X_(x), X_(y). To an X-isomorphism σ of η̄_x with η̄_y one associates a morphism (4.3.5.1) H*_c(X − {x}, K) = H*(X mod {x}, K) → H*(X_(y) mod η̄_y, K), using the diagram of spaces {x} → X_(x) ← η̄_x ↔ η̄_y = η̄_y over X = X = X = X = X_(y), whose first arrow can be reversed because H*(X_(x), K) ≅ H*({x}, K).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13' (implicit, as for (4.3.4)). Replaces Morse theory for a growing ball in P¹(C).

items.name: Injectivity of the product of local relative H¹ maps on P¹
items.statement: Let t ∈ P¹ and K ∈ D^b(P¹) such that the 𝓗^iK are constructible and the support of 𝓗^i(K) is finite for i < 0. Let S be a finite subset of P¹ such that the 𝓗^iK are locally constant outside S. Then the product of the morphisms (4.3.5.1), for X = P¹, x = t and y ∈ S, is injective: H¹(P¹ mod t, K) ↪ ∏_{s∈S} H¹(P¹_(s) mod η̄_s, K).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13' (implicit). Application has t ∉ S. Proof: kill the part of K with finite support (K' ⊂ K; H¹(K) ≅ H¹(K/K')), reduce via 0 → H¹(𝓗⁰K) → H¹(K) → H⁰(𝓗¹K) to 𝓗 = 𝓗⁰K without punctually supported sections, locally constant off S; H¹(P¹ mod t, 𝓗) classifies 𝓗-torsors on P¹ trivialized at t (no automorphisms), built in stages over P¹_(t), P¹ − (S − {t}) via a continuous action σ*(h+p) = σ(h) + σ*p of π₁(P¹−S, η̄_t), and over P¹_(s); conclude by (4.2.5)-type generation of π₁(P¹−S, η̄_t) by local monodromy groups. The H⁰ case is left to the reader.

items.name: Obstruction group as relative H¹ over P¹ (plan of proof of (4.3.3))
items.statement: In the notation of (4.3.1), the injection Hⁿ(X) → Hⁿ(Y) factors through H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z/m) ⊂ Hⁿ(Y), and it suffices to show that for α in this H⁰ the obstruction dα ∈ H^{n+1}_c(X − Y) to extending α from Y to X vanishes. One has X − Y = X̃ − Y − Δ̃ and, with φ the projection of X̃ − Δ̃ to P¹, H^{n+1}_c(X − Y) = H¹(P¹ mod 0, Rφ_!Z/m[n]). If t ∉ S, φ⁻¹(t) is a smooth affine variety purely of dimension n, so its H^i_c vanishes for i < n; hence R^iφ_!Z/m has finite support (⊂ S) for i < n. Thus (4.3.6) applies, reducing to local obstructions, which are the (α, δ_σ).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'.

items.name: Local obstructions vanish for α ∈ H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z/m)
items.statement: Let α ∈ Hⁿ(Y) and α̃ its pull-back to Y ∪ Δ̃. The obstruction dα ∈ H^{n+1}_c(X − Y) to extending α to X coincides with the obstruction to extending α̃ to X̃, which lies in H¹(P¹ mod 0, s(K → L)[n]) where K = f_*(Z/m)^•, L = f_*((Z/m)^•|Δ̃) for a flasque resolution (Z/m)^•, and s(K → L) represents Rφ_!Z/m. Its image under (4.3.5.1) at s ∈ S is the obstruction to extending the transported class α_σ ∈ Hⁿ(Y_{η̄_s}) over the inverse image of P¹_(s) in X̃ (since Δ̃ is smooth over P¹, the 𝓗^i(L) are constant and RΓ(P¹_(s), L) → L_{η̄_s} is a quasi-isomorphism). These obstructions vanish if α comes from H⁰(P¹, Rⁿf_!Z/m); hence (4.3.3).
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'. Uses the 'derived category' form of the Leray spectral sequence of f.

items.name: Orthogonal decomposition Hⁿ(Y) = Hⁿ(X) ⊕ Ev(Y)
items.statement: In Q_ℓ-cohomology one has a decomposition into an orthogonal direct sum (for the intersection form Tr(x ∪ y)): Hⁿ(Y) = Hⁿ(X) ⊕ Ev(Y).
items.note: Reformulation of hard Lefschetz, from (4.3.3) and (4.1.2). EDC.4: 'leave any direct-sum splitting requiring hard Lefschetz to DWP.9'; DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'. Used in (4.4) (nondegeneracy of the form on Ev(Y)) and (4.5.1).

items.name: Intersection of the vanishing and fixed parts
items.statement: In Z_ℓ-cohomology, the cross (4.3.3.2) shows that the intersection of the vanishing part Ev(Y) of Hⁿ(Y) with the fixed part Hⁿ(X) = Hⁿ(Y)^{π₁(P¹−S,0)} is the subgroup Ker(η∪ : Hⁿ(X) → H^{n+2}(X)). In Q_ℓ-cohomology this kernel is zero (hard Lefschetz for X): Lefschetz's 'fundamental lemma' — a cycle both invariant and vanishing is zero.
items.note: DWP.9 ('Absolute hard Lefschetz after weights') lists 'Sources: Weil II4.1.1–4.1.6,4.3,6.2.8–6.2.13'.

items.name: Lefschetz's fundamental lemma is false in Z_ℓ-cohomology (Morgan)
items.statement: The kernel Ker(η∪ : Hⁿ(X) → H^{n+2}(X)) can be nonzero in Z_ℓ-cohomology (hence, over C, in integral cohomology): replacing η by a multiple (changing the projective embedding) one can make it coincide with the whole torsion subgroup of Hⁿ(X). Thus Lefschetz's 'fundamental lemma' is false in Z_ℓ-cohomology (and over C in integral cohomology).
items.note: Remark attributed to J. Morgan; Deligne concludes one may doubt Lefschetz's claimed proof. Not planned in any stage; no proof beyond the one-line argument is given.

items.name: Automorphism group G of Ev(Y) and geometric monodromy group M
items.statement: Notation of (4.3.1), Q_ℓ-cohomology. G is the group of automorphisms of Ev(Y) preserving the intersection form (,), which is nondegenerate by hard Lefschetz (4.3.9). The group π₁(P¹ − S, 0) acts on (the cohomology of) Y respecting (,); M denotes its image in G.
items.note: G is Sp(Ev(Y)) for n odd and O(Ev(Y)) for n even. LPV.4/LPV.5 work with the radical quotient E/(E∩E^⊥) of Deligne I rather than Ev(Y) with hard Lefschetz; no stage plans this even-n orthogonal setting ('No even-dimensional orthogonal openness claim is substituted').

items.name: Monodromy of a Lefschetz pencil: open or finite
items.statement: Suppose X irreducible. If p = 2 and n is even, suppose moreover the pencil sufficiently general (= with axis in a suitable open subset of a Grassmannian; i.e. such that (4.2.8) applies). Then exactly one of: a) M is open in G; b) n is even and M is finite.
items.note: Case n odd (M open in Sp) corresponds to LPV.5 'For odd n, prove that the compact monodromy image is **open** in Sp(V)', there with V = E/(E∩E^⊥) (equal to Ev(Y) given (4.3.9)); the n even orthogonal/finite dichotomy is explicitly unplanned in LPV.5. Proof: G is semisimple over Q_ℓ, so the compact subgroup M is open once Zariski-dense; after extending scalars to Q̄_ℓ (≅ C) apply (4.4.2^a) (n odd) and (4.4.2^s) (n even) to the Zariski closure of M and the conjugacy class of Picard–Lefschetz transformations, hypotheses from (4.2.5) and (4.2.8).

items.name: Zariski-dense compact subgroups of a semisimple ℓ-adic group are open (fact used)
items.statement: The group G is a semisimple algebraic group over Q_ℓ; for the compact subgroup M of G to be open it suffices that it be Zariski-dense. Zariski density may be checked after extension of scalars from Q_ℓ to Q̄_ℓ.
items.note: Stated without proof. LPV.5 plans an ℓ-adic Lie-algebra/inverse-function route to openness for Sp only ('Build the necessary ℓ-adic analytic matrix-group/closed-subgroup and exponential-logarithm lemmas'), not this general fact.

items.name: Algebraic subgroups of Sp(V) generated by an orbit of transvections
items.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional C-vector space with a nondegenerate alternating form (,), M an algebraic subgroup of Sp(V) and R an orbit of M in V which spans V. Suppose M is the smallest algebraic subgroup of Sp(V) containing the transvections x ↦ x + (xδ)δ (δ ∈ R); in other words, M is generated by the one-parameter subgroups of transvections U_δ = {x ↦ x + λ(xδ)δ | λ ∈ C} for δ ∈ R. Then M = Sp(V).
items.note: LPV.5 plans the Lie-algebra analogue (Deligne I 5.11: 'an irreducible symplectic Lie subalgebra generated by these operators is all sp(V)') but not this algebraic-group lemma. Tau Ceti has symplectic transvection units (TauCeti/Algebra/Lie/Symplectic/StandardCarrier/Generation.lean) but not this statement. Proof (4.4.4^a): R ≠ {0} ⇒ all nonzero multiples of δ ∈ R lie in R (via (4.4.3^a)); take W maximal with R ∩ W dense in W; R = (R∩W) ∪ (R∩W^⊥), W nondegenerate, M ⊂ Sp(W) × Sp(W^⊥), R one orbit ⇒ W = V, R dense in V, all U_δ (δ ∈ V) in M.

items.name: Non-orthogonal pairs in R span a plane contained in R
items.statement: In the situation of (4.4.2^a), let δ', δ'' ∈ R be non-orthogonal. Then the nonzero linear combinations of δ' and δ'' lie in R.
items.note: Proof: the subgroup generated by U_{δ'} and U_{δ''} is the SL(2) of the plane spanned by δ', δ''; it lies in M, and the nonzero vectors of this plane form a single SL(2)-orbit.

items.name: Algebraic subgroups of O(V) generated by an orbit of reflections
items.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional C-vector space with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form (,), M an algebraic subgroup of O(V) and R an orbit of M in V which spans V. Suppose the elements of R satisfy (δ, δ) = 2, and that M is the smallest algebraic subgroup of O(V) containing the reflections s_δ : x ↦ x − (xδ)δ for δ ∈ R. Then M is finite or M = O(V).
items.note: Proof (4.4.4^s): take W not totally isotropic, maximal with R ∩ W dense in the sphere (δ,δ)=2 of W; for δ ∈ R − W the linear form (δ, x) must be locally constant on the sphere, forcing a) dim W = 1, b) δ ⊥ W, or c) W isotropic with W∩W^⊥ of codimension 1 and δ ⊥ W∩W^⊥; if dim W ≠ 1 one gets W = V, M = O(V); if always dim W = 1, all (δ',δ'') are 2cos θ with θ ∈ 2πQ, finitely many values since R is algebraic, so R and M ⊂ Perm(R) are finite. In the application (δ,δ) = (−1)^{n'}·2;

items.name: Pairs in R with irrational angle span unit vectors in R
items.statement: In the situation of (4.4.2^s), let δ', δ'' ∈ R. If (δ', δ'') is not of the form 2cos θ with θ a rational multiple of 2π, the linear combinations δ of δ' and δ'' with (δ, δ) = 2 are in R. The same conclusion holds if (δ', δ'') = ±2.
items.note: Proof: in the first case the form is nondegenerate on the plane, s_{δ''}s_{δ'} is a rotation of infinite order, its algebraic hull is the SO of the plane (dimension 1); in the case ±2, reduce to (δ',δ'') = 2 (replace δ' by −δ'), assume δ' ≠ δ''; the form on the plane has kernel C(δ''−δ') and s_{δ'}s_{δ''} is a nonzero transvection parallel to it, whose algebraic hull is the group of all such transvections. Deligne notes the ±2 case is not needed.

items.name: Finite monodromy is independent of ℓ with integral character
items.statement: If M is finite, the analogous group in ℓ'-adic cohomology is also finite, for every ℓ' ≠ p. As a quotient of π₁(P¹ − S, 0) it is independent of ℓ', and the character of its representation on Ev(Y, Q_ℓ') has integer values independent of ℓ'.
items.note: Proof: π₁ acts trivially on H^i(Y) (i ≠ n) and on a complement of Ev in Hⁿ(Y); the action on Ev is semisimple without trivial constituent, so Ev is recovered from the virtual representation Σ(−1)^iH^i(Y) by removing trivial factors; by specialization ((1.11)) reduce to k = F̄_q; with notation (0.7) the virtual representation comes from π₁(P¹₀ − S₀, 0), and at Frobenius F_x (x rational over F_{q^m}) its character is the number of F_{q^m}-points of the fibre of X̃ at x (Lefschetz trace formula, planned at SF.2/WC.0 per the Weil I conventions); conclude by (4.4.6).

items.name: Rational characters agreeing on Frobenius powers (different ℓ)
items.statement: Let U₀ be a normal geometrically connected algebraic variety over F_q with a base point u, G the quotient of W(U₀, u) by a subgroup of finite index of π₁(U, u), and V a virtual ℓ-adic representation of G. Let V' be a virtual ℓ'-adic representation of W(U₀, u). Suppose that on the powers of the Frobenius elements F_x ∈ W(U₀, u) (x ∈ |U₀|) the characters of V and V' take rational values and coincide. Then V' comes by inflation from a virtual representation of G, and the characters of V and V' have rational values and are equal.
items.note: Proof: by Čebotarev every element of G of large enough degree is an F_x (cf. (3.5.3)); a character of G is determined by its values on elements of large degree (for g central of degree > 0, n ↦ χ(gⁿh) is a combination of n ↦ λⁿ, and a Vandermonde determinant gives linear independence on n ≥ N); so V's character is rational, V is realizable over a number field, replaced by an ℓ'-adic V₁ reducing to ℓ = ℓ', then (4.4.7). DWP.3 plans the function-field Chebotarev input ('export it for future geometric monodromy/rationality consumers') but not this lemma.

items.name: Virtual ℓ-adic representations of W(U₀,u) determined by Frobenius traces
items.statement: Let V' and V'' be two virtual ℓ-adic representations of W(U₀, u). If their characters coincide on the powers of the Frobenius elements, they coincide.
items.note: Proof: V the sum of the constituents, G⁰ the Zariski closure of the image of π₁(U, u) in GL(V), G as in (1.3.7); cut V', V'' by the ℓ-adic valuations v of the eigenvalues of a central g ∈ G of degree d > 0; the characteristic polynomial of F_x on V'_v keeps eigenvalues of valuation (deg(x)/deg(g))·v (cf. (1.3.14)); by log det(1 − Ft, V') = −Σ Tr(Fⁿ, V') tⁿ/n the pieces have the same Frobenius characters; twist (1.2.7) to representations of π₁(U₀, u) and apply Čebotarev (density of Frobenius). Relies on §1 (1.2.7), (1.3.7), (1.3.14).

items.name: Setup for finite monodromy, n even
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (4.4.1), suppose moreover n even, n = 2n₁, M finite and Ev(Y) nonzero (i.e. S ≠ ∅). The form (,) on Ev(Y) has values in Q_ℓ(−n); it corresponds to a form, still denoted (,), on Ev(Y)(n₁) with values in Q_ℓ. The vanishing cycles δ are elements of Ev(Y)(n₁) and satisfy (δ, δ) = (−1)^{n₁}·2.
items.note: No stage plans the even-dimensional finite-monodromy case.

items.name: The lattice of vanishing cycles
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (4.4.8): the Z-module L generated by the vanishing cycles δ satisfies L ⊗ Q_ℓ ≅ Ev(Y)(n₁), and the form (,) takes integer values on L.
items.note: Proof: in M the reflections s_δ are characterized independently of ℓ as conjugates of nontrivial elements of an inertia group at some s ∈ S; Tr(s_δ s_δ') is an ℓ-independent integer (4.4.5) and (δ,δ')² = Tr(s_δs_δ') − dim Ev(Y) + 4 (printed '+2', (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E57)) has a square root in Q_ℓ for all ℓ ≠ p, hence is a square of an integer, so (δ,δ') ∈ Z; choosing δ_i ∈ R forming a Q_ℓ-basis, every δ ∈ R is a rational combination of the δ_i.

items.name: Finite monodromy is a Weyl group of type A, D or E
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (4.4.8): the vanishing cycles ±δ form in L a root system R of type A, D or E, and the group M is the corresponding Weyl group.
items.note: Proof: the s_δ form one conjugacy class in M, M is finite and generated by the reflections s_δ of L; so R is an irreducible root system with all roots of the same length (type A, D or E) and M its Weyl group. Tau Ceti has Dynkin types and simply-laced predicates (TauCeti.DynkinType.IsSimplyLaced, TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/RootSystem/DynkinType.lean) and uniqueness of Cartan type (TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/RootSystem/Classification.lean:514 eq_of_valid_of_cartanMatrix_eq) but the classification step 'irreducible, one root length ⇒ A, D, E' and this geometric theorem are not present.

items.name: The gcd (lcm) theorem for Lefschetz pencils over F_q
items.statement: Let X₀ be a smooth projective absolutely irreducible variety of dimension n+1 over F_q, and (X_t)_{t∈P¹} a Lefschetz pencil of hyperplane sections of X, defined over F_q. For p = 2 and n even, suppose it sufficiently general. Let S ⊂ P¹ be the set of t for which X_t is singular. Then the polynomial det(1 − FT, Hⁿ(X)) is the lcm of the polynomials f(T) = ∏(1 − α_iT) having the following property: (∗) for t a point of P¹ − S defined over F_{q^k}, and F the Frobenius endomorphism of X_t relative to its natural F_{q^k}-structure, ∏(1 − α_i^kT) divides det(1 − FT, Hⁿ(X_t)).
items.note: Notation (0.7). Used by Katz and Messing [7] to compare ℓ-adic and crystalline cohomology. WC.6 only says equality of ℓ-adic and crystalline characteristic polynomials 'requires its own source-qualified theorem and construction'; no stage plans (4.5.1). Proof: det(1 − FT, Hⁿ(X)) satisfies (∗) by the decomposition below, and every polynomial satisfying (∗) divides it by (4.5.2) with P = f, Q = det(1 − FT, Hⁿ(X)).

items.name: Splitting of the characteristic polynomial of a smooth fibre
items.statement: Write Hⁿ(X_t) = Hⁿ(X) + Ev(X_t) (4.3.9). If the β_i are the eigenvalues of Frobenius on Hⁿ(X) (counted with multiplicity), for t defined over F_{q^k}: det(1 − FT, Hⁿ(X_t)) = ∏(1 − β_i^kT) · det(1 − FT, Ev(X_t)). In particular ∏(1 − β_iT) = det(1 − FT, Hⁿ(X)) satisfies (∗).
items.note: Consequence of (4.3.9) and Frobenius-compatibility of Hⁿ(X) → Hⁿ(X_t).

items.name: Divisibility lemma for the gcd theorem
items.statement: Whatever the polynomials P(T) = ∏(1 − γ_iT) and Q(T) = ∏(1 − δ_jT) (the γ_i and δ_j assumed ≠ 0), if for every point t ∈ P¹ − S defined over F_{q^k} one has ∏(1 − γ_i^kT) | ∏(1 − δ_j^kT) · det(1 − FT, Ev(X_t)), then P | Q.
items.note: Reduction to deg P = 1 by induction on deg P: if γ is one of the γ_i, the degree-1 case shows γ equals some δ_j; apply induction to P/(1−γT), Q/(1−γT). Degree-1 case by contradiction via (4.5.3), (4.5.4) and Lemma (4.5.4).
