items.name: Divisibility of the vanishing characteristic polynomial for k ≡ 1 (N)
items.statement: Suppose P = 1 − γT with γ distinct from all δ_j. For each j let k_j be the generator of the ideal of integers k with γ^k = δ_j^k, and N the product of the nonzero k_j. For k ≡ 1 (N) one has γ^k ≠ δ_j^k, hence (4.5.3): 1 − γ^kT | det(1 − FT, Ev(X_t)) (t over F_{q^k}, k ≡ 1 (N)). In particular γ is an ℓ-adic unit.
items.note: Step in the proof of (4.5.2).

items.name: Arithmetic monodromy group G as an extension of Ẑ by M
items.statement: Let u be a geometric point of P¹ − S. The group π₁((P¹ − S)₀, u) acts on E = Ev(X_u) and maps to π₁(Spec(F_q)) = Gal(F̄/F_q) = Ẑ. Let G be the image of π₁((P¹ − S)₀, u) under the diagonal map to GL(E) × Ẑ; it is an extension of Ẑ by the geometric monodromy group M of (4.4). Let ρ be its projection to GL(E) and deg its projection to Ẑ. For t ∈ (P¹ − S)₀(F_{q^k}) and F_t the image in G of the corresponding Frobenius, deg(F_t) = k and det(1 − FT, Ev(X_t)) = det(1 − ρ(F_t)T).
items.note: Construction used for the density argument; Frobenius conventions as in (0.7).

items.name: γ^{deg g} is an eigenvalue of ρ(g) when deg g ≡ 1 (N)
items.statement: Since the F_t are dense in G (Čebotarev), by continuity (4.5.3) gives: (4.5.4) for g ∈ G with deg(g) ≡ 1 (N), γ^{deg(g)} is an eigenvalue of ρ(g). This is absurd even restricting to g with deg(g) = 1: since ρ(g) normalizes M and the ρ(g) with deg(g) = 1 form a coset of M, it suffices to verify Lemma (4.5.4).
items.note: Function-field Chebotarev density planned at DWP.3 ('Construct the function-field closed-point Chebotarev/density input in §6.13 ... export it for future geometric monodromy/rationality consumers'), but this consequence is not planned. Label (4.5.4) is used twice on this page (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E59).

items.name: Elements of a coset gM have no common eigenvalue
items.statement: If g ∈ GL(E) normalizes the geometric monodromy group M, the gm for m ∈ M have no common eigenvalue.
items.note: Proof: M may be replaced by its Zariski closure M⁻, which by (4.4.1)/(4.4.9) is the symplectic group of a nondegenerate alternating form on E, the orthogonal group of a nondegenerate quadratic form on E, or a Weyl group of type A, D or E; g is correspondingly a symplectic similitude, an orthogonal similitude, or a scalar multiple of an automorphism of the root system. Replacing g by gm and by λg: in the Sp/O cases Id and −Id already have no common eigenvalue; in the Weyl case only the class ḡ of g mod W (a Dynkin-diagram automorphism) matters; see the next items.

items.name: Weyl group cosets: trivial ḡ and the opposition involution
items.statement: If ḡ is trivial, the elements of the Weyl group W have no common eigenvalue: since e ∈ W it suffices to find an element without eigenvalue 1, e.g. a Coxeter transformation. The case where ḡ is the opposition involution (trivial for A₁, D_{2k}, E₇, E₈; of order 2 for A_k (k > 1), D_{2k+1}, E₆) reduces to the previous one by replacing g by −g. It remains to treat D_{2k} with ḡ of order 2, and D₄ with ḡ of order 3.
items.note: The fact that a Coxeter element has no eigenvalue 1 is used without proof; not found in Mathlib/Tau Ceti (Mathlib has CoxeterSystem but no Coxeter-element eigenvalue results).

items.name: Case D_{2k}, ḡ of order 2
items.statement: For D_{2k}, the root system is the set of vectors ±e_i ± e_j (i ≠ j) of Z^{2k}; W ∪ gW is the group of permutations, with possible sign changes, of the e_i, and W is the subgroup of permutations with an even number of sign changes. The elements (e₁,…,e_{2k−1},e_{2k}) ↦ (e₁,…,e_{2k−1},−e_{2k}) and (e₁,…,e_{2k−1},e_{2k}) ↦ (e₂,…,e_{2k},−e₁) of gW have respectively eigenvalues ±1 and the (2k)-th roots of −1, so have no eigenvalue in common.
items.note: Elementary linear algebra.

items.name: Case D₄, ḡ of order 3
items.statement: For D₄, the root system is the set of Hurwitz integral quaternions of norm 2, and one may take for g multiplication by ½(1 + i + j + k). Its eigenvalues are ½(1 ± √−3), and g and −g have no common eigenvalue; hence the result since −1 is in the Weyl group.
items.note: Mathlib has quaternions (Quaternion) but no Hurwitz order/D₄ model.

items.name: Goal: a Q_ℓ-DG algebra A(X) modelling the Q_ℓ-homotopy type
items.statement: To each algebraic variety X over an algebraically closed field k one attaches a commutative differential graded Q_ℓ-algebra A(X), well defined up to quasi-isomorphism and functorial in X, which 'is' the Q_ℓ-homotopy type of X. In particular H*A(X) = H*(X, Q_ℓ). If k = C, the minimal model of A(X) is deduced from Sullivan's minimal model [6] of the rational homotopy type of X(C) by extending scalars from Q to Q_ℓ.
items.note: Programme statement justifying results announced in [3] (Deligne, ICM Vancouver 1974). The method uses a construction due independently to Grothendieck and Miller [8]. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Divided-power polynomial ring Z{t} and its t-grading
items.statement: The algebra of divided-power polynomials over Z is the subring Z{t} of Q[t] with Z-basis the tⁿ/n! (n ≥ 0). The t-grading of Z{t} is the one for which tⁿ/n! has degree n.
items.note: Mathlib has the universal divided power algebra Γ_R(M) (DividedPowerAlgebra, Mathlib/RingTheory/DividedPowerAlgebra/Init.lean:100, defined as a quotient of MvPolynomial (ℕ × M) R); for M = R = Z this is abstractly Z{t}, but the concrete subring of Q[t] with basis tⁿ/n!, its grading and the identification are not in either library. Used as the coefficient ring of the Grothendieck–Miller de Rham complex.

items.name: Convention: DG algebras are graded-commutative
items.statement: 'Differential graded' is abbreviated DG; DG algebras are always assumed commutative in the sense of the Koszul sign rule (model example: exterior differential forms on a manifold).
items.note: Neither library has commutative (Koszul-sign) DG algebras as such; DGAInfinity Layer 1 plans DG algebras but not graded-commutative ones or Sullivan algebras.

items.name: A{t}-algebras t-graded DG
items.statement: Let A be a commutative ring and put A{t} = A ⊗ Z{t}; for A = Q this is simply Q[t]. An A{t}-algebra t-graded DG is an A{t}-DG-algebra each homogeneous component of which is equipped with a grading, the t-grading, which makes it a graded A{t}-module, and such that the product and the differential d are homogeneous of t-degree 0.
items.note: Bigraded (exterior degree, t-degree) formalism of the construction. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: The Z{t}-de Rham complex functor Ω on simplicial sets
items.statement: The 'Z{t}-de Rham complex' construction (defined in (5.1.8)) is a contravariant functor associating to each simplicial set X a Z{t}-algebra t-graded DG, X ↦ Ω(X). Ωᵖ(X) denotes the part of degree p for the DG structure (exterior degree). The t-degree and exterior degree of a bihomogeneous element satisfy (5.1.4.1): 0 ≤ exterior degree ≤ t-degree.
items.note: Construction attributed to Grothendieck and Miller [8]. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Cohomology of the Z{t}-de Rham complex
items.statement: There is a functorial morphism of bigraded Z{t}-algebras (5.1.4.2) H*Ω(X) → H*(X, Z) ⊗ Z{t}, which identifies the cohomology of Ω(X) with the sum of the Hᵖ(X, Z) ⊗ tⁿ/n! for p ≤ n.
items.note: Proof referred to Miller [8]; key input is (5.1.9 b). Mathlib has simplicial sets but no singular/simplicial cohomology ring of a simplicial set with this comparison. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: A{t}-de Rham complex Ω(X, A) and comparison with Sullivan's de Rham complex
items.statement: For every commutative ring A (the cases of interest are A = Z, Z/ℓⁿ, Q) there is a functor 'A{t}-de Rham complex' Ω(X, A) obeying the formalism (5.1.4) with Z replaced by A. It is covariant in A and the isomorphism (5.1.4.2)_A is functorial in A. For A = Q there is a morphism from Ω(X, Q) to the Q[t]-algebra t-graded DG deduced from the de Rham–Sullivan complex Ω_DRS(X) of X by extending scalars from Q to Q[t]; it is compatible with (5.1.4.2) and identifies the part of t-degree n of Ω(X, Q) with tⁿ ⊗ (the subcomplex of Ω_DRS(X) formed by the forms of degree ≤ n in the barycentric coordinates of each simplex).
items.note: Ω_DRS is Sullivan's complex of polynomial forms (not in either library). The text calls this morphism 'Cet isomorphisme'; (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E61) No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Base change of Ωᵖ(X, A) to a quotient ring
items.statement: If B is a quotient of A, the natural morphism Ωᵖ(X, A) ⊗_A B → Ωᵖ(X, B) is an isomorphism, except in the component of t-degree p.
items.note: Used in (5.2.1 b) for surjectivity of transition maps and the Mittag-Leffler condition when passing from Z/ℓⁿ to Z_ℓ.

items.name: Relative polynomial divided-power forms Ω(σ) on R^σ
items.statement: For a finite set σ, Z{(x_i)_{i∈σ}} denotes the subring of Q[(x_i)_{i∈σ}] with Z-basis the monomials ∏_{i∈σ} x_i^{n_i}/n_i!. Ω′(σ) is the corresponding de Rham complex: the subcomplex of the de Rham complex of Q[(x_i)_{i∈σ}] with Z{(x_i)}-basis the products of dx_i (one product for each finite subset of σ). Put t = Σ x_i and let Ω(σ) be the quotient of Ω′(σ) by the ideal generated by dt. It is a Z{t}-algebra t-graded DG if one takes as t-grading the grading in which x_i and dx_i have t-degree 1; it is called the Z{t}-algebra t-graded DG of relative (rel. t), polynomial, integral divided-power differential forms on R^σ.
items.note: Building block of the simplicial DG algebra Ω of (5.1.8). No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Ω(σ, A)
items.statement: For any ring A one puts Ω(σ, A) = Ω(σ) ⊗ A.
items.note: Coefficient extension for (5.1.8).

items.name: Intrinsic description via Γ*(L) ⊗ ΛL
items.statement: a) If L is a free A-module, consider Ω(L) = Γ*(L) ⊗ Λ*L; the exterior degree is that of the exterior power, and the t-degree is the sum of the exterior and symmetric (divided-power) degrees; the differential, compatible with divided powers, is characterized by d(x ⊗ 1) = 1 ⊗ x. b) If M is a free quotient of L, consider the quotient Ω(L, M) := Γ*(L) ⊗ Λ*M of Ω(L). c) One takes Ω(σ, A) = Ω(A^σ, A^σ modulo the diagonal A).
items.note: Mathlib has Γ_R(M) (DividedPowerAlgebra, Init.lean:100) and exterior algebras, but not this DG algebra with divided-power-compatible differential. Used in (5.1.9 b) to compute the homotopy of Ω.

items.name: Ω(σ) is contravariant in σ
items.statement: The Z{t}-algebra t-graded DG Ω(σ) is a contravariant functor of σ: this is clear from (5.1.6.3), the pair (Z^σ, Z diagonal) being contravariant in σ. Concretely, to φ: τ → σ one associates φ* sending x_i to Σ_{φ(j)=i} x_j. For example, for τ ⊂ σ and φ the inclusion, φ* is obtained by setting x_i = 0 for i ∉ τ.
items.note: Gives the simplicial object of (5.1.8).

items.name: Heuristic: forms on a simplicial complex as compatible families
items.statement: Idea in the parallel context of Godement's 'simplicial schemes': given a set S and a set 𝒮 of finite nonempty subsets of S (the simplices), with every one-element subset a simplex and every nonempty subset of a simplex a simplex, let |σ| be the standard simplex in R^(S) spanned by e_i, i ∈ σ, X = ∪|σ|, X̂ the cone on X. Replace these by the homotopic spaces X′ (union of the affine spans σ′ of the |σ|) and X̂′ (union of the linear spans σ̂′); with t: R^(S) → R the sum of coordinates, X′ is the fibre at t = 1 of t restricted to X̂′. With Ω(σ) the Z{t}-DG algebra of relative, polynomial, integral divided-power forms on σ̂′, a p-form α ∈ Ωᵖ(X) is by definition a family α_σ ∈ Ωᵖ(σ) (σ ∈ 𝒮) such that for τ ⊂ σ, α_τ is the restriction of α_σ to Ωᵖ(τ).
items.note: Motivation only; the formal definition is (5.1.8).

items.name: Formal definition Ω(X, A) = Hom(X, Ω ⊗ A)
items.statement: Restrict the functor Ω(σ) of (5.1.6.4) to the finite sets Δ_n = [0, n] and increasing maps between them; one obtains a simplicial Z{t}-algebra t-graded DG Ω. For a simplicial set X and ring A one puts Ω(X, A) = Hom(X, Ω ⊗ A) (the sum over i, p of the groups of morphisms of simplicial sets from X to the (i, p)-bihomogeneous component of Ω ⊗ A).
items.note: Mathlib has SSet and simplicial objects, but not this simplicial DG algebra. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Explicit comparison map to Ω_DRS(X) ⊗ Q[t]
items.statement: The morphism (5.1.5) into Ω_DRS(X) ⊗ Q[t] is obtained by sending x_i to (barycentric coordinate x_i) ⊗ t.
items.note: Proofs of the fundamental properties are referred to Miller [8].

items.name: Homotopy of the simplicial group Ω
items.statement: The homology (homotopy) groups of the simplicial group Ω are as follows: each H_i is isomorphic to Z, placed in exterior degree and t-degree i. This follows easily from (5.1.6.3), recalling that the simplicial group σ ↦ A^σ is homotopic to 0 (its normalization reduces to A → A (iso) in homological degrees 0 and 1): one has Γ*(A^σ) ∼ Γ*(0) = (σ ↦ A), and Λ*(A^σ modulo A diagonal) is computed by Quillen's décalage theorems: its normalization is the symmetric algebra of the A-module A, with Symⁿ placed in homological degree n.
items.note: The 'key point' behind (5.1.4.2). Quillen's décalage theorems are an unstated external input (not in the bibliography). Not in either library.

items.name: Cohomology and Ω of a filtering projective system of simplicial sets
items.statement: Let 𝐗 be a filtering projective system of simplicial sets X^α. Put (5.2.1.1) Hⁱ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) = lim ind Hⁱ(X^α, Z/ℓⁿ) and (5.2.1.2) Ω(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) = lim ind Ω(X^α, Z/ℓⁿ), a Z/ℓⁿ{t}-algebra t-graded DG; relation (5.1.4.2) still holds between these (exactness of inductive limits).
items.note: Pro-object setting needed because étale hypercoverings form a pro-system. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Under (F): Hⁱ(𝐗, Z_ℓ) finitely generated, universal coefficient sequences
items.statement: Assume (F): the Hⁱ(𝐗, Z/ℓ) are finite groups. Then (arguments of SGA5 V (5.3.1)) each (5.2.1.3) Hⁱ(𝐗, Z_ℓ) = lim proj Hⁱ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) is a Z_ℓ-module of finite type, and one has the usual exact sequences (universal coefficients) 0 → Hⁱ(𝐗, Z_ℓ) ⊗ Z/ℓⁿ → Hⁱ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) → Tor₁^{Z_ℓ}(Hⁱ⁺¹(𝐗, Z_ℓ), Z/ℓⁿ) → 0.
items.note: Input: SGA5 V (5.3.1). The printed right side of (5.2.1.3) has a non-bold X (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E62). Mathlib has Mittag-Leffler systems (CategoryTheory.Functor.IsMittagLeffler, Mathlib/CategoryTheory/CofilteredSystem.lean:137) but not this statement.

items.name: Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ) and its cohomology
items.statement: Put (5.2.1.4) Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ) = lim proj_n Ω(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) (bigraded projective limit); it is a Z_ℓ{t}-algebra t-graded DG. One has: a) the Hⁱ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) are finite, so their projective system satisfies Mittag-Leffler (ML); b) in each bidegree (i, p) with i ≠ p the transition maps between the _iΩᵖ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) are surjective ((5.1.5)) so ML holds; for i = p there is an exact sequence _pΩ^{p−1}(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) →d _pΩᵖ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) → Hᵖ(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) → 0, whence ML since the cohomology satisfies ML. By a), b) the passage to the projective limit (5.2.1.4) is exact, whence a morphism (5.2.1.5) H*Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ) → H*(𝐗, Z_ℓ) ⊗_{Z_ℓ} Z_ℓ{t} which identifies the cohomology of Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ) with the sum of the Hᵖ(𝐗, Z_ℓ) ⊗ tⁿ/n! for p ≤ n. It is essential that the inductive limit over α precede the projective limit over n.
items.note: Here the left index i in _iΩᵖ is the t-degree. Uses (F) and (5.1.5). Mittag-Leffler condition exists in Mathlib (CofilteredSystem.lean:137), not the exactness of lim for complexes.

items.name: A(𝐗) and H*A(𝐗) = H*(𝐗, Q_ℓ)
items.statement: For a t-graded module M over Q[t] (e.g. over Q_ℓ[t]) let lim_t M be the inductive limit of the homogeneous components M_k of M with transition maps M_n → M_{n+m} multiplication by t^m. Put (5.2.1.6) H*(𝐗, Q_ℓ) = H*(𝐗, Z_ℓ) ⊗_{Z_ℓ} Q_ℓ and (5.2.1.7) A(𝐗) = lim_t Q_ℓ ⊗ Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ). Passing to the limit in (5.2.1.5) gives an isomorphism (5.2.1.8) H*A(𝐗) = H*(𝐗, Q_ℓ).
items.note: A(𝐗) is a commutative DG Q_ℓ-algebra. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: A(X) for a variety X via countable étale covers
items.statement: Let X be an algebraic variety over an algebraically closed field k. It can be defined over a countable algebraically closed subfield k₁ of k: X₁ over k₁, from which X is deduced by extension of scalars. Because k₁ is countable one can find a countable projective system, indexed by the integers, of étale surjective morphisms φ_α: X₁^α → X₁ such that for every étale surjective φ: U → X₁ there are α and a factorization of φ_α through φ. For each α and finite set σ let (X₁^α/X₁)^σ be the fibre product over X₁ of a family indexed by σ of copies of X₁^α; for σ = Δ_n these form a simplicial scheme. Put (5.2.2.1) 𝐗 = (π₀((X₁^α/X₁)^{Δ_n}))_α and (5.2.2.2) A(X) = A(𝐗).
items.note: The printed text says 'Parce que k est dénombrable' and 'φ: U → X' and writes X^1_α for X^α_1 (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E63, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E64). Čech nerves exist in Mathlib (CategoryTheory.Arrow.cechNerve, Mathlib/AlgebraicTopology/CechNerve.lean:56) but not this étale construction.

items.name: H*A(X) ≅ H*(X, Q_ℓ)
items.statement: With 𝐗 as in (5.2.2.1): H*(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) = H*(X₁, Z/ℓⁿ) (by definition of étale cohomology if one used hypercoverings, and by Artin with the chosen definition); H*(X₁, Z/ℓⁿ) → H*(X, Z/ℓⁿ) is an isomorphism; condition (F) holds by SGA4½ [Th. finitude] (1.1). By definition of ℓ-adic cohomology one therefore has an isomorphism H*A(X) ⥲ H*(X, Q_ℓ).
items.note: Inputs: Artin's Čech-versus-hypercovering comparison (unreferenced 'd'après Artin'), invariance of étale cohomology under extension of algebraically closed base field, and finiteness SGA4½ [Th. finitude] (1.1) (the brief's SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2 / WC.0 convention stages import finiteness, but none plans A(X)). No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Galois action on A(X)
items.statement: Suppose X defined over a countable subfield k₀ of k, and take for k₁ the algebraic closure of k₀ in k. One can then choose the projective system of the X₁^α defined over k₀. The Galois group Gal(k₁/k₀) then acts on 𝐗 and hence, by transport of structure, on A(X), compatibly with the Galois action on the ℓ-adic cohomology of X. A(X) is enormous, so one can hardly speak of continuity of the Galois action; one can only say that Galois acts continuously on the Ω(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) (with the discrete topology), for every n.
items.note: Feeds the Frobenius gradings of (5.3).

items.name: Comparison system of nerves for k = C
items.statement: Take k = C and a projective system X₁^α as in (5.2.2). One can find a projective system of spaces X^α over X(C) and morphisms a_α: X^α → X₁^α(C) such that each X^α is the disjoint union of the opens of an open covering of X(C), the p-fold intersections of these opens being empty or contractible (for all p ≥ 1). Let 𝐗(C) be the projective system of the nerves N^α = π₀(X^α/X(C)^{Δ_n}) of the coverings X^α; each nerve has the homotopy type of X(C). The projective system of the a_α gives a morphism 𝐗(C) → 𝐗.
items.note: Text writes 'recouvrement ouvert de X' for X(C) and later N_α for N^α (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E65). Uses existence of good covers of X(C).

items.name: Minimal models of A(X) are the Q_ℓ-scalar extensions of Sullivan's minimal model of X(C)
items.statement: Construction of isomorphisms between the minimal models of the Q_ℓ-DG algebra A(X) and the tensor product with Q_ℓ of the minimal models 𝓜(X(C)) of Sullivan [6] of the rational homotopy type of the topological space X(C). By SGA4 XVI (4.1), Ω(𝐗, Z/ℓⁿ) → Ω(𝐗(C), Z/ℓⁿ) is a quasi-isomorphism inducing on cohomology the comparison isomorphisms Hⁱ(X, Z/ℓⁿ) ⥲ Hⁱ(X(C), Z/ℓⁿ); Ω(N_α, Z/ℓⁿ) → Ω(𝐗(C), Z/ℓⁿ) are quasi-isomorphisms; in the limit Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ) → Ω(𝐗(C), Z_ℓ) ← Ω(N_α, Z_ℓ) are quasi-isomorphisms; Ω(N_α, Z) ⊗ Z_ℓ → Ω(N_α, Z_ℓ) and lim_t Ω(N_α, Z) ⊗ Q → Ω_DRS(N_α) ∼ Ω_DRS(X(C)) are quasi-isomorphisms; whence a chain of quasi-isomorphisms A(𝐗) → A(𝐗(C)) ← (lim_t Ω(N_α, Z) ⊗ Q) ⊗ Q_ℓ → Ω_DRS(N_α) ⊗ Q_ℓ ∼ Ω_DRS(X_C) ⊗ Q_ℓ. Passing to minimal models turns these quasi-isomorphisms into isomorphisms.
items.note: Inputs: Artin comparison theorem SGA4 XVI (4.1) (no atlas stage found plans the étale–singular comparison in this form), Sullivan's theory of minimal models [6]/[13]. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Filtration of a minimal model by finite-type subalgebras
items.statement: Let A be a DG algebra over a field K of characteristic 0 (for us K = Q or Q_ℓ) with H⁰(A) = K and the Hⁱ(A) finite-dimensional. For minimal models 𝓜 → A see [6]. The inductive construction of 𝓜 easily gives an increasing exhaustive filtration of 𝓜 by sub-algebras of finite type 𝓜_n (n ≥ 0) such that (*) every automorphism of 𝓜 is homotopic to an automorphism of 𝓜 respecting each 𝓜_n.
items.note: No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones). Proof only sketched ('On déduit facilement').

items.name: Generalized-eigenspace grading of 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ by an automorphism
items.statement: If the automorphism σ of 𝓜 respects the filtration by the 𝓜_n, its eigenvalues and the grading of 𝓜 by generalized eigenspaces make sense: after extending scalars to an algebraic closure K̄ of K, 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ is the direct sum of the 𝓜(a) = ∪_m Ker(σ − a)^m (a ∈ K̄*), and these form a grading of 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ of type K̄*.
items.note: Printed with k̄ for K̄ (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E66). Finite-dimensionality of each 𝓜_n is what makes generalized eigenspaces available; Mathlib has Module.End.maxGenEigenspace for finite-dimensional spaces but nothing for this DG setting.

items.name: Eigenvalues on 𝓜 are products of eigenvalues on cohomology
items.statement: Every eigenvalue of σ on 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ is a product of eigenvalues of σ on the Hⁱ(A) ⊗ K̄, indeed on the spherical quotients of the Hⁱ(A) ⊗ K̄. More precisely, an eigenvalue of σ on 𝓜ⁿ ⊗ K̄ is a product ∏ α_i of eigenvalues α_i of σ on H^{n(i)}, with Σ n(i) ≥ n.
items.note: Asserted as following easily from the inductive construction of 𝓜.

items.name: Z-grading from a homomorphism v: Γ → Z and its descent
items.statement: Let Γ be the subgroup of K̄* generated by the eigenvalues of σ. If v: Γ → Z is a homomorphism, the 𝓜(n) = ⊕_{v(a)=n} 𝓜(a) form a grading (of type Z) of 𝓜 ⊗ K̄. If v(α) ≥ 0 for every eigenvalue α of σ on H*(A), this grading is in degrees ≥ 0. If v(α) ≥ i for every eigenvalue α of σ on Hⁱ(A) (for all i), then 𝓜ⁿ ⊗ K̄ is entirely in degrees ≥ n. If Γ is contained in Γ′, stable under Gal(K̄/K), and v extends to a Galois-invariant v′: Γ′ → Z, this grading of 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ is defined over K, i.e. comes from a grading of 𝓜.
items.note: Printed '𝓜 ⊗ K̄*' for 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E66); also 𝓜(n) reuses n.

items.name: Γ′ = q-Weil numbers and v′ = weight
items.statement: The case of interest: K = Q_ℓ and, for a suitable integer q > 1, a power of a prime, one can take for Γ′ the set of algebraic numbers α all of whose complex conjugates have the same absolute value, of the form q^{n(α)/2} (an integer power of q^{1/2}); take v′(α) = n(α). The ℓ-adic weight gradings mentioned in [3] are obtained by this method with σ a Frobenius.
items.note: Weil q-numbers of integer weight: DWP.0 'Define Weil q-numbers of an integer weight on actual algebraic-number carriers and their all-embeddings absolute-value property'. The grading of minimal models itself is not planned.

items.name: Frobenius gradings of 𝓜 ⊗ Q_ℓ split the Hodge weight filtration
items.statement: Let X be a complex algebraic variety, defined over a subfield k₀ of C of finite type over Q (X deduced from X₀/k₀). Gal(k̄₀/k₀) acts on A(X) (5.2). Let 𝓜 be Sullivan's minimal model of the rational homotopy type of X(C). By (5.2.5), 𝓜 ⊗ Q_ℓ is a minimal model of A(X); more precisely there is a natural homotopy class of quasi-isomorphisms φ from 𝓜 ⊗ Q_ℓ to A(X), inducing on cohomology the natural isomorphisms H*(X(C), Q) ⊗ Q_ℓ ≅ H*(X, Q_ℓ). For every automorphism σ of A(X) there is an automorphism σ̃ of 𝓜 ⊗ Q_ℓ, well defined up to homotopy, with φσ̃ homotopic to σφ, and σ̃ can be chosen to respect a filtration as in (5.3.1). If σ is a Frobenius as in [3], the hypotheses of (5.3.2) hold for σ̃ and the corresponding grading of 𝓜 ⊗ Q_ℓ induces on cohomology a grading which splits the Q_ℓ-scalar extension of the Hodge-theoretic weight filtration on H*(X(C), Q) (loc. cit.).
items.note: Uses (5.2.5), Frobenius eigenvalues being q-Weil numbers (mixedness of H*(X, Q_ℓ), cf. (6.1.2)), and the compatibility of the ℓ-adic and Hodge weight filtrations from [3] and Hodge II/III [2]. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Existence and conjugacy of weight gradings of Sullivan's minimal model
items.statement: There exist gradings 𝒲 of 𝓜 compatible with the weight filtration of the Hⁱ(𝓜) = Hⁱ(X(C), Q), in the sense that W_n Hⁱ(X(C), Q) = ⊕_{j≤n} 𝒲_j Hⁱ(𝓜). Two such gradings are conjugate by an automorphism of 𝓜 inducing the identity on Gr^W H*(X(C), Q).
items.note: Printed with ⊕_{j≤m} (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E67, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E68). Proof: gradings respecting (𝓜_n) are homomorphisms 𝐆_m → G₁ = Aut((𝓜, 𝓜_n)) = lim proj Aut((𝓜_k))_{k≤n}; G₂ ⊂ G₁ × 𝐆_m is the subgroup of (g, λ) with g respecting the weight filtration and acting on Gr^W_j Hⁱ by λ^j; the kernel U of (g, λ) ↦ λ is unipotent; after extension to Q_ℓ, α: G₂ → 𝐆_m has a section (5.3.3), so α is surjective over Q, and an extension of 𝐆_m by a unipotent U is trivial with U-conjugate sections (Levi-type input, unreferenced). This gives existence and uniqueness among gradings inducing a grading on each 𝓜_n; the full uniqueness needs Lemma (5.3.5). No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Lemma: a common (5.3.1)-filtration for finitely many automorphisms
items.statement: For every finite set of automorphisms of 𝓜 there exists a filtration (5.3.1) of 𝓜 stable under all these automorphisms.
items.note: Its 'somewhat painful' verification is left to the reader (a gap, PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E68). Needed to conclude (5.3.4).

items.name: Weight gradings of the minimal model of A(X) over any algebraically closed field
items.statement: For X an algebraic variety over an arbitrary algebraically closed field, one can still define a weight filtration on H*(X, Q_ℓ), in terms of generalized eigenspaces of suitable Frobenius automorphisms, and the preceding constructions provide gradings of the minimal model of A(X) inducing on cohomology a grading which splits the weight filtration.
items.note: Sketch only; relies on spreading out to a finite-type base and mixedness (6.1.2). No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Formality: for X proper and smooth, A(X) has the minimal model of (H*(X, Q_ℓ), d = 0)
items.statement: For X proper and smooth, a minimal model of A(X) is a minimal model of H*(X, Q_ℓ) equipped with the DG structure for which d = 0.
items.note: Proof: let W be a weight grading of a minimal model 𝓜 of A(X). Since Hⁱ(X, Q_ℓ) is pure of weight i (Weil I), 𝓜ⁿ is entirely of degrees ≥ n ((5.3.1)); hence dW_n(𝓜ⁿ) ⊂ W_n(𝓜ⁿ⁺¹) = 0; W_n(𝓜ⁿ) consists of cycles and projects onto Hⁿ(X, Q_ℓ) (surjective since Hⁿ is pure of weight n); φ_n: 𝓜ⁿ → Hⁿ(X, Q_ℓ) is this projection composed with the projection of 𝓜ⁿ onto W_n(𝓜ⁿ) killing the W_i(𝓜ⁿ), i > n; φ = (φ_n) is a quasi-isomorphism of DG algebras. ℓ-adic analogue of the DGMS formality theorem [6]. Purity input is planned (DWP.4/DWP.7), but formality itself is not planned anywhere.

items.name: Analogue of Morgan's theorem for unipotent ℓ-adic quotients of π₁ (X normal)
items.statement: For X normal one obtains in the same way a theorem analogous to Morgan's theorem on the system of quotients of π₁(X) which are unipotent ℓ-adic Lie groups, cf. [9].
items.note: Statement not made precise in the paper; reference Morgan [9]. No atlas stage plans the ℓ-adic/rational homotopy type, Sullivan minimal models of algebraic varieties or the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex (grep of all atlas and Tau Ceti roadmaps for Sullivan / minimal model / rational homotopy / de Rham finds only elliptic-curve minimal Weierstrass models and the A∞ minimal models of DGAInfinity Layer 3, which are A∞-transfer minimal models, not Sullivan's commutative ones).

items.name: Proalgebraic group Aut h(𝓜) and the Galois homomorphism (5.3.9.1)
items.statement: For 𝓜 a minimal model and (𝓜_n) a filtration as in (5.3.1), let G be the proalgebraic group of automorphisms of 𝓜 respecting the 𝓜_n and H the subgroup of those homotopic to the identity; Aut h(𝓜) = G/H is a proalgebraic group. If X over k algebraically closed comes by extension of scalars from X₀/k₀ with k₀ countable, the natural action of Gal(k̄₀/k₀) on A(X) gives a group homomorphism (5.3.9.1) Gal(k̄₀/k₀) → Aut h(𝓜)(Q_ℓ). One should verify (question left open) that this homomorphism is continuous, i.e. that for every algebraic quotient (= of finite type) Q of Aut h(𝓜), the induced Gal(k̄₀/k₀) → Q(Q_ℓ) is continuous for the usual topology on Q(Q_ℓ). The author does not believe there is a reasonable action of Gal(k̄₀/k₀) on 𝓜 itself.
items.note: Listed among 'questions passées sous silence'; continuity is an open question, not a result.

items.name: Open question: conjugacy and Q-rationality of weight filtrations
items.statement: One should verify that the increasing filtrations attached to the weight gradings of (5.3.3) or (5.3.6) are all conjugate under the group of automorphisms of 𝓜 (the ℓ-adic minimal model) homotopic to the identity. In the setting (5.3.3), where 𝓜 is the ℓ-adification of Sullivan's rational minimal model 𝓜_Q, their conjugacy class should be defined over Q (equivalently, be the orbit of a filtration obtained by extension of scalars from a filtration of 𝓜_Q).
items.note: Open question; recorded so the assembler does not treat it as a result.

items.name: The two contexts for mixed sheaves
items.statement: a) Equal characteristic p: only schemes of finite type over F_p are considered; 'sheaf' means Weil sheaf. b) 'Equal characteristic 0': one considers schemes of finite type over Z and sheaves (in the sense of: Q̄_ℓ-constructible sheaf), allowing oneself at every moment to replace X by X[1/n]. For schemes this amounts to schemes of finite type over Q, whose category is the 2-inductive limit of the categories of schemes of finite type over the Z[1/n]; this is not known for sheaves (the author does not know whether a constructible sheaf on X_Q always comes from a constructible sheaf on some X[1/n]).
items.note: DWP.8 lists 'Weil II … 6.1.1–6.1.12' among its sources and plans 'stability of the mixed category under six operations with finite-type and coefficient hypotheses'. Weil sheaves are §1 material (DWP.5).

items.name: Hom over X_Q is the colimit of Hom over X[1/n]
items.statement: If X is of finite type over Z and 𝓕, 𝓖 are constructible sheaves on X, then Hom over X_Q(𝓕, 𝓖) = lim ind Hom over X[1/n](𝓕, 𝓖). In other words, the 2-inductive limit of the categories of sheaves on the X[1/n] identifies with a full subcategory of that of sheaves on X_Q.
items.note: Limit argument for constructible sheaves (SGA4 IX/VII type), covered by DWP.8's 'finite-type and coefficient hypotheses' for the Q-variant (DWP.8 sources 6.1.1–6.1.12).

items.name: Mixed/pure sheaves in context b)
items.statement: For X_Q a scheme of finite type over Q deduced by base change from X of finite type over Z, and 𝓕_Q a sheaf on X_Q, one says 𝓕 is mixed, pure, … if 𝓕_Q is deduced from a sheaf 𝓕 on some X[1/n] and the restriction of 𝓕 to X[1/nm] is mixed, pure, … for suitable m. Results in context b) are presented as variants of those in context a); potential variants ((3.4.10)) could also be given but are not made explicit.
items.note: DWP.8 sources include Weil II 6.1.1–6.1.12.

items.name: R^i f_* preserves mixedness
items.statement: Let f: X → Y be a morphism of schemes of finite type over F_p (resp. Q), and 𝓕 a mixed sheaf on X. Then the sheaves R^i f_* 𝓕 are mixed.
items.note: DWP.8: 'Prove stability of the mixed category under six operations with finite-type and coefficient hypotheses … Derive these estimates from DWP.7 and the actual comparison morphisms'. Deduced from Lemma (6.1.3) by generic base change SGA4½ [Th. finitude] (1.9). Also used in §5 ((5.3.3), (5.3.6)) for mixedness of H*(X, Q_ℓ).

items.name: Lemma: generic mixedness of R^i f_* over a base S
items.statement: Let S be a scheme of finite type over Z[1/ℓ], f: X → Y a morphism of S-schemes of finite type, and 𝓕 a mixed sheaf on X. Then there is a dense open U of S over which the sheaves R^i f_* 𝓕 are mixed.
items.note: Proof follows SGA4½ [Th. finitude] (2.1)–(2.8) (Deligne's generic constructibility argument), in steps (6.1.4)–(6.1.9). DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12.

items.name: Case X smooth over Y = S, 𝓕 lisse, R^i f_! 𝓕 lisse
items.statement: If X is smooth over Y = S, 𝓕 is lisse and the R^i f_! 𝓕 are lisse, then the R^i f_* 𝓕 are deduced by Poincaré duality from the R^i f_! 𝓕, to which (3.3.1) applies; hence they are mixed.
items.note: Uses Poincaré duality (EDC.2) and the fundamental theorem (3.3.1) (DWP.7). DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12.

items.name: Case X smooth over Y = S, 𝓕 lisse
items.statement: If X is smooth over Y = S and 𝓕 is lisse, one reduces to (6.1.4) by replacing S by a suitable dense open (generic lissity of R^i f_! 𝓕).
items.note: DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12. Generic lissity is an input from SGA4½ [Th. finitude].

items.name: Induction statement (∗)_n for open embeddings
items.statement: (∗)_n: the conclusion of (6.1.3) holds if S is integral with generic point η, f is an open embedding with dense image, and dim X_η ≤ n. For n = 0, after shrinking S, X = Y and (∗)₀ is evident. In (∗)_{n−1} one may replace 'open embedding' by 'embedding' (factor into an open and a closed embedding).
items.note: DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12.

items.name: Lemma: (6.1.3) holds on Y′ ⊂ Y with complement finite over S
items.statement: Assuming (∗)_{n−1}: after shrinking S, the conclusion of (6.1.3) holds over some open Y′ ⊂ Y whose complement Y₁ is finite over S.
items.note: Proof: local on Y, assume Y ⊂ A^n_S; apply (∗)_{n−1} to X → Y → A¹_S via each coordinate pr_i, get dense opens U_i ⊂ A¹_S over which the conclusion holds on pr_i^{-1}(U_i); it holds over their union. DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12.

items.name: (∗)_n for X smooth over S and 𝓕 lisse
items.statement: (∗)_n holds when X is smooth over S and 𝓕 is lisse. Proof: local on Y, assume Y affine, then projective (replace Y by its closure in a projective space); take i: Y₁ ↪ Y and j: Y′ ↪ Y from (6.1.7), b: Y → S. Applying Rb_* to the triangle of 0 → j_! j^* Rf_* 𝓕 → Rf_* 𝓕 → i_! i^* Rf_* 𝓕 → 0 gives a triangle Rb_* j_! j^* Rf_* 𝓕 → Ra_* 𝓕 → b_{1*} i^* Rf_* 𝓕 →, whose first two terms have mixed cohomology sheaves on a dense open of S, by (3.3.1) (b proper) and (6.1.5); so the third is mixed, whence i^* Rf_* 𝓕 and then Rf_* 𝓕 are mixed. The derived-category argument is justified by writing 𝓕 as a projective limit of locally constant free R/mⁿ-sheaves (as in (1.1.1)) and repeating the argument on the projective system of triangles.
items.note: Here a = b∘f and b₁ = b∘i, not named in the diagram (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E69). DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12; DWP.8 asks to derive estimates 'not assumed exactness of a six-functor package', matching the paper's finite-level justification.

items.name: (∗)_n in general
items.statement: (∗)_n holds in general. Reduce to X having a dense open V smooth over S (for S the spectrum of a perfect field replace X, Y by X_red, Y_red; in general shrink S, make a finite radicial surjective base change S′ → S and pass to reduced schemes, harmless since the étale topology is insensitive to finite radicial surjective morphisms); shrinking V, assume 𝓕 lisse on V, j: V ↪ X. Apply (6.1.8) to j and fj. Define Δ by the triangle → 𝓕 → Rj_* j^* 𝓕 → Δ →. The cohomology sheaves of Δ are supported in X − V, with dim(X − V)_η < n, so by induction Rf_* Δ is mixed; in the triangle → Rf_* 𝓕 → R(fj)_* j^* 𝓕 → Rf_* Δ → two vertices are mixed, hence so is the third.
items.note: DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12.

items.name: Proof of (6.1.2) from (∗)_n and (3.3.1)
items.statement: The problem is local on Y (assume Y affine); using an affine covering of X and its Leray spectral sequence one reduces to X affine; then factor f = gj as an open embedding followed by a proper morphism, so Rf_* = Rg_* Rj_*: the open embedding is handled by (∗)_n, the proper morphism by (3.3.1).
items.note: DWP.8 sources include 6.1.1–6.1.12. Nagata compactification is an implicit input.

items.name: The four operations and local Ext preserve mixedness
items.statement: The four operations R^i f_*, R^i f_!, f^* and R^i f^! transform mixed sheaves into mixed sheaves. The same stability holds for the local Ext functors.
items.note: Formal consequence of (6.1.2) (cf. SGA4½ [Th. finitude] (1.5)). DWP.8: 'Prove stability of the mixed category under six operations'.

items.name: Vanishing-cycle setting and mixedness of sheaves with Gal(η̄/η)-action
items.statement: Let S be a smooth curve over F_q (resp. Q), s a closed point, X an S-scheme of finite type and 𝓕 a sheaf on X; base change to S_(s) gives (X′, 𝓕′) over the henselian trait S_(s), with generic point η, geometric point s̄ over s and geometric generic point η̄ of the strict localization S_(s̄). The vanishing-cycle sheaves R^iΨ(𝓕′) are sheaves on X_s̄ with a continuous action of Gal(η̄, η) over its action on X_s̄ (via Gal(s̄/s)); the restriction to inertia is automatically quasi-unipotent. For a sheaf 𝓖 with such an action ρ of Gal(η̄/η): a) a sheaf on X_s̄ with continuous Gal(s̄/s)-action is a sheaf on X_s (SGA7 XIII (1.1.3)); if ρ factors through Gal(s̄/s), (𝓖, ρ) is mixed if the corresponding sheaf on X_s is; b) if (𝓖, ρ) has a finite filtration F with Gr_F(ρ) factoring through Gal(s̄/s) (unipotent case), (𝓖, ρ) is mixed if Gr_F(𝓖) is, in the sense of a); c) hypothesis b) becomes true after replacing Gal(η̄/η) by a subgroup of finite index (quasi-unipotence), i.e. replacing S_(s) by a trait finite over S_(s); (𝓖, ρ) is mixed if it becomes so, in the sense of b), after such a change of trait.
items.note: DWP.8 lists Weil II 6.1.1–6.1.12 as sources. Nearby-cycle functors themselves come from LPV.0–2 (imported by R34.3).

items.name: Nearby-cycle sheaves of a mixed sheaf are mixed
items.statement: With the notation of (6.1.12), if 𝓕 is mixed, the vanishing-cycle sheaves R^iΨ(𝓕′) are also mixed.
items.note: Proof: by the monodromy theorem, after a finite cover of S_(s), inertia I acts unipotently via Z_ℓ(1); by (1.6.1), (1.6.14) it suffices that the (R^iΨ𝓕′)^I are mixed; with u: X_s ↪ X and v the complementary open, as in (3.6.1) these are quotients of u^* R^i v_*(v^*𝓕), and (6.1.11) applies. DWP.8's source list stops at 6.1.12; LPV.0–2/R34.3 plan the nearby-cycle functors but no stage plans their mixedness, so this is missing.

items.name: Dualizing complex K_X and duality functor D
items.statement: (Context (6.1.1 a).) For every scheme X of finite type over F_p, a: X → Spec(F_p), put K_X = Ra^! Q̄_ℓ, the dualizing complex. D denotes the contravariant functor 'dual with values in the dualizing complex': D: D^b_c(X) → D^b_c(X), K ↦ RHom(K, K_X).
items.note: EDC.1:adjoint: 'For a:X→Spec(k), define K_X=a^!Λ and D_X(K)=RHom(K,K_X)'.

items.name: Dualizing complex of a smooth scheme
items.statement: If X is smooth of pure dimension n, K_X reduces to the sheaf Q̄_ℓ(n) placed in degree −2n: K_X = Q̄_ℓ(n)[2n].
items.note: EDC.2:trace-purity: 'Construct Tr_f:Rf!Λ(d)[2d]→Λ for smooth pure relative dimension d and prove that its adjoint f*Λ(d)[2d]→f^!Λ is an isomorphism'.

items.name: D is involutive and exchanges the operations
items.statement: The functor D is involutive. For every morphism f: X → Y it exchanges the functors Rf^! and f^*, and the functors Rf_! and Rf_*. One also has D(K ⊗ L) = RHom(K, DL).
items.note: EDC.1:biduality: 'Prove the bounded constructible restrictions and biduality … Prove localization and the exchange isomorphisms relating D to f*, Rf*, Rf! and f^!, including D_Y Rf!≅Rf* D_X'.

items.name: Complexes mixed of weight ≤ n
items.statement: A complex K is mixed of weight ≤ n if for every i the sheaf ℋⁱK is mixed of punctual weights ≤ i + n.
items.note: DWP.8: 'define K of weights≤w by H^i(K) having stalk weights≤w+i'.

items.name: Rf_! preserves 'mixed of weight ≤ n'
items.statement: Let f: X → Y be a morphism of schemes of finite type over F_p. If K ∈ Ob D^b_c(X) is mixed of weight ≤ n, then Rf_! K is mixed of weight ≤ n.
items.note: Proof: spectral sequence R^p f_! ℋ^q K ⇒ ℋ^{p+q} Rf_! K (printed as an E₁ term, (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E70)); by (3.3.1) the initial term is mixed of punctual weights ≤ p + (q + n), so the abutment is mixed of weights ≤ (p + q) + n. DWP.8: 'f* and Rf_! preserve upper weights'.

items.name: Pure complexes and pure sheaves
items.statement: A complex K is pure of weight n if it is mixed of weight ≤ n and DK is mixed of weight ≤ −n. A sheaf 𝓕 is pure of weight n if the complex reduced to 𝓕 in degree 0 is.
items.note: DWP.8: 'define weights≥w by DK of weights≤−w, using EDC.1's actual dualizing complex. Purity means both bounds.'

items.name: Twist-shift invariance of weight bounds
items.statement: Whatever N, a complex K is mixed of weight ≤ n if and only if K(N)[2N] is. In the definition (6.2.4) of purity one may therefore replace the dualizing complex K_X by a complex locally of the form K_X(N)[2N], and DK by DK(N)[2N].
items.note: DWP.8: 'Prove that F[m] tensor ℚ_ℓ(r), for pure lisse F of weight w, has complex weight w+m−2r'; DWP.8 sources include 6.2.1–6.2.6.

items.name: Purity on a smooth scheme; complexes with lisse cohomology
items.statement: For X smooth, the condition on DK in (6.2.4) may be replaced by: 'RHom(K, Q̄_ℓ) is mixed of weight ≤ −n'. If the cohomology sheaves of K ∈ Ob D^b_c(X) are lisse, K is pure of weight n if and only if each ℋⁱK is punctually pure of weight i + n.
items.note: DWP.8 (sources 6.2.1–6.2.6); it warns 'A stalkwise pure sheaf on a singular base need not be pure in this duality sense', consistent with the smoothness hypothesis here.

items.name: j_* of a pure sheaf on an open of a smooth curve is pure
items.statement: Let X be a smooth curve and j: U ↪ X a dense open. If 𝓕 is a pure sheaf of weight n on U, then j_*𝓕 is pure of weight n (apply (1.8.8.1) and the formula RHom(j_*𝓕, Q_ℓ) = j_* Hom(𝓕, Q_ℓ)).
items.note: Local weights of j_*𝓕 at boundary points come from DWP.5 ('the weights of boundary invariants of j_*F'); DWP.8 sources include 6.2.1–6.2.6.

items.name: j_* across a smooth divisor of a tame pure lisse sheaf is pure
items.statement: For X smooth, j: U ↪ X the complement of a smooth divisor D, and 𝓕 a lisse sheaf on U, punctually pure of weight n and tamely ramified along D, the sheaf j_*𝓕 is again pure of weight n (same argument).
items.note: DWP.8 sources include 6.2.1–6.2.6. 'Same argument' needs the local weights along D and the duality formula RHom(j_*𝓕, Q_ℓ) = j_*Hom(𝓕, Q_ℓ) in the tame smooth-divisor case, which is only asserted.

items.name: Proper direct image preserves purity
items.statement: If f: X → Y is proper and K ∈ Ob D^b_c(X) is pure, then Rf_* K is pure of the same weight.
items.note: Proof: apply (6.2.3) to K and to DK, using DRf_*K = Rf_*DK since f is proper. DWP.8: 'Proper direct image preserves purity by duality.'

items.name: Variant: purity over Z[1/ℓ]
items.statement: For every scheme X of finite type over Z[1/ℓ], a: X → Spec(Z[1/ℓ]), put K′_X = Ra^! Q̄_ℓ. There is again a duality functor D′K = RHom(K, K′_X) and a definition of purity parallel to (6.2.4). If X is of finite type over F_p, K′_X = K_X(−1)[−2]: the functors D and D′ are deduced from one another by shift and twist and, by (6.2.5 a), the above definition of 'pure of weight n' generalizes (6.2.4). Proposition (6.2.6) remains true.
items.note: No stage plans K′_X over Spec Z[1/ℓ] or purity relative to it: DWP.8's sources stop at 6.2.6 and EDC.1 works over a field; LPV.7:invariant-cycles only 'retain[s] the specified arithmetic model over an integral finite-type Z[1/ℓ]-base' for 6.2.8. K′_X = K_X(−1)[−2] needs absolute purity for Spec F_p ↪ Spec Z[1/ℓ] (regular codimension one). Used in (6.2.8 d).

items.name: Potentially pure complexes on a proper family over a henselian trait
items.statement: Let k be algebraically closed, S the spectrum of the henselization of k[T] at (T), s the closed point, η the generic point and η̄ a geometric generic point; let f: X → S be proper. A complex K ∈ Ob D^b_c(X) is called potentially pure if (X/S, K) comes from an arithmetic situation of the following type: a) Spec(k) is a geometric generic point of an integral scheme A₀ of finite type over Z[1/ℓ]; b) S comes by extension of scalars to k and henselization from a smooth curve S₀ over A₀ equipped with a section; c) f comes from a proper morphism f₀: X₀ → S₀; d) K comes from a pure complex K₀ ∈ Ob D^b_c(X₀).
items.note: LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'prove the potentially pure-complex extension 6.2.8–6.2.9, retaining the specified arithmetic model over an integral finite-type Z[1/ℓ]-base rather than treating “potentially pure” as an empty label'. Purity in d) is in the sense of (6.2.7).

items.name: Local invariant cycle theorem for pure complexes
items.statement: With the notation of (6.2.8), let K be a potentially pure complex on X. Then the specialization morphism sp*: H*(X_s, K) → H*(X_η̄, K)^{Gal(η̄/η)} is surjective.
items.note: Generalizes (3.6.1). Proof parallel to (3.6.1): the cross (3.6.1)(8) with row 0 → H^{i−1}(X_η̄, K)_I(−1) → Hⁱ(X_η, K) → Hⁱ(X_η̄, K)^I → 0 and column Hⁱ(X_s, K) → Hⁱ(X_η, K) → H^{i+1}_{X_s}(X, K), where H^{i+1}_{X_s}(X, K) = [H^{−i−1}(X_s, DK)]^∨ (D exchanges Ri^! and i^*, commutes with RΓ(X_s, −)); the analogues of (3.6.2), (3.6.3) use (6.2.6), (6.2.3) instead of (3.3.9), (3.3.4). LPV.7:invariant-cycles plans 6.2.8–6.2.9 (quoted under s6-6.2.8).

items.name: Geometric setting: dualizing complex over k and the universal hyperplane section
items.statement: For the rest of the section arguments are geometric except for one reference to (6.2.9) and one to (3.4). Let k be algebraically closed; for X of finite type over k, a: X → Spec(k), define K_X = Ra^!Q̄_ℓ and D(K) = RHom(K, K_X) as in (6.2.1); the same formalism holds. Let X ⊂ 𝐏 be a projective variety; hyperplane sections are parametrized by the dual projective space 𝐏̌, and each line D of 𝐏̌ parametrizes a pencil. Diagram (6.2.10.1): X ←q Z ←i X̃, f: Z → 𝐏̌, f: X̃ → D, i: D ↪ 𝐏̌, where Z is the universal hyperplane section and X̃ its restriction to D.
items.note: DWP.9 lists 'Weil II … 6.2.8–6.2.13' as sources; LPV.3–4 construct pencils/blowups. Printed with 𝐏 instead of 𝐏̌ in the diagram (PAPER-DELIGNE-80/E71).

items.name: Generic lissity and monodromy of a general pencil
items.statement: For K in D^b_c(X), the R^i f_* q^* K are lisse on a dense open U of 𝐏̌; a hyperplane section Y_u with u ∈ U is called general. π₁(U, u) acts on H*(Y_u, K). If D is general enough and u ∈ V = U ∩ D, the image of π₁(V, u) in GL H*(Y_u, K) coincides with that of π₁(U, u). In particular (6.2.10.2) H*(Y_u, K)^{π₁(U,u)} = H*(Y_u, K)^{π₁(V,u)} (D general enough).
items.note: Generic lissity is SGA4½ [Th. finitude]; the Lefschetz-type surjectivity π₁(V) → π₁(U) for a general line is asserted without reference. DWP.9 sources include 6.2.8–6.2.13.

items.name: Weak Lefschetz for complexes with support bounds
items.statement: With the preceding notation, let n be an integer (in good cases, the dimension of Y_u), and suppose that for each i the support of ℋⁱ(DK[−2n−2]) has dimension ≤ n + 1 − i. Then (i) for every hyperplane section Y: Hⁱ(X, K) ⥲ Hⁱ(Y, K) for i < n, and Hⁿ(X, K) ↪ Hⁿ(Y, K).
items.note: Proof parallel to (4.1.6): weak Lefschetz Hⁱ_c(X − Y, K) = 0 for i ≤ n, reduced by duality to vanishing of H^{−i}(X − Y, DK) for −i ≥ −n, then the long exact sequence. That vanishing follows from the support hypothesis on the affine X − Y by Artin's affine vanishing theorem, which the text does not cite. LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'Prove the support-bound weak-Lefschetz refinement 6.2.11'.

items.name: Image of Hⁿ(X, K) in a general pencil
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (6.2.11), (ii) for D a general pencil and u ∈ D, the image of Hⁿ(X, K) in Hⁿ(Y_u, K) coincides with the image of H⁰(D, Rⁿf_*(i^*q^*K)).
items.note: Proof: for a general enough Y the restriction of K to Y satisfies the hypothesis with n replaced by n − 1 (generic acyclicity SGA4½ [Th. finitude] for Z/𝐏̌ and q^*K; D(K|Y) = ((DK)|Y)(−1)[−2]), which allows applying (4.3.7) as in (4.3.8) and concluding as in (4.3.9). LPV.7:invariant-cycles plans 6.2.11.

items.name: Global invariant cycle theorem for pure complexes
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of (6.2.11), if K is potentially pure then, for Y_u a general hyperplane section of X, Hⁿ(X, K) identifies with the subgroup Hⁿ(Y_u, K)^{π₁(U,u)} of monodromy invariants in Hⁿ(Y_u, K).
items.note: Proof: for a general enough pencil D, i^*q^*K on X̃ is potentially pure (D i^*q^*K = i^*q^*DK: the twists from q and i cancel); apply (6.2.9) at each point of D − V to get H⁰(D, Rⁿf_*(i^*q^*K)) ↠ Hⁿ(Y_u, K)^{π₁(V,u)}; by (6.2.11) Hⁿ(X, K) maps onto Hⁿ(Y_u, K)^{π₁(V,u)} ⊃ Hⁿ(Y_u, K)^{π₁(U,u)}; combine with (6.2.10.2) and injectivity (6.2.11 i). LPV.7:invariant-cycles: 'global invariant-cycle result 6.2.12'.

items.name: Hard Lefschetz for potentially pure complexes
items.statement: Let X ⊂ 𝐏 be a projective scheme, η the first Chern class of 𝒪(1) and K ∈ Ob D^b_c(X) a potentially pure complex. Identify Z_ℓ with Z_ℓ(1) over k, so as to regard η as lying in H²(X, Z_ℓ). Let n be an integer and suppose K and DK[−2n] satisfy: for all i, the dimension of the support of the sheaf ℋⁱ is ≤ n − i (with dim ∅ = −∞). Then for all i ≥ 0 the iterated cup product ηⁱ: H^{n−i}(X, K) → H^{n+i}(X, K) is an isomorphism.
items.note: DWP.9: 'construct the absolute theorem for a projective X and a potentially pure bounded complex K satisfying both explicit support-dimension inequalities … for every j require dim Supp H^j(K)≤n−j and dim Supp H^j(DK[−2n])≤n−j'. Proof parallel to (4.1.1), induction on dim X: in dim 0 the hypotheses force ℋⁱK = 0 for i ≠ n; a general hyperplane section Y satisfies the hypotheses with n − 1, reducing to η: H^{n−1}(X, K) → H^{n−1}(Y, K) → H^{n+1}(X, K), whose second arrow is the transpose of restriction H^{n−1}(X, DK[−2n]) → H^{n−1}(Y, DK[−2n]); one checks the perfect duality between H^{n−1}(Y, K) and H^{n−1}(Y, DK[−2n]) (with DK[−2n] = (D(K|Y))[−2(n−1)]) induces a perfect duality on the fixed parts ((6.2.12)), by (4.1.4), since π₁(U, u) acts semisimply on H*(Y_u, K) ((6.2.6) and (3.4.1)(iii)).

items.name: Added in proof: Gabber's purity of the intersection complex
items.statement: Let X be an irreducible normal complex algebraic variety. The intersection cohomology of MacPherson and Goresky of X can be defined as the hypercohomology of X with coefficients in a certain complex of sheaves I_X. The construction of I_X has an analogue in étale cohomology, over an arbitrary base field. O. Gabber has just proved the purity of I_X; his theorem allows the results of this section to be applied to MacPherson–Goresky cohomology.
items.note: EDC.7: 'For pure lisse L of weight w on a smooth d-dimensional dense open, prove IC_X(L) is pure of weight w+d in the perverse normalization'. Gabber's theorem is cited without reference (published later in BBD).

prerequisites.citation: P. Deligne, P. Griffiths, J. Morgan, D. Sullivan, Real homotopy theory of Kähler manifolds, Invent. Math. 29 (1975), 245–274
prerequisites.why: Minimal models and formality; the notion used in (5.2.5), (5.3.1) and the model for the formality theorem (5.3.7).

prerequisites.citation: D. Sullivan, Infinitesimal computations in topology, Publ. Math. IHÉS 47 (1977), 269–331
prerequisites.why: Rational homotopy theory, the de Rham–Sullivan complex and minimal models used throughout §5.

prerequisites.citation: E. Miller, De Rham cohomology with arbitrary coefficients, Topology 17 (1978), 193–203
prerequisites.why: The divided-power Z{t}-de Rham complex of §5.1 and the proofs of its properties (5.1.4)–(5.1.9).

prerequisites.citation: J. Morgan, The algebraic topology of smooth algebraic varieties, Publ. Math. IHÉS 48 (1978), 137–204 (corrections: Publ. Math. IHÉS 64 (1986))
prerequisites.why: The theorem on unipotent quotients of π₁ whose ℓ-adic analogue is (5.3.8).

prerequisites.citation: P. Deligne, Théorie de Hodge II and III, Publ. Math. IHÉS 40 (1971), 5–57 and 44 (1974), 5–77
prerequisites.why: Mixed Hodge structures and the weight filtration on H*(X(C), Q), which the Frobenius gradings of (5.3.3)–(5.3.4) split, and the Hodge analogues cited in §§1.8–1.9.

prerequisites.citation: J. Steenbrink, Limits of Hodge structures, Invent. Math. 31 (1976), 229–257
prerequisites.why: Limit mixed Hodge structures, the complex analogue behind the local invariant cycle theorem (3.6.4).

prerequisites.citation: N. Katz, W. Messing, Some consequences of the Riemann hypothesis for varieties over finite fields, Invent. Math. 23 (1974), 73–77
prerequisites.why: Bibliography [7]: consequences of the Weil I purity theorem (independence of ℓ and crystalline comparisons for smooth projective varieties), cited in Weil II alongside the p-adic statements.

prerequisites.citation: P. Deligne et al., Cohomologie étale (SGA 4½), Lecture Notes in Math. 569 (1977)
prerequisites.why: [Th. finitude]: finiteness, generic base change and generic constructibility used throughout §§1–6.

routes.reason: DWP.5–DWP.8 were written for this paper. DWP.5 covers the local weights and the analytic preparation, 'especially 1.8.4' and 'the Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin positivity argument'. DWP.6 covers pure local systems on curves, DWP.7 the fundamental direct-image theorem and DWP.8 mixed complexes and semisimplicity. The paper is their principal source, and the missing items are the steps those stages rely on but do not name. From §1: Weil sheaves and the Weil group (1.1), totally real sheaves, the conjectures (1.2.9)–(1.2.10), determinantal weights with Grothendieck's theorem that the radical of the monodromy group is unipotent (1.3), the corollaries (1.8.5)–(1.8.12), non-archimedean bounds and Newton polygons (1.10), and specialization of monodromy with the proof of (1.3.1) (1.11). From §2: the abstract Hadamard–de la Vallée-Poussin method, compact forms and equidistribution. From §3: the Kummer description of the vanishing cycle, p-adic couples, and the equidistribution theorem (3.5.3) with the function-field Sato–Tate theorem (3.5.7), which DWP.10's arithmetic interfaces should export. From §6: mixedness of nearby cycles (6.1.13) and the Z[1/ℓ] variant (6.2.7).

LPV.1 owns inertia, variation and the monodromy operator. The linear algebra of the monodromy filtration it needs is in (1.6)–(1.7) and (1.9) and is not stated there: primitive parts, the Lefschetz decomposition, Jacobson–Morozov, the relative monodromy filtration, the tame restriction along a normal-crossings divisor and several-variable weight filtrations. §4's pencil theory extends LPV.2–LPV.5: the p = 2, n even local formula, transverse pencils, the integral failure of Lefschetz's fundamental lemma (4.3.10), and the monodromy theorem (4.4.1), open or finite, including the orthogonal case with finite monodromy a Weyl group of type A, D or E (4.4.9). LPV.5 plans only the odd, symplectic case. Also the gcd theorem (4.5.1). The complex local invariant cycle theorem (3.6.4) is the comparison for LPV.7:invariant-cycles.

(3.7) revisits the exponential sums of Weil I (8.4) in a family. It uses the universal family of polynomials with smooth leading form and proves the lissity of the R^i f_! of the Artin–Schreier sheaf (3.7.3). This is the family form of FF.2's trace-function bounds.
(4.1.6) refines the weak Lefschetz theorem EDC.4 plans to Z_ℓ coefficients: H_c^{n+1}(X − Y, Z_ℓ) and Hⁿ(Y, Z_ℓ)/Hⁿ(X, Z_ℓ) are torsion-free for a smooth hyperplane section Y.

The conventions of §0 (geometric points, henselisation and strict henselisation, traits, closed points, finite filtrations, limits in ind- and pro-categories) and the filtered derived category and truncation of (1.1.2) are the site-theoretic background SF.2 owns ('construct sheaf cohomology, localization, proper/smooth base change and compact support'). They are listed so that nothing in the paper is unowned.

Nothing in the atlas plans the ℓ-adic homotopy type of a variety, Sullivan-style models built from étale hypercovers, or weights on them. The Tau Ceti DGAInfinity roadmap supplies DG algebras, A∞ minimal models, Massey products and formality, but not Sullivan's graded-commutative minimal models, their construction from varieties, or the weight theory. A Tau Ceti roadmap is never re-planned, and this is a different direction: arithmetic geometry of homotopy types rather than algebra of A∞ structures. So §5 becomes a new roadmap that imports DGAInfinity's DG-algebra theory.
routes.title: ℓ-adic homotopy types of varieties and their weights
routes.brief: Design a roadmap for the ℓ-adic homotopy type of an algebraic variety and its weights, following Deligne, Weil II §5. (1) Construct the Grothendieck–Miller divided-power de Rham complex: the ring Z{t} of divided-power polynomials, the simplicial graded-commutative DG algebra Ω of polynomial divided-power forms on the standard simplices (5.1.1–5.1.6), Ω(X, A) = Hom(X, Ω ⊗ A) for a simplicial set X (5.1.8), the computation of its cohomology (5.1.4.2), and the comparison with Sullivan's rational de Rham complex Ω_DRS (5.1.5, 5.1.9). (2) For a filtering projective system of simplicial sets 𝐗 satisfying the finiteness condition (F), define Ω(𝐗, Z_ℓ) and the Q_ℓ-DG algebra A(𝐗), and prove H*A(𝐗) = H*(𝐗, Q_ℓ) (5.2.1). For a variety X over an algebraically closed field k, define A(X) through countable étale hypercovers and prove H*A(X) ≅ H*(X, Q_ℓ) (5.2.2), with its Galois action when X is defined over a subfield (5.2.3). For k = C, prove that the minimal models of A(X) are the Q_ℓ-scalar extensions of Sullivan's minimal model of X(C) (5.2.4–5.2.5). (3) Weights: for X defined over a finite field, state and prove Theorem 5.3.4 exactly as printed, with the index corrected as in the paper's sourceIssues: the minimal model of A(X) admits weight gradings, and any two are conjugate. Include the generalized-eigenspace grading of 𝓜 ⊗ K̄ (5.3.1), Lemma 5.3.5 on a common filtration (left to the reader in the paper; prove it), the splitting of the Hodge weight filtration (5.3.3), the arbitrary-base-field version (5.3.6), formality of A(X) for X proper and smooth (5.3.7, the ℓ-adic analogue of Deligne–Griffiths–Morgan–Sullivan), and the analogue of Morgan's theorem for normal X (5.3.8). Record (5.3.9)–(5.3.10) as open questions, not targets. Import, never re-plan: DG algebras, homological transfer (A∞ minimal models), Massey products and formality from the Tau Ceti roadmap on DG and A∞ algebras (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/DGAInfinity, layers 1, 3 and 8). Sullivan's graded-commutative minimal models (existence, uniqueness up to non-unique isomorphism, homotopies) are not planned there and belong to this roadmap; étale cohomology with Z_ℓ and Q_ℓ coefficients and hypercovers from SchemeAndStackFoundations (SF.2); Frobenius weights, Weil numbers and the weight bounds of Weil II Theorem 1 from DeligneWeightsAndPurity (DWP.0, DWP.7); purity for proper smooth X from DWP.4/WeilConjectures; abstract mixed Hodge structures from tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/HodgeStructures (milestone L2, which covers only the linear algebra of Théorie de Hodge II §§1–2); the mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of complex varieties, which (5.3.3) uses, has no atlas owner, so the design must plan it or take it as a prerequisite; divided-power algebras from Mathlib (DividedPowerAlgebra). Acceptance tests: the circle and a torus (formal, weights 1 and 2 on H¹ and H²); P¹ minus three points over F_q, where A(X) has weight-2 generators in degree 1; and a proper smooth curve of genus ≥ 1, which is formal.

More simply: H²_c(X, 𝐐_ℓ) = 𝐐_ℓ(−1) gives the factor (1 − qt)^{−1}, and H¹_c cannot cancel it because its weights are ≤ 1.

So 'borné' does not follow as stated, and a lower bound for the point count is needed to reach a contradiction. sourceIssues.printed: The source deduces from (3.4.1) that every smooth mixed sheaf has a pointwise weight filtration by smooth subsheaves, and that every pure sheaf is geometrically semisimple.

sourceIssues.reason: The source (3.4.1)(iii) (p. 208) explicitly assumes ℱ₀ lisse and X₀ normal, and normality cannot be dropped. Counterexample: let X₀ be a nodal cubic with split node over 𝐅_q. The normalisation P¹ is simply connected, so π₁(X) has a quotient Ẑ (the loop through the node) on which Frobenius acts trivially. Choose a rank-2 representation of W(X₀) = π₁(X) ⋊ 𝐙 in which π₁(X) acts through Ẑ → 𝐙_ℓ by non-trivial unipotent matrices and Frobenius acts trivially. It is lisse and pure of weight 0 (all Frobenius eigenvalues are 1), but not geometrically semisimple. Similarly, if 'faisceau' is read in the category of all constructible sheaves, 𝐐_ℓ on P¹ has the non-split subsheaf j_!𝐐_ℓ. So the second clause needs the lisse and normal hypotheses of (3.4.1)(iii). sourceIssues.locator: §4, proof of Théorème (4.4.9), p. 230 last display and p. 231 first line (published text, Numdam scan)
sourceIssues.printed: The source gives Tr(s_δ s_δ') = (dim Ev(Y) − 2) + (δ, δ')² and concludes that the integer Tr(s_δ s_δ') − dim Ev(Y) + 2 admits a square root in 𝐐_ℓ for every ℓ ≠ p.
sourceIssues.correction: Tr(s_δ s_δ') = (dim Ev(Y) − 4) + (δ, δ')², and the integer is Tr(s_δ s_δ') − dim Ev(Y) + 4.
sourceIssues.reason: Let ε = ±1 with (δ,δ) = (δ',δ') = 2ε (by (4.4.8)), so s_δ(x) = x − ε(x,δ)δ. Put a = (δ,δ'). In general Tr(s_δ s_δ') = dim − 2 − 2 + (2/(δ,δ))(2/(δ',δ'))a² = dim − 4 + a². Directly, on span(δ,δ'): s_δs_δ'(δ) = (a²−1)δ − εaδ' and s_δs_δ'(δ') = −δ' + εaδ, giving plane trace a² − 2, and the identity on the orthogonal complement adds dim − 2. Checks: δ' = δ gives s_δ² = 1 with trace dim (the printed formula gives dim + 2), and δ ⊥ δ' gives dim − 4. The conclusion (δ,δ')² ∈ 𝐙 is a square, hence (δ,δ') ∈ 𝐙, is unaffected.
